verses.1:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse calls all people, rather than believers alone, to fear their Lord because they share one human reality. Men and women, strong and weak, young and old are alike in their humanity; therefore neither men may oppress women nor the strong wrong the weak. The divinely inspired laws and social order are intended to secure an easy, protected, and enduring human life, both individually and collectively. “Lord” is especially fitting because creation, governance, and perfection encompass all humanity, whereas the verse is not restricted to those who worship God.

“Being” translates al-Nafs, the thing itself or that by which man is man: in worldly life, the union of soul and body, and in al-Barzakh, the soul alone. In context, the “single being” is Adam and its mate is his wife. All human beings consequently return to these two parents. Al-Mizan rejects the interpretation that the two expressions merely mean the male and female parents of every person. The verse in 49:13 establishes equality because all people are born of a human male and female, and denies superiority except through piety; this verse instead establishes a more specific unity, namely that the multitude of men and women are branches of one original root. Interpreting the pair generally would lose the force of “and spread from these two, many men and women,” and would not suit the chapter’s purpose.

The mate was created “of the same (kind),” meaning of the same human species as the original being, and min indicates origin. Thus all people descend from two similar human beings. The words do not establish that Adam’s wife was made from a part of him, notwithstanding traditions said to place her creation in one of Adam’s ribs. The verse itself does not support that view.

The phrase “and spread from these two” apparently confines the origin of the present human race to Adam and his wife, with no other male or female participating. “Many men and women” includes all their descendants, immediate and remote. On this reading, their first children married one another, since they alone constituted the available males and females. Al-Mizan holds that this involved no objection at that time: marriage rules are legislative rulings, subject to God’s judgment, and He may permit something when necessary and later prohibit it. Such a ruling is not an unchangeable creative decree.

To demand something of another “by Allah” is to adjure him by God, and reveals the reverence and love with which people regard Him. The more apparent construction joins “and relationship” to “Allah”: fear God and be mindful of kinship. A reading attributed to Ḥamzah, wa al-arḥāmi, has been used to make relationship another thing by which people adjure one another, but Al-Mizan rejects that explanation. Its grammar is unsound in one possible construction; in the other, it would place relationship alongside God in majesty, contrary to Qur’anic propriety. There is, however, no difficulty in coupling fear of God with heedfulness toward kinship, which is itself His creation.

The first command grounds fear of God in His lordship and in the common human root preserved through propagation. The repeated command adds attention to His majesty and power and to the unity of relationship that He has created. Al-Riḥm originally means the womb and came to mean relationship because relatives issue from it; al-arḥām means relatives. Kinship is a small society, as a nation is a larger one, and the Qur’an treats both society and the individual as real entities with their own characteristics and effects. The repeated command therefore particularly emphasizes the importance of preserving ties of relationship.

Allah’s name al-Raqīb does not mean mere observation. It denotes attentive supervision of people’s acts and omissions, whether to rectify defects or preserve their record for recompense. The reminder that God vigilantly watches follows the command to preserve human unity and is a grave warning to transgressors. The severe Qur’anic condemnation of oppression, mischief, and exceeding limits is closely connected with the divine purpose of protecting humanity’s unity from disorder, decline, and collapse.

Al-Mizan reports that Jewish history places the present human species at no more than seven thousand years and argues that reflection supports this. Starting from a pair, ordinary reproduction could produce a thousand people in a century; even if disasters killed 999 of every thousand, the population would still grow by fifty percent each century. Beginning with two people and applying that minimal increase over seventy centuries would yield more than two and a half billion people, which the commentary treats as corresponding to the then world population.

Geologists, by contrast, date human fossils, bodies, and artifacts to more than five hundred thousand years and therefore make humanity millions of years old. Al-Mizan answers that this does not demonstrate uninterrupted descent of the present race from those ancient groups. Earlier human races may have appeared, multiplied, and become extinct before the present one arose. The Qur’an does not clearly settle whether humanity is confined to the present cycle or whether previous cycles occurred, though 2:30 may suggest a humanity before this one. Traditions narrated from the Imāms of the Ahlu al-bayt likewise indicate that many human cycles preceded the one that began with Adam.

The commentary rejects arguments that differences of human color require several independent original pairs. If evolution and adaptation can cause changes within a species, differences of blood and color might likewise have arisen within one species; moreover, scientific discussion does not assign such differences the claimed importance. Nor does the early human population of the Western Hemisphere disprove a common origin: over the vast period proposed by those who date human life to millions of years, prehistoric geological changes could have separated lands and populations. The contrary argument ultimately rests on a sense of improbability.

For the present race, however, Al-Mizan regards the Qur’an as clear that all people descend from one male and one female. The Qur’an names the father Adam; traditions, like the present Torah, call his wife Ḥawwāʾ, though the Qur’an does not name her. Human propagation normally occurs through sperm, while Adam was originally created from dust; the present species thus ends in Adam and his wife, even though other interpretations may be advanced for some verses.

Al-Mizan also rejects the claim that Adam in the accounts of creation and angelic prostration denotes the human species rather than an individual. Plural pronouns in passages such as 7:11 do not overcome the evident meaning of the relevant verses. In particular, the address to the children of Adam concerning Satan’s expulsion of “your parents” from the Garden establishes Adam’s individual identity through its dual pronouns. Iblīs’s reference to Adam’s progeny and the verse under discussion likewise show that Adam was an individual from dust and the father of his descendants. Otherwise the comparison between Jesus’ exceptional creation and Adam’s in 3:59 would fail. To treat Adam as the species is therefore an inordinate extreme; Al-Mizan also identifies as an opposite extreme the Sunnī scholar Zayn al-ʿArab’s view that affirming more than one Adam is al-kufr.

The commentary holds that the Qur’anic account establishes mankind as an independent species: the race propagated through sperm ends with Adam and his wife, who were created from earth and not derived from an analogous species. It presents the scientific evolutionary account as a theory in which the earth cooled from a molten condition, life developed from simple cells through aquatic plants and animals, amphibious forms, land animals, and finally homo sapiens. Its proponents appeal to a graded appearance of perfection among creatures and to experiments producing partial changes. Yet Al-Mizan argues that this does not prove evolution to be the sole possible explanation. Species could have been created separately, and the observed or experimental changes may concern conditions and characteristics rather than the essence of a species. No experiment has produced an actual transformation of an individual from one species into another, such as an ape into homo sapiens. Evolution is thus, in its view, a hypothesis devised to answer certain problems rather than a conclusion established by decisive proof; the Qur’anic teaching of man’s separate creation remains academically unrefuted.

Al-Mizan returns to the consequence that Adam’s sons married his daughters. Although Islam, and reportedly earlier shariah, prohibit such unions, the prohibition rests on benefits and harms and can change with divine legislation. The initial permission could have been necessary when only brothers and sisters existed and divine will intended their multiplication; once that necessity ended, retaining it would have fostered indecency. Present norms cannot simply be imposed upon that original situation.

The objection that sibling marriage is contrary to natural religion is also rejected. Nature’s opposition is said to arise not from an innate loathing of such intercourse, but from its tendency, in ordinary society, to spread indecency, undermine chastity, and erase decency. Historical reports of such marriages among Zoroastrians, their reported legalization in Russia, and the reported prevalence of incest in Europe are offered as evidence that no inherent aversion is decisive. The further claim that family familiarity naturally extinguishes sexual inclination is defective because its premises are disputed; its alleged undesirability applies where the union is not essentially necessary; and it presupposes the absence of legislated rules that secure society’s essential welfare. Al-Mizan concludes that many currently governing laws and principles are themselves unnatural in that sense.
verses.2: Al-Mizan considers the opening command either a prologue to the two prohibitions or a rule they explain; because the closing declaration of grave crime refers to both prohibitions or at least the last, the prologue reading is favored. The governing rule forbids managing an orphan’s property to the orphan’s detriment and prepares for the ensuing inheritance and marriage laws. “Do not substitute worthless for good” most obviously forbids keeping an orphan’s good property while returning one’s own inferior property in exchange; interpreting it as exchanging the unlawful for the lawful is less evident. Al-ḥūb, “sin” or “crime,” functions as both an infinitive verb and a verbal noun.
verses.3:
Al-Mizan explains the verse against the pre-Islamic practice by which powerful men married orphan girls under their care, absorbed their property, treated them unjustly, and sometimes discarded them after impoverishing them. The Qur’an had already severely forbidden injustice toward orphans and the consumption of their property. Muslims reportedly then became so fearful of wrongdoing that they separated orphans’ food and property completely, even allowing unused food to spoil; [2:220] relieved this hardship by permitting orphans to live with and mingle with their guardians as brethren, provided their affairs were set right.

In this context, the verse intensifies the prohibition: if a man fears he cannot deal equitably with orphan girls and therefore does not wish to marry them, he should not marry them, but should marry other women who seem good to him, up to two, three, or four. “Then marry” stands in place of the implied consequence, “then do not marry the orphans”; “such women” already indicates women other than those orphan girls. The verse thus substitutes the stated cause—fear of inequity—for its implied effect, reluctance to marry them.

The commentary rejects several proposed explanations: that the limit of four was imposed merely to prevent guardians from exhausting their own wealth and consuming orphans’ property; that concern for orphans is simply made analogous to justice toward wives; that reluctance over orphan guardianship is linked to avoiding fornication; that the verse means marrying other orphan relatives; or that reluctance to eat with orphans requires avoiding plural marriage. None properly fits the wording.

Mathnā wa thulātha wa rubāʿa means twos, threes, and fours. Since the address is to individuals and the numbers are joined in a way that indicates choice, each believer may marry two, three, or four wives. The words neither permit marrying several women in a single contract, repeated groups of two, three, or four, polyandry, nor nine wives by adding the numbers. As Majmaʿ al-bayān observes, saying that people entered in twos, threes, and fours does not mean groups of nine; moreover, Arabic has a word for nine.

A man who fears he will not be just between several wives must marry only one. The condition is fear rather than certain knowledge because certainty in such matters is difficult, especially where temptation clouds judgment; making the rule depend on knowledge would defeat its benefit. “Or what your right hands possess” means slave-girls possessed and lived with by virtue of possession, not marriage. They are not entitled to a division of nights, which makes equitable treatment easier, but this does not license injustice toward them; their marriage is addressed separately in [4:25]. Al-ʿawl means deviation from the right course, not burden. Thus the marriage law is founded on justice, equity, and the rejection of oppression and usurpation of women’s rights.
verses.4:
Al-Mizan explains that al-Ṣaduqah, al-Ṣadaqah, al-Ṣadāq, and al-Ṣidāq mean dowry, while al-Niḥlah means a gift given freely and without bargaining. By saying “their dowries,” the verse endorses the established marriage custom of assigning the wife property or something of value as dowry. Seemingly, its place in the conjugal relation resembles that of a price in a sale: customarily the man proposes marriage and brings the dowry as a buyer brings the price.

The permission to take a portion of the dowry applies only when the wife herself is pleased to relinquish it. It removes any possible assumption that the husband may not use it even with her consent. “Then eat it with enjoyment (and with) wholesome (result)” reinforces the basic command to give the dowry and shows that this permission is elective, not compulsory. Al-hanāʾ denotes what is agreeable or easily digested and is used of food; al-Marīʾ derives from quenching thirst and concerns drink. In the combined expression hanīʾanmarīʾan, the first relates exclusively to food and the second to drink.
verses.5:
Al-Mizan explains al-safah as feeble-mindedness or weakness of understanding in worldly affairs, although the word’s implication changes with its context and can, in a religious context, denote a dissolute person. Here, because the surrounding verses concern property held for orphans, it most likely denotes orphans whose minds are immature, and “your property” means their property, attributed to their guardians. If the term is taken generally, it includes both orphans and others, but the former reading is weightier.

The attribution of the ward’s property to guardians rests on the reality that worldly wealth belongs to human society as a whole. Particular persons hold particular portions for the general good, which underlies individual ownership and exclusive possession. People must therefore preserve wealth and not leave it under the management of those, such as minors or the insane, who cannot administer it properly.

The verse establishes a general social rule: society, as a legal personality, possesses the riches God has made its support and must administer, preserve, and profitably invest them. Guardians must manage the affairs of those weak of understanding, rather than surrendering their property to be wasted. They should develop it through earning, trade, and profit-sharing, maintaining wards from its growth and profit rather than consuming the capital, lest the capital gradually disappear and leave the ward destitute. The wording “out of it,” rather than “from it,” indicates this point, as al-Zamakhsharī notes.

The commentary further infers a principle of general guardianship. A father or paternal grandfather is guardian where present; otherwise responsibility falls upon the Islamic government, and finally upon other believers. Ultimately, all property belongs to God, who made it a means of livelihood for mankind. He permits individuals an exclusive relation to portions of this common wealth through lawful means such as inheritance, possession, and trade, subject to conditions including sanity and majority. Private interests are to be respected while they do not conflict with the common good; where they do conflict, public welfare decisively takes precedence. This principle underlies many Islamic rules, and is confirmed by: He it is Who created for you all that is in the earth [2:29].

“Maintain them” and “clothe them” cover food, clothing, housing, and the other material necessities of life. The command to speak kindly is an ethical rule for guardianship: wards deprived of control over their property remain human beings, not beings to be addressed harshly or insultingly. It may also be understood as an instruction to good treatment and commendable social intercourse generally.
verses.6:
Al-Mizan explains that guardians must test orphans continuously from the time they show some discretion until they reach marriageable age. A single test cannot establish whether maturity of intellect has become settled in the child’s nature. Reaching marriageable age is the basis for returning property, but al-rushd—maturity of intellect, the ability to find one’s way to the goals of life—is the necessary condition for granting independent authority to manage it.

Islam thus applies two standards of al-bulūgh. For worship and matters such as the penal code, adulthood begins at a prescribed age; for financial affairs, acknowledgements, and similar dealings, age alone is insufficient without maturity of intellect. This protects orphans and other wards from disorder, deception, and fraud by those who could exploit their inexperience. Such additional maturity is unnecessary for worship and penal matters, since people understand the evil of crimes and sins, and the need to avoid them, before attaining this financial maturity.

Guardians may not consume a ward’s property extravagantly or hastily in fear that the ward will grow up and stop them. Extravagant consumption is unjust, careless taking without need or entitlement. Hasty consumption is taking even the ordinary fee for one’s service while anticipating the ward’s majority. Both are forbidden, except that a poor guardian who is maintaining the ward’s affairs may take a reasonable amount from the estate for his livelihood, as a worker takes wages from his employer; a rich guardian must abstain altogether. The commentary rejects the view that the poor guardian should simply eat from his own property, since this would make the distinction between rich and poor purposeless.

Witnesses must be called when property is returned, so that the transfer is properly established and future disputes or claims against the guardian are prevented. Yet witnesses may fail through injustice or other causes. The concluding words, “and Allah is sufficient as a Reckoner,” therefore return the rule to its divine source: God’s meticulous reckoning and the monotheistic training that should restrain guardian, witnesses, and ward even when external legal safeguards fail.

Together with the preceding verse, this passage sets out guardianship: taking and preserving property in trust, developing it profitably, maintaining the ward, determining when guardianship begins and independent management is restored, and returning the estate. These rules rest on the common benefit that God has made property a means of support for mankind; they cultivate the ethical duty to speak to wards with kind words; and they are governed by monotheism, whose influence endures even when legal and ethical restraints weaken.
verses.7:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse establishes a comprehensive and previously unfamiliar inheritance system. al-Naṣīb denotes a separately allotted share; al-Tarikah is the property left by the deceased; al-Aqrabūn indicates that nearness of relation between deceased and heir is an essential condition; and al-Farḍ denotes a determined, fixed portion.

Islam introduced this system only after preparing the believers by strengthening love in God and religious brotherhood, under which one believer initially inherited from another. Once the faith had become established and believers had abandoned former pride and prejudice, the final inheritance system based on relatives was instituted.

The verse deliberately removes every possible ambiguity. Its unrestricted statement that men inherit includes minors as well as adults; its equally unrestricted statement that women inherit includes every woman. Repeating that the property is what parents and near relatives leave, specifying that it may be little or much, and ending with “a decreed share” all emphasize that the allotted portions are fixed and cannot be disregarded because an estate is small. The verse also proves that the general inheritance law includes the Prophet’s estate and invalidates al-taʿṣīb, the preference of agnates.
verses.8:
Al-Mizan holds that the verse concerns relatives, orphans, and needy people who are present when the heirs divide the estate, not when a dying person makes a bequest. “Relatives” accordingly refers to their poor members, as their mention alongside orphans and the needy indicates. The exhortation to give them something and address them kindly is directed to heirs and executors and calls them to mercy and kindness.

Whether this giving is legally obligatory or recommended is a juristic question outside the commentary’s scope. The verse has not been abrogated by the inheritance verses: those verses fix the shares of heirs, whereas this one concerns non-heirs and specifies no share. This is especially clear if the giving is, as the verse apparently suggests, recommended.
verses.9:
Al-Mizan says that (4:9) is probably connected with the preceding inheritance ruling and warns those who would revive the former practice of depriving minor heirs and consuming their rights. “Let them speak right words” apparently alludes adversely to that conduct: “words” commonly stands for deeds, and “right” words are words that can be believed and acted upon, rather than merely courteous words. The phrase may also refer to sound views, ideas, and advice.

The verse’s image of people fearing for weak offspring left behind is a simile intended to awaken compassion for orphaned children who have lost their guardian and protector. It is not restricted to those who actually have weak children, since the conditional is hypothetical. Those who have human sympathy should fear God concerning orphans, care for their welfare, and neither oppress them nor usurp their rights. Yet the command is not simply to show compassion; it is a threat that what one does to others’ orphans, including unjustly taking their property, will return upon one’s own orphans after one’s death.

The commentary treats this as a Qur’anic reality arising from a connection between good and evil deeds and natural phenomena. Deeds return to their doers even in this world, but their effects may extend to their progeny: the righteous father of the two orphan boys is presented as having contributed to the mercy shown to them in And as for the wall, it belonged to two orphan boys in the city, and there was beneath it a treasure belonging to them, and their father was a righteous man; so your Lord desired that they should attain their maturity and take out their treasure, a mercy from your Lord [18:82]. Thus a person’s blessing or misfortune may result from his own actions or from those of his forebears.

Al-Mizan explains this through invocation. Whatever comes from God comes in response to an invocation, and the causes and preliminaries a servant brings about are themselves a practical supplication. In doing good or evil to another human being, one shows approval that the same thing befall oneself and thus practically asks God for it. Good done to others is therefore a request for the same good for oneself; injustice done to their children or orphans is likewise a request that it be done to one’s own. Since humankind shares one origin and progeny is a single unit, an affliction affecting one part reaches the whole. Accordingly, what one does to another or that person’s descendants is bound to return to oneself or one’s descendants, unless God decides otherwise; unknown and opposing causes may intervene, as hinted by And whatever affliction befalls you, it is on account of what your hand have wrought, and (yet) He pardons most (of your faults) [42:30].

On (4:10), Al-Mizan states that the verse threatens those who consume orphans’ inheritance shares and that saying they swallow it “into their bellies” is more emphatic. It is evidence for the embodiment of deeds: their swallowing fire is literal, not a mere comparison to one who swallows fire. The objection that the present tense requires a metaphor, since the following “soon they shall enter burning fire” refers to the future, overlooks embodiment of deeds. The final clause points specifically to punishment in the hereafter; al-Saʿīr is a name for the fire of the hereafter.

verses.11:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse establishes the inheritance shares of the first class of heirs: children and parents. Its use of al-awlād rather than al-abnāʾ restricts the rule of one male share to two female shares to the deceased’s immediate children. Descendants, however remote, take the share of the parent through whom they are connected when no nearer heir intervenes: thus a son’s daughter takes two shares while a daughter’s son takes one. The descendants of brothers and sisters likewise take through their respective progenitor. The term for son, unlike al-awlād, may extend beyond an immediate child, just as al-ab may denote more than an immediate father.

The wording, “The male shall have the equal of the portion of two females,” deliberately overturns the pre-Islamic exclusion of women from inheritance. It treats the female share as confirmed and as the measure by which the male share is fixed, rather than merely saying that a woman receives half of a man’s portion. This is reinforced by the fact that the Qur’an expressly details women’s portions, while men’s portions are generally stated in relation to them. The definite forms denote categories: whenever male and female children inherit together, every male takes two shares and every female one, regardless of their number. The following provision for more than two daughters is understood as contrasting with an omitted clause concerning the mixed case, a familiar ellipsis in Arabic usage.

A single daughter receives one-half, and more than two daughters receive two-thirds. Although the verse does not expressly state the portion of exactly two daughters, Al-Mizan holds that they receive two-thirds. The rule can generally be inferred from the mixed case, where a son and daughter receive two-thirds and one-third respectively; yet this inference alone would not make the ruling conclusive, since the verse could theoretically have prescribed another share for two daughters. Its intentional silence, alongside its explicit ruling for more than two daughters, confirms the inference. The Prophet’s uninterrupted practice and the consensus of Muslim jurists, apart from a reported dissent by Ibn ʿAbbās, further confirm it. Al-Kulaynī in al-Kāf and the exegete Abū Muslim are reported to have derived the same result from the male’s double share, but Al-Mizan considers their explanation incomplete unless this confirmation by the verse’s deliberate silence is added. It rejects as unworthy the claims that “more than two” means two or more, or that two daughters’ share is established by analogy with two sisters at the end of the chapter.

Parents are joined to children as co-heirs in the first class. Each receives one-sixth when the deceased has a child. When only the parents inherit, the mother receives one-third; when there are brothers, she receives one-sixth. Brothers therefore belong to a later class and cannot inherit while a first-class heir is present, though they partially exclude the mother by reducing her share. The phrase that only the two parents inherit indicates that they are then the sole heirs.

Although the verse mentions a bequest before a debt, Al-Mizan says this does not conflict with the sunnah requiring payment of debt before execution of a bequest. Speech may mention the less weighty matter first in order to emphasize it, then rise to the more weighty one. The qualifying words, “he may have bequeathed,” further emphasize the bequest and require respect for the deceased’s expressed wish.

The address, “your parents and your children, you know not which of them is the nearer to you in usefulness,” is directed to heirs, for usefulness here concerns benefiting from inherited property. It both explains the differing shares of parents and children and educates the inheritors. Mentioning parents before children hints that parents are nearer in benefit. Although a person naturally feels stronger compassion for children, the parents’ connection to him is stronger than the children’s connection to him; on this basis one may naturally receive more from a parent than from a child, despite a superficial impression to the contrary. Al-Mizan takes this as evidence that inheritance law rests upon a real creative and natural basis rather than imagination. It may also possibly imply that descendants, however remote, precede grandfathers and grandmothers.

“An ordinance from Allah” emphasizes that these portions are decreed, fixed, and not alterable. Explicitly, the verse assigns each parent one-sixth in the presence of children; gives the mother one-third or one-sixth in their absence according to the stated conditions; gives one daughter one-half; gives several daughters two-thirds; and assigns sons and daughters the two-to-one ratio. It also establishes two daughters’ two-thirds share. Implicitly, an only son receives the whole estate, and several sons alone divide it equally. Al-Mizan regards this as a remarkably comprehensive ruling in brief language.

Finally, the commentary holds that the verse’s unrestricted wording makes no inheritance distinction between the Prophet and other people, rejecting the suggestion that general Qur’anic declarations did not apply to him because he proclaimed them. It notes, without pursuing it here, the Sunni-Shiʿah dispute arising from Abū Bakr’s report in the case of Fadak over whether prophets are inherited by their heirs or leave their property as charity.
verses.12:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse gives the husband one-half of his wife’s estate when she has no child and one-fourth when she has a child; it gives wives one-fourth of the husband’s estate when he has no child and one-eighth when he has a child. These shares follow payment of bequest and debt. In the case of al-kalālah, a brother or sister receives one-sixth, while several of them share one-third, after a non-harmful bequest or debt.

A translator’s note attached to the passage rejects the reported rule attributed to Abū Bakr that prophets neither inherit nor are inherited. The note says that this conflicts with the general inheritance verses and with And Solomon inherited from David (27:16) and Zachariah’s prayer for an heir who would inherit him and the children of Jacob (19:5–6). It maintains that these inheritances concern property, or in Solomon’s case the Kingdom, rather than prophethood or divine knowledge, which come directly from God.

Al-Mizan distinguishes the Qur’anic styles used for shares. A half or two-thirds is expressed in a possessive construction, while smaller portions such as a fourth, sixth, or third are expressed with or understood to include min, “from.” It takes this min to suggest taking from and beginning with a smaller part of the whole, and therefore considers the differing constructions appropriate to the relative size of the prescribed shares. It also understands “the half” as meaning the half of what the deceased left.

A translator’s note disputes that explanation as incomplete and arbitrary, since similar constructions are explained differently to fit it. The note proposes that min denotes al-tabʿīd, or portioning: possessive wording assigns a share from the whole estate, whereas wording with “from” assigns it from only a portion. On this view, the eldest son first receives al-habwah—specified personal effects of his father, such as a ring or sword—so parents and, where there is a child, the husband receive their fractions from the remaining portion. The note further states that wives do not receive a share in land and receive only the price, rather than the property itself, of their allotted share of other immovable property; their one-fourth or one-eighth therefore always comes from only a portion of the estate. It concludes that the two styles express distinct legal circumstances, not literary variation or the mere size of a share.

Al-Mizan defines al-kalālah as a verbal noun whose basic sense is encompassing, so that it may apply both to the inheritor and to the inherited person. Al-Rāghib is reported to define it as an heir other than a child and father, while a report from the Prophet defines it as one who dies without leaving child or parent; Al-Mizan accepts both descriptions. It offers two grammatical analyses of kāna and al-kalālah, each yielding the same result: the deceased is neither a parent nor an offspring of the heirs. It also reports al-Zajjāj’s distinction between readings of yūrithu and yūrathu, under which al-kalālah is respectively an object or a circumstantial subject.

The condition that the bequest or debt must not harm others forbids a dying person from borrowing in order to injure the heirs and deprive them of inheritance. It may also mean that he must not harm them by bequeathing more than one-third of his property.
verses.13:
Al-Mizan explains that Allah’s “limits” are the boundaries that preserve distinctions and prevent things from mixing. Here they are the inheritance laws and their apportioned shares. The promise of everlasting gardens for obeying Allah and His Messenger in this matter, and of abiding in the Fire with an abasing punishment for transgression, displays the exceptional gravity of these rules.

The commentary holds that the inheritance verses, together with the verse concerning one who has neither parents nor offspring, the declaration that men and women have shares in what parents and relatives leave, and the rule that possessors of relationship have the better claim, establish Islam’s basic inheritance principles; traditions clarify their detailed application. The first principle is nearness to the deceased. Nearer kin exclude remoter kin and may also receive a larger or smaller share accordingly. Father, mother, son, and daughter form the first class because their relationship is direct. Children exclude grandchildren, though grandchildren take their parents’ place when no child remains. The second class consists of brothers, sisters, grandfathers, and grandmothers, who are connected through one link; children of brothers and sisters take their parents’ place in their absence. Paternal and maternal uncles and aunts form the third class, connected through a parent and grandparent. Each nearer generation excludes the more remote one. Moreover, a relative connected by both parents excludes one connected only through the father, although a uterine brother or sister is not thereby excluded.

Al-Mizan identifies another precedence when assigned shares crowd one another and exceed the estate. Some heirs already have specified reductions for stated circumstances: the husband falls from one-half to one-fourth when there is a child; the wife from one-fourth to one-eighth; and the mother from one-third to one-sixth when there is a child or brothers. The father, however, remains at one-sixth whether there is a child or not. Daughters and sisters, by contrast, receive stated portions of one-half or two-thirds without a prescribed reduction for crowding. Al-Mizan infers that the first group cannot suffer a further reduction when the total shares exceed the estate; the deficiency falls upon daughters and sisters. Conversely, when the estate exceeds the assigned shares, the surplus returns only to those who would bear the deficiency. Thus, if father and daughter inherit, the father takes one-sixth, and the daughter receives her one-half plus the remaining one-third by return, making her share five-sixths.

The traditions of the Imāms of Ahl al-bayt are said to state this rule clearly. Al-Mizan contrasts it with al-‘awl, introduced during the reign of ʿUmar b. al-Khattāb, by which all shares are proportionately reduced when they exceed the estate, and with the early resort to al-taʿsīb, which gives preference to agnatic relatives.

The commentary then considers why men generally receive twice women’s share, while the mother may equal or exceed the father. It suggests that the mother’s greater attachment to the child, together with the burdens of pregnancy, childbirth, care, and upbringing, explains her exceptional position. The general two-to-one rule is said to rest on two considerations: men’s excellence in rational management of worldly affairs and their obligation to maintain and spend on women. Al-Mizan understands the description of men as maintainers of women to refer to management of livelihood and to superiority in rational thought. It portrays men’s lives as predominated by intellect and women’s by emotions and sentiments, and judges financial management, saving, exchange, production, and investment more suited to rational deliberation.

On this account, two-thirds of the world’s inheritable wealth comes under men’s ownership and management, while one-third comes under women’s. Yet the difference in ownership is compensated by the requirement that men treat women with justice and equity and share their means with them. A woman therefore owns one-third but has the benefit and usufruct of two-thirds—her own third plus half of the man’s two-thirds—whereas a man owns two-thirds but uses only one-third. Al-Mizan presents this inverse relation between possession and usufruct as the reason for the distinction between inheritance and maintenance: rational management is given predominance in property, while women’s sentiments are more directly relevant to benefiting from property.

The “excellence” attributed to men is, in Al-Mizan’s view, intellectual rather than an excellence in strength, toughness, or courage. Men’s roughness and endurance are important for defence, security, hard labour, hardship, and composure amid danger. Women are described as having the contrasting qualities of tender emotion and benevolent feeling, qualities indispensable for love, mercy, childbirth, childrearing, nursing, and household life. Neither quality can by itself sustain human society: hardness requires softness, and repulsion requires attraction. Their mutual complementarity maintains social balance, and God cannot be unjust in His judgment.

The commentary further presents men as those who go forth to seek livelihood and procure life’s necessities, even through conflict and war, while women provide rest, love, compassion, and the attraction that prevents human life from becoming merely a contest between attackers and attacked. It calls women a primary cause and basic agent of civilization, and therefore regards domestic life and marriage as the basis from which the wider human society of nations and tribes develops.

For Al-Mizan, these functional differences concern the proper ordering of worldly life, not true honor before God. Material amplitude, bodily strength, and social functions are only instruments. The superiority that matters in Islam is nearness to God, and that depends wholly on piety and fear of God, whether found in a man or a woman.
