verses.15:
Al-Mizan explains that atāh and atā bihi mean doing the act, while al-Fāhishah denotes indecent conduct and is generally used for fornication, though elsewhere it can refer to sodomy or to sodomy and lesbianism. Here it apparently means fornication, as the exegetes hold. Reports say that, when the verse of flogging was revealed, the Prophet identified flogging as the way God had opened for those guilty of fornication. The wording, “or Allah makes some way for them,” also indicates that the ruling was soon to be superseded. Since no later ruling is said to have abrogated a punishment for lesbianism or to have imposed flogging for it, the verse concerns neither lesbianism nor sodomy. “Four (witnesses) from among you” indicates male witnesses, because the pronoun is masculine.

Confinement is perpetual imprisonment, as shown by “until death takes them away,” but it is imposed only upon the required testimony, not merely upon known guilt. This evidentiary condition, and the mild expression fa-amsikūhunna, “then restrain them,” rather than a word for imprisonment, display God’s forbearance toward the ummah. The alternative, that God make a way for them, means release from perpetual confinement and signals its probable abrogation. In practice, fornicating women were later punished by flogging rather than house confinement; thus the verse’s “way” undoubtedly refers to flogging, which replaced this ruling.
verses.16:
Al-Mizan holds that the pronoun “it” refers to indecency and that the two verses are interrelated, apparently concerning fornication. On an initial reading, the first verse gives the rule as it concerns women and the second completes it for both parties: both are to be afflicted, while women are confined. Yet “then if they repent and amend, turn aside from them” cannot straightforwardly accord with lifelong confinement. It would therefore have to mean ending their other punishment while confinement remains.

A view based on certain traditions assigns the first verse to non-virgins and the second to virgins: virgins would be confined until repentance and amendment, then released. Al-Mizan rejects this because the wording gives no basis for distinguishing virgins from non-virgins, and because the first verse addresses women alone while the second addresses both parties. Abū Muslim’s view that the first verse concerns lesbianism and the second sodomy, neither being abrogated, is also rejected. The earlier explanation rules out lesbianism, while the well-established sunnah prescribes death for sodomy. The Prophet’s hadīth states: “Whoever among you commits the sin of the people of Lot, kill (both) the doer and (the man) done to.” Whether that law was original and unabrogated or later abrogated the verse, it refutes Abū Muslim’s interpretation.

Considering the apparent meaning and the problems in those explanations, Al-Mizan tentatively interprets the first verse as concerning adultery by married women. Its reference to women rather than men supports this, since “women” commonly means wives, particularly in the construction “you [that is, you men’s] women.” The initial confinement was temporary, and stoning was later ordained. This does not establish that the Book is abrogated by the sunnah, as al-Jubbāʾī claimed: “or Allah makes some way for them” itself announces a later ruling, and the Prophet explains the honored Qur’an. Even if this were termed abrogation, it would not entail the difficulties of abrogating the Book by the sunnah.

The second verse concerns fornication other than adultery. Its affliction includes confinement, striking with shoes, admonition, public shaming through harsh words, and similar injuries; it was abrogated by the verse of flogging in the chapter of ‘The Light’. The tradition identifying it with virgin girls is a weak khabar al-wāhid and al-mursalah. Al-Mizan adds that this interpretation is not free from weakness, because advance indication of later abrogation does not lessen the fact of abrogation. Repentance must be joined to amendment: it is not mere words or passing remorse, but definite reform of conduct and character.
verses.17:
Al-Mizan explains al-tawbah as return. The servant’s repentance is a remorseful return to God accompanied by a firm resolve to abandon the course that had drawn him away from servitude. God’s tawbah, by contrast, is His merciful turning toward the servant, involving forgiveness. A servant’s one repentance is surrounded by two divine turnings: first, God grants the strength and ability by which the servant can sever the causes of estrangement and return; then, after the servant repents, God turns again to cleanse him of sin and bring him near.

“Repentance with Allah is only for those” means that God has made acceptance of repentance incumbent upon Himself by His own promise. It does not mean that anything external can impose a duty on Him. Whenever acceptance is called obligatory for God, the meaning is that He does not break the promise He has voluntarily given.

The verse primarily concerns God’s merciful return, though its conditions necessarily disclose the conditions of the servant’s repentance. It embraces both return from polytheism and disbelief to faith and return from a believer’s disobedience to obedience. Thus “those who do evil in ignorance” includes unbelievers as well as sinful believers: disbelief is an act of the heart, or necessarily produces evil acts. Yet this applies provided that disbelief or sin is not wilfully obstinate.

“Ignorance” here does not simply mean absence of information. A person may knowingly and voluntarily commit evil, but when desire, anger, or other impulses overpower the knowledge that should distinguish good from evil, that knowledge is treated as ineffective and thus as ignorance. Such a person ordinarily returns to awareness and remorse once the agitation subsides. The unrepentant sinner, however, whose evil arises from obstinacy and refusal of truth, is not described in this sense as ignorant but as wilful and stubborn. Still, when an apparently obstinate person abandons that stance and submits to the truth, this shows that even his obstinacy was grounded in ignorance. In the fullest sense, every disobedience proceeds from human ignorance; the truly obstinate sinner is the one who does not turn away from evil until the end of life and health.

“Then turn (to Allah) soon” means that the sinner returns before death and the signs of the next world appear, not necessarily immediately after the sin. A person whose sin arose from ignorance does not persist in it until death as an indifferent and obstinate person would. Regret forced by punishment or fear is not true repentance, because it is only a device to escape consequences; if these were removed, the person would resume the evil. When death’s signs appear, worldly free choice—the basis on which obedience, disobedience, and a voluntary return to God are meaningful—has ended.

Accordingly, “in ignorance” and “soon” are, on the more apparent interpretation, two exclusive conditions: the sin must not arise from arrogant obstinacy, which destroys the spirit of submission, and repentance must not be postponed through negligence until death. The commentary notes an alternative: “in ignorance” may merely explain that every evil is ignorance because its doer does not know its true reality and danger. On that reading, “soon” would simply mean before death’s signs, while excluding obstinacy. But Al-Mizan judges the first reading closer to the verse’s apparent sense.

It rejects the reported view that “soon” requires repentance to remain temporally close to the sin. The paired verses state only two cases in which repentance is refused: that of one who delays until death, and that of one who dies an unbeliever. Treating every delayed repentance as invalid would create an additional excluded case not mentioned by the verses.

The distant demonstrative in “so these it is” suggests the honour accorded to those whose repentance is accepted, and the singular “evil” suggests leniency in counting their sins. The ending, “Allah is All-knowing, Wise,” rather than “Forgiving, Merciful,” explains that God opened repentance because He knows His servants’ weakness and ignorance and, in His wisdom, provides a means to restore the proper order. It also warns that God examines hearts and cannot be deceived by an outward or insincere repentance.
verses.18:
Al-Mizan holds that this verse excludes two kinds of repentance from acceptance: repentance deferred until death arrives, and the supposed return of one who dies an unbeliever. The omission here of “with Allah” hints that such people have been cut off from especial divine mercy and care; the plural “evil deeds” indicates that all their misdeeds are retained for final reckoning.

The phrase “who go on doing evil deeds” denotes continued conduct. This may mean that postponing repentance is itself a continually renewed sin, that such a person is effectively incessant in sin, or that indifference to repentance leads him repeatedly into the same or similar sins. The wording “until when death comes to one of them” exposes their contemptuous neglect: they treat repentance as unimportant, live as they please, and suppose that uttering or entertaining “Surely, now I repent” at life’s end will avert sin’s consequences.

“Now” shows that this remorse is compelled by the sight of death and the next world’s unavoidable recompense. It is not a genuine reform of character or a freely chosen return, but despair at the loss of worldly life and fear of the new reality confronting the sinner. Since no worldly life or practical freedom of choice remains, there is no opportunity for the return that repentance requires.

The second excluded case is the one who continues in disbelief and dies an unbeliever. At that point his repentance, that is, his belief, cannot benefit him; there is no deliverance after death for one who dies in unbelief, nor can ransom or appeal avail him. The qualification “while they are unbelievers” nevertheless indicates a possible merciful return for a disobedient believer who dies in disobedience without arrogance or negligence. Though death ends the servant’s voluntary repentance, God may still turn to such a servant with forgiveness and mercy through intercession. This confirms that the verses principally describe God’s return to the servant, and only incidentally discuss the servant’s return. The distant demonstrative in “These are they” marks their remoteness from divine proximity and honour, while al-Iʿtād means to prepare or promise.

Al-Mizan presents the Qur’anic teaching of repentance in its full scope as distinctive. Earlier revealed religions recognized conversion from disbelief and polytheism, but treated it simply as belief rather than analysing repentance and extending it beyond that. It appears, moreover, from the foundations of Christianity as an independent religion that repentance is of no benefit; yet the Church made it a commodity through indulgence certificates and priestly absolution. The Qur’an instead begins with man’s utter neediness before God and his distance from the perfection, honour, and everlasting happiness for which he is called. To reach divine proximity, he must return from the root of unhappiness, polytheism, and from its branches, other sins, to true faith and righteous deeds. This comprehensive return is repentance, and success depends upon it.

Because the servant possesses no good or happiness independently of God, his repentance requires a prior divine turning that supplies aid and support, followed by a divine turning that accepts his return, forgives sin, and purifies him. Considered in relation to the servant, these are two divine turnings; in reality they are one mercy encompassing him before and after his repentance. God’s merciful turning can also occur without the servant’s repentance, as in intercession for a sinful servant. Since nearness is relative, repentance may even be attributed to sinless prophets and other near servants when they rise from one degree of nearness to a higher one.

Divine mercy that removes the darkness of polytheism or other sin is God’s return to the servant; the servant’s seeking forgiveness and removal of disobedience is his return to God. Therefore a true divine call must address sins no less than polytheism and disbelief. Both the prior and subsequent divine turnings are gratuitous divine grace, not actions forced upon God. Calling acceptance of repentance obligatory means only that God has promised acceptance and does not break His promise; He retains unrestricted sovereignty to accept what He promises and reject what He has declared unacceptable, such as repentance after an increase in unbelief.

The commentary rejects a writer’s claim that Pharaoh’s repentance at drowning was not rejected because divine mercy should receive one who humbles himself in desperation. Repentance at death, it replies, is false remorse produced by the direct sight of sin’s consequences and approaching punishment. Not every regret is repentance, and not every repentance is accepted; the guilty who ask to return after seeing punishment would, if returned, resume what they had been forbidden.

This account is not merely theoretical. In individual and social reform alike, a person must first be rescued by the requisite favourable causes from evil conditions, then withdraw from those conditions, and finally have the stains of corruption removed so that goodness may take their place. This corresponds respectively to God’s prior help, the servant’s repentance, and divine acceptance and forgiveness.

Repentance has a real effect upon the soul: when effective, it removes spiritual evils that produce misery in this world and the next and prepares a person for felicity. It does not, however, abolish the rules of sharīʿah; divine laws remain in force despite repentance, just as they are not removed by disobedience. Some particular rulings connected with repentance may be waived when a person repents, but this is legislated for the welfare of creation and does not mean that repentance itself cancels divine law.

Its fundamental purpose is deliverance from the ruin of sin and disobedience and attainment of success. It also preserves hope against despair. Human life requires a balance of hope and fear: without hope that effort can bear fruit, a person loses vigour, abandons action, and falls into pessimism. Repentance revives the heart even at the brink of ruin. It does not encourage sin on the assumption that one can repent afterward. A person who plans repentance before, during, and after committing the sin has not renounced it or felt true remorse; sin and the alleged repentance are one intended act of deception, whose evil returns upon its author.

Genuine repentance begins when a person recognizes with certainty the evil of his sin. That knowledge produces remorse, and remorse leads him to change direction by doing good opposed to the evil. Such changed conduct proves that he has returned to God. This underlies the prescribed practices of expressing regret, seeking forgiveness, forming habits of good deeds, and abandoning evil deeds.

Repentance is a voluntary return from evil to obedience and can occur only in this worldly life, where choice between good and evil remains. It is ineffective regarding violations of other people’s rights: repentance concerns God’s rights, whereas a wronged person’s satisfaction must be obtained for injury to his property, honour, or life. God cannot remit such a wrong by depriving its victim of a due right. Islam, as repentance from polytheism, nevertheless cuts away prior sins concerning the branches of religion. Conversely, a person who originates an evil custom or leads others astray can scarcely realise a true return while its enduring effects continue, since he remains burdened with the wrongdoing of those who follow it.

Where repentance is effective and admissible, it erases sin and may change evil deeds into good ones, whether by itself or together with belief and righteous deeds. Yet abstaining from sin is better than sin followed by repentance. Sins are connected to Satanic temptation, whereas God’s sinless, pure-hearted servants have a distinctive and unmatched rank in servitude, beyond that of even good servants who repent.
verses.19:
Al-Mizan holds that the prohibition on inheriting women “against (their) will” does not directly concern the pre-Islamic practice of treating a deceased man’s widow herself as inherited property. Under that practice, an heir could claim a widow without a new dowry, marry her, give her to another and take her dowry, or prevent her remarriage until her death in order to inherit her property. Yet the qualifying phrase “against (their) will” cannot mean that inheriting widows was always unwilling, nor that it was lawful when they consented. The verse rather forbids contriving to inherit a woman’s property against her will, as occurred when heirs restrained widows from remarriage in expectation of their property. Thus “women” is metaphorical for their property, or “property of” is understood before it.

The verse does not address marrying a father’s widow by inheritance; that is prohibited by “And marry not women whom your fathers married ...” Nor does it directly prohibit giving her to another man and taking her dowry, which is discredited by such verses as and women shall have the benefit of what they earn (4:32) and ... then when they have fully attained their term, there is no blame on you for what they do for themselves in a proper manner (2:234).

“Do not straiten them in order that you may take part of what you have given them” concerns a husband’s effort to recover some of the dowry he himself gave, not restraint of remarriage to obtain property from other sources. It forbids making a wife’s life difficult in any manner in order to force her to ransom herself through returning dowry for dissolution of the marriage. The exception is manifest indecency, understood as adultery: in that case he may impose restrictions so that she pays something to obtain divorce. This does not conflict with and it is not lawful for you to take any part of what you have given them, unless both fear that they cannot keep within the limits of Allah; then if you fear that they cannot keep within the limits of Allah, there is no blame on them for what she gives up to become free thereby. The verse in ‘The Women’ specifies the other by restricting coercive recovery to fornication, while the payment mentioned in ‘The Cow’ is one made by mutual agreement and therefore cannot particularize this verse.

Al-Maʿrūf denotes what society recognizes and does not disapprove; living with women in a proper manner therefore requires a socially recognized mode of life. In a sound society, every person is an equally important integral part, contributing what benefits society, taking according to need, and giving the surplus; to nullify someone’s identity as such a part is to exploit that person as a vassal. Men and women alike belong to one human root and one species, and society needs each sex equally, as stated in you are (sprung) the one from the other (4:25).

Their distinct natural characteristics do not contradict this equality: men are generally marked by strength and hardiness, women by stronger sentiment and soft-heartedness; human life needs both strength and love, the forces of repulsion and attraction. The sexes are consequently equal in social weight, effect, and influence, just as individual men remain equal in their basic social value despite differences in ability, knowledge, rank, or condition. Islam establishes this equality, or social freedom, for women as for men.

Social freedom means that a person endowed with understanding and free will may choose what benefits him, provided that it does not harm society, and is not compelled to adopt another’s choice. It does not negate specialization or different laws based on differing social weight: Islam reserves judiciary, administration, and jihād for men and makes them responsible for maintaining women; similarly, minors cannot make acknowledgements or transactions and are exempt from the sharīʿah’s obligations. Such distinctions do not alter the basic human value shared by all, and comparable exclusions occur in all civil codes and human systems.

The statement that one may dislike something in which Allah has placed abundant good presents a certain fact in the form of a possibility in order to prevent antagonism and prejudice. Al-Mizan notes that women at the Qur’an’s revelation were often denied full human status—treated either as exploitable appendages or as permanently inferior dependants. It is probably with this social outlook in view that the verse says “if you hate them,” rather than “if you dislike their marriage.”
verses.20: Al-Mizan explains al-Istibdāl as replacing one wife with another, hence the meaning: if a man wishes to divorce a wife and take another in her place, he must not recover any of the dowry paid to the divorced wife, even if it was a heap of gold and he seeks only a small part. The interrogative condemns such recovery as taking it by al-Buhtān—ordinarily a false accusation, but here the act of taking back dowry itself—and manifest wrong.
verses.21:
Al-Mizan explains that the question, “And how can you take it,” expresses astonishment at recovering dowry after intimate union. al-Ifdāʾ denotes intimate touching. Since marriage and sexual intimacy make spouses like one being, taking the dowry back is oppression and injustice, like one part of a body oppressing another.

The “firm covenant” apparently means the union firmly established by the marriage tie, of which the stipulated dowry, received by the woman as her right, is a concomitant. The interpretations that it means either a promise to retain her properly or release her fairly, or their becoming lawful to one another through marriage, are regarded as far-fetched from the wording. The passage also prohibits marrying women previously married by one’s fathers, apart from what has already passed, calling this indecent, hateful, and an evil way.
verses.22:
Al-Mizan explains that the question, “And how can you take it,” expresses astonishment at recovering dowry after intimate union. al-Ifdāʾ denotes intimate touching. Since marriage and sexual intimacy make spouses like one being, taking the dowry back is oppression and injustice, like one part of a body oppressing another.

The “firm covenant” apparently means the union firmly established by the marriage tie, of which the stipulated dowry, received by the woman as her right, is a concomitant. The interpretations that it means either a promise to retain her properly or release her fairly, or their becoming lawful to one another through marriage, are regarded as far-fetched from the wording. The passage also prohibits marrying women previously married by one’s fathers, apart from what has already passed, calling this indecent, hateful, and an evil way.
verses.23:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse prohibits conjugal relations with specified women. Its seven blood-relatives include every ascendant mother, however remote, and every descendant daughter, however remote; sisters share a father, mother, or both without an intermediary; paternal and maternal aunts include the sisters of grandparents as well. Although the immediate context may suggest marriage, the later exception for those whom the right hands possess shows that what is ultimately implied by “Forbidden” is cohabitation or a similar expression, not marriage alone. The divine wording leaves this unspoken out of moral decorum.

The plural wording distributes the ruling individually: each man is forbidden his own mother, daughter, sister, and so on, not every mother or daughter to every man. The address is to men because, by nature, men seek women and propose marriage.

Suckling establishes real legal relationships parallel to blood-relations. A sound tradition, narrated by both sects from the Prophet, states: “Verily God has prohibited through suckling what He has prohibited through blood-relationship.” Thus it creates the corresponding seven prohibited groups: foster-mother, foster-daughter, foster-sister, foster paternal and maternal aunts, and the daughters of foster-brothers and foster-sisters. “Your sisters from suckling” specifically means sisters suckled by one’s mother with milk flowing because of one’s father. The detailed conditions by which suckling establishes this prohibition belong to jurisprudence.

A wife’s mother is prohibited whether or not the marriage was consummated. A step-daughter is her mother’s daughter by an earlier husband, and is prohibited only after intercourse with her mother. “Who are in your guardianship,” literally “in your lap,” describes the usual situation and is not a restriction: a step-daughter remains prohibited even if she was not raised by her stepfather. It may indicate the rationale that constant domestic mixing with such women would otherwise make avoidance of incest impossible. The decisive condition is consummation with the mother; had guardianship been a legal condition, it too would have been expressly qualified. “There is no blame on you” thus implies “in marrying them.”

The wives of biological sons, including descendants through sons or daughters, are prohibited; “who are of your own loins” excludes the wives of adopted sons. Having two sisters in marriage is forbidden only simultaneously. A man may marry a wife’s sister after the first wife’s divorce or death.

“Except what has already passed” most plainly pardons the pre-Islamic practice of having two sisters at once, but does not allow an existing union to continue after the prohibition. Its purpose is to preserve the legal effects of the former union—especially children’s legitimacy, kinship, inheritance, and family rights—not to validate the dissolved marriage itself. It is also possible, though less evidently intended, that the exception extends to all the listed prohibitions: Islam recognizes marriages prevailing in non-Muslim societies when their religion or custom regarded them as lawful, thereby recognizing children and kinship when people enter Islam. Allah’s forgiveness here concerns the external legal effects of past acts, rather than sins and disobedience.
verses.24:
Al-Mizan holds that al-muhsanāt in this verse means women presently married to husbands, not chaste women or free women. Apart from the prohibited groups already listed, the relevant prohibition is that of marrying a woman whose existing marriage continues; neither chastity nor free status itself prevents marriage. “Except those whom your right hands possess” consequently excludes a man’s married slave woman from this prohibition. Traditions report that her master may remove her from her husband, leave her untouched for the prescribed period, have intercourse with her, and then return her to him. The alternative view that the exception means chaste women possessed through marriage or slavery is rejected, since al-muhsanāt does not mean chaste here and the Qur’an uses “those whom your right hands possess” specifically for slaves. The reported view, based on a weak narration from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, that it concerns only captive unbelieving married women is likewise rejected as an unsupported particularization.

“Allah’s ordinance to you” commands adherence to what God has prescribed. “Lawful for you is (all) besides that” refers, through its grammatical form and connection with “that you seek (them) by means of your wealth,” to the cohabitation implied by “Forbidden”: intercourse is lawful with women outside the fifteen prohibited groups after marriage, or after acquiring a slave woman. It does not concern a numerical limit, merely other relatives, or slave women alone. The subsequent clause excludes fornication from the possible ways of approaching women and confines lawfulness to marriage and possession by slavery. Wealth means dowry in marriage and price in acquiring slaves; muhsinīn means chastity, not married or free status, and chastity is the opposite of every illicit sexual relation, not celibacy.

The commentary rejects the claim that “not committing fornication” literally forbids intercourse without an intention to procreate, and that chastity therefore means permanent marriage. It distinguishes the underlying benefit of a law from the scope of the law established by the Law-giver’s wording. Marriage serves, in most cases, the combined benefit of procreation and protection from indecency: sexual desire impels union, while reason restrains deviation that ruins life, family, and procreation. Yet not every union produces children, and the permanent rules of marriage apply to all persons and times, not only to instances that achieve its usual benefit. Making lawfulness depend on an intention or capacity for procreation would absurdly invalidate marriages involving infertility, menopause, pregnancy, or intercourse without ejaculation. Marriage is a lawful institution with fixed rules, even where its common benefits do not arise.

Al-Mizan states unequivocally that al-istimtāʿ in “Then as to such of them with whom you have mutʿah” means mutʿah marriage. Grammatically, mā may be the relative pronoun referring to women with whom mutʿah is contracted; alternatively, it may mean “whenever,” referring to the implied cohabitation. In either case, the clause branches from the preceding general permission by specifying a component or particular case. At the verse’s Medinite revelation, mutʿah was a prevalent Muslim practice known by this exact name, a fact unanimously accepted in the traditions. As with established terms such as hajj, trade, interest, salāt, sawm (fast), zakāt, and hajjuʿt-tamattuʿ, a Qur’anic use of an established religious or social term must bear its recognized meaning rather than its original literal one. Whether mutʿah was later abrogated is a separate question.

This interpretation is also reported from early exegetes among the Companions and their disciples, including Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd, Ubayy b. Kaʿb, Qatādah, Mujāhid, al-Suddī, Ibn Jubayr, and al-Hasan, and is the madhhab of the Imams of the Ahl al-bayt. The interpretations that al-istimtāʿ simply means marriage for enjoyment, or that istamtaʿtum means merely “you enjoy,” are untenable because the current technical usage of mutʿah would have governed the hearers’ understanding. They also make the dowry clause unsuitable: in ordinary marriage, dowry becomes due upon the marriage formula, rather than upon intercourse or merely seeking enjoyment, and earlier verses had already established its rules. The verse therefore is not merely restating the obligation of dowry.

Al-Mizan rejects the proposed Qur’anic abrogations. The verse in the chapter of ‘The Believers’ cannot abrogate this verse because it is Meccan whereas the mutʿah verse is Medinite; moreover, mutʿah is a marriage and its woman a wife, as early Muslim usage itself calls it mutʿah marriage. The inheritance, divorce, waiting-period, and numerical-marriage verses stand to this verse as general to particular, or unrestricted to restricted, not as abrogators. Tradition may exclude a mutʿah wife from inheritance without removing her status as wife; the same applies to the other rules. In any event, the cited general verses of divorce, number, and inheritance precede this particular verse.

It is especially untenable to claim that the preceding clauses of this same interconnected verse abrogate its later permission of mutʿah. The verse lists prohibited women and then permits all others through marriage or possession; since mutʿah is a marriage, no contradiction exists. Nor does the requirement of chastity create a difficulty: al-ihsān here means chastity because the clause includes slave women. Even if it meant marriage, the consequence would only be that the tradition, not the Qur’an, excludes a man with a mutʿah wife from the stoning rule; stoning itself is not mentioned in the Qur’an. Finally, abrogation by tradition is invalid from the outset because it conflicts with mutawātir traditions requiring reports to be tested by the Qur’an and rejected when they do not accord with it.
verses.25:
Al-Mizan explains that al-Ṭawl may mean riches or ample ability, while al-muhsanāt here means free women, being contrasted with slave women. It cannot mean chaste women, married women, or Muslim women: the first would be contrasted with unchaste women, married women cannot be remarried while their marriage remains, and “believing” would be redundant if it meant Muslim. The verse requires belief in both the free woman and the slave girl, and thus indicates the unlawfulness of marrying a nonbelieving woman, whether Jewish, Christian, or polytheist.

“Those whom your right hands possess” means slave women owned by believers other than the suitor, since one cannot marry his own slave girl. Possession is nevertheless ascribed to all believers because Islam regards them as one body, united in religion and interest. A man unable to pay a free believing woman’s dowry and maintenance may marry a believing slave girl, so as not to fall into indecency and spiritual ruin.

The verse is commonly understood to speak of permanent marriage and to present marriage to a slave girl as an inferior alternative to permanent marriage with a free woman. Permanent marriage is the ordinary choice for one who intends a household, offspring, and heirs. Mutʿah, by contrast, is a divinely provided facility that relieves people’s burden, blocks indecency, and uproots social evils. The Qur’an often confines legislation to its most familiar cases; accordingly, its wording may also apply to marriage generally, including temporary marriage. Even if the present verse concerns permanent marriage alone, its concession is contained wholly within its own clause and cannot prove that the preceding mutʿah verse excluded temporary marriage.

Because true faith is inward and known to God, “Allah knows best your faith” means that dealings must rest on outward signs of belief, such as the two witnessing, congregational prayer, and common religious duties, rather than inaccessible inner reality. “You are (sprung) the one from the other” removes the social aversion to marriage with slaves. Slave and free person are equally human; their difference lies only in certain social regulations and has no standing before God, who recognizes piety. The opening sequence is therefore not a binding condition that a man must first be impoverished before he may marry a slave girl. It speaks in the audience’s customary manner, while affirming the common humanity of slave and free. For this reason, “and that you abstain is better for you” cannot mean that abstaining from marriage with slave women is preferable because such marriage supposedly brings disgrace.

Marriage to a slave woman requires her master’s permission, because he controls her affairs; he is called her “people” in accordance with their shared humanity. Her dowry must be fixed and paid properly, without reduction, delay, or offence; though paid to her, it is in fact paid to her master. In this clause, al-muhsanāt means chaste women. “Not fornicating, nor receiving paramours” may distinguish open illicit relations from secret liaisons, the latter having been common in Arabia.

Regarding the punishment for a slave woman’s indecency, uhsinna may mean that she is married, or, on the preferable active recitation, that she is Muslim. If it means marriage, it has no independent legal effect: a slave woman who fornicates receives half the punishment of a free woman whether married or not. The punishment is flogging, not stoning, since stoning cannot be halved; al-muhsanāt consequently means unmarried free women here, and the penalty is fifty stripes. It is also possible that al-ihsān denotes chastity: slave women were often compelled by masters into prostitution for profit, but a believing slave woman not compelled would normally preserve outward chastity; if she then committed fornication, she would receive half the free woman’s punishment. Taking uhsinna to mean that they simply become chaste would make the condition superfluous, since an unchaste slave would then be presumed compelled.

Al-ʿAnat means affliction, hardship, and perdition, and here denotes falling into fornication under the pressure of desire. “This” apparently refers to marriage with slave girls; “and that you abstain is better for you” may thus mean abstaining from such marriage or from fornication, and perhaps refers to marriage more generally, God knows better. In either case patience is superior: abstention from marrying slave women avoids the masters’ rights over them and their offspring, while abstention from illicit relations purifies character and strengthens piety. God’s forgiveness erases evil thoughts’ effects from the minds of His pious servants, and He has mercy on them.
verses.26:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse states the ultimate purpose and benefit of the preceding laws: God wishes to explain the rules of religion, which bring good in this world and the next and rest on many benefits and reasons. The omitted object of “to explain to you” may emphasize the greatness of what is explained, or “to explain” and “to guide” may share the object, “the ways of those before you.”

“The ways of those before you” most naturally means the general way of life of the prophets and righteous people who sought God’s pleasure and attained felicity in both worlds, rather than every detail of earlier customs. Thus it does not require retaining earlier laws that have been revoked. Another possible interpretation is that God explains the customs of prior societies, both right and wrong, guides people to what is right among them, and turns mercifully to them regarding wrong practices they had adopted. Although this can fit if all three verbs share that object, the commentary considers it less suited to Qur’anic usage, since guidance normally means conveying or showing the truth, rather than merely informing people of all earlier customs.

God’s turning mercifully to His servants includes His favor in ordaining the sharīʿah, explaining reality, and guiding to the right way, as well as accepting repentance and removing sin’s effects and consequences. “Allah is Knowing, Wise” qualifies every clause of the verse, not merely the final one.
verses.27: Al-Mizan explains that the repeated statement that Allah desires to turn mercifully to the believers makes the following contrast specifically with the preceding clause about God’s merciful turning; without the repetition, the statement about those who follow lusts would seem awkwardly parallel to all the preceding clauses. Their desired “great deviation” is transgression of the limits set out in these verses: incest, disregard for the consequences of blood and marital relations, licentiousness and debauchery, and refusal to follow God’s prescribed path.
verses.28:
Al-Mizan explains human weakness as the presence of desire within human nature, continually inciting lust and causing inward turmoil. In mercy, God has made lawful means of calming that desire: marriage and possession, included in “and lawful for you is (all) besides that,” and the further concession of mutʿah marriage, which lacks such burdens of permanent marriage as a heavy dowry and regular maintenance. These are the means by which He lightens the believers’ burdens.

The view that the verse refers only to permitting marriage with slave girls in necessity is rejected. Such marriages already occurred among pre-Islamic Arabs, despite their social contempt for them. The verses instead remove that stigma by teaching that a slave girl is as fully human as a free woman and is not unworthy of social intercourse or family ties.

The lightening of burdens is addressed specifically to this ummah, whereas the stated cause—humanity’s created weakness—is universal. The verse therefore gives a general cause while leaving unspoken the factor that had restricted its effect among earlier nations: human weakness always called for this mercy, but impediments had prevented its full extension until divine mercy encompassed this ummah. This is indicated by “Our Lord! do not lay on us a burden as Thou didst lay on those before us” (2:286) and “He has chosen you and has not laid upon you any hardship in religion” (22:78). The general cause thus also indicates that the favors granted to humanity have appeared in their complete form in this ummah.
verses.29:
Al-Mizan explains “swallow up” property as exercising such complete control over it that others’ control is removed, just as food is consumed by eating. “Wrongful” denotes what lacks a rightful, wise purpose, while al-Tijārah means a sale-and-purchase transaction undertaken to gain profit. By saying “your property among yourselves,” the verse treats wealth as circulating through the collective life of society; it therefore prohibits transactions that harm and corrupt society rather than conduce to its welfare, such as interest, gambling, and deceptive trade.

The commentary holds that “except that it be trading by your mutual consent” is a disjointed, not a connected, exception. The prohibition of wrongful transfers might otherwise suggest that social life could not be sustained; the clause answers this implied objection by identifying mutually consenting, properly conducted trade as a transaction capable of fulfilling society’s needs. In this reading, “by wrongful means” is a basic qualification, so the verse need not be further qualified by listing other lawful transfers, such as gifts, compromise, prizes, dowry, or inheritance.

Al-Mizan considers the connected-exception reading grammatically possible but less fitting to the context. It rejects as remote the views that the verse merely forbids spending wealth in ways displeasing to God, or that it originally prohibited eating another’s food without compensation and was later abrogated. It also rejects the claim that wrongful acquisition means taking property without an exactly equal exchange, while trade is an indulgence allowing such inequality. al-Bātil is what fails to achieve its intended effect; the intended effect of trade is the reciprocal transfer of goods and price in a way that meets both parties’ needs. That effect can obtain despite an unequal monetary valuation when another factor compensates for it, such as the buyer’s desire for the item, fear of losing it, or another benefit; mutual agreement shows that such factors are present, and the exchange is not thereby void or wrongful. The Qur’an cannot ordain what it has judged void and false, nor can rightly guided human nature require falsehood in order to meet its needs. Thus, even on the connected-exception reading, “by wrongful means” would have to be merely explanatory.

The commentary likewise rejects the view that the disjointed exception declares all worldly trade and affairs vain because they are impermanent. Besides tending instead toward the connected reading, that interpretation imports ideas suited to other verses into a legal context and would result in legalizing wrongful conduct; the Qur’an cannot permit wrongfulness.

Although “do not kill yourselves” apparently forbids suicide, its connection with the preceding communal treatment of property indicates that the believers form one self: each person’s life is both his own and, in this sense, that of the others. It therefore covers both suicide and murder. “Surely Allah is Merciful to you” may further indicate that the prohibition includes exposing oneself to danger or doing what may lead to one’s death; the mercy clause is especially suited as the reason for this prohibition of killing.
verses.30:
Al-Mizan explains that al-ʿUdwān literally means exceeding a limit and is broader than injustice; here it means transgressing the limits set by God. Nuslihi nāran means, “We shall burn him into fire.”

The commentary holds that this verse addresses the Messenger of God rather than the believers because of dhālika, “this,” which contains the singular addressee. One who commits the act, although the believers are one self and should not seek their own destruction, is no longer part of the believing community; thus the punishment is not addressed to the believers themselves. For the same reason, the statement is general—“whoever does this”—rather than “whoever among you.”

“And this is easy to Allah” supports referring “this” primarily to the prohibition of killing. The preceding assurance of divine mercy is especially appropriate to that command, and together the two endings mean that God mercifully forbids people to kill themselves, though He could easily cast a murderer into the Fire. Nevertheless, both the mercy clause and the threat may be related to both preceding prohibitions: wrongful consumption of property and killing. Al-Mizan finds no support for extending the threat to all the prohibitions from the beginning of the chapter, or from verse 19 onward.

The verse also shifts style: God is first mentioned in the third person in “surely Allah is Merciful to you,” then speaks in the first person in “We will soon cast him into fire,” because the address has turned directly to the Prophet; it returns to the third person in “this is easy to Allah,” explaining that this is easy because He is God.
verses.31:
Al-Mizan explains that al-ijtināb, “to avoid” or “shun,” is metaphorically derived from al-janb, the side of the body: one turns one’s front toward what one seeks and turns it aside from what one avoids. It is therefore more expressive than merely “leaving.” Al-Takfir derives from covering or hiding and is generally used in the Qur’an for forgiveness of sins. Al-Kabāʾir, “great sins,” necessarily implies smaller forbidden sins, because greatness is relative to smallness. Thus the verse establishes that sins, when compared with one another, are great or small, and that al-Sayyiʾah in its second clause means the small sins parallel to the great ones.

Every act of disobedience is great when the insignificance of the servant is compared with the greatness of God; this does not conflict with the relative distinction between sins themselves. A sin is great when its prohibition is more strongly emphasized than that of others, as shown by severe wording, repeated emphasis, or a threat such as punishment by fire. The promised “honorable place of entering” is either paradise or nearness to God, whose final result is the same.

The commentary further notes that al-Sayyiʾah may mean an evil occurrence causing grief, the consequences of sin in this world or the next, or sin itself. It can denote sins generally, but in this verse it denotes small sins, since avoidance of great sins leaves these remaining. The verse is a divine favor to believers: God promises to expiate minor slips, which people can scarcely avoid altogether because of weakness, ignorance, desire, and similar influences. It does not license small sins. Whoever commits one while considering it insignificant and harmless displays contempt for God’s command; that contempt is itself among the gravest sins. Like the promise of forgiveness to those who return to God, the verse gives hope to hearts without encouraging sin.

Al-Mizan rejects the claim that great sins cannot be identified and that one must therefore avoid every sin lest one perish. The verse presupposes that people can recognize major sins from their prohibitory commands, and at minimum obliges them to learn them in order to guard against them. Knowing them also reveals God’s limits and warns that transgressing them is not forgiven without definite remorse and sincere repentance. Intercession is real, but it does not benefit one who disdains divine commands or treats repentance lightly; committing sins in reliance on intercession is itself a great sin that closes the way to it.

Several proposed definitions are then assessed. The definition of great sins as those carrying both an afterlife punishment and a fixed worldly penalty fails because persistence in a minor sin becomes great, although no fixed punishment is prescribed for it; friendship with unbelievers and usury are likewise among the gravest Qur’anic prohibitions without such a penalty. Defining them solely as sins threatened with fire in the Qur’an—or adding traditions—is neither comprehensive nor exclusive. Defining them as sins that demonstrate indifference to religion and heedlessness of the sharīʿah identifies transgression and rebellion, which are indeed mortal sins, but does not account for other grave sins that remain grave even without obstinacy, such as consuming an orphan’s property, incest, and unlawfully killing a believer. The view that only acts prohibited in themselves, rather than through incidental circumstances, are great is in one respect opposite to the preceding view; indifference and transgression are themselves grave concomitants that can make any sin mortal.

The restriction of “great sins” to sins mentioned earlier in this chapter is incompatible with the verse’s generality. The view attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās that every forbidden deed is great is valid only when one compares the servant’s disobedience with the majesty of the Lord, not when one compares sins with one another. Taking the phrase to mean all forbidden sins would make the verse say, in effect, that if people avoid all sins, God will expiate their small sins—although none would remain. Limiting this to sins before revelation would restrict the verse to those then present, while construing it as a general promise to one who wholly resolves and succeeds in avoiding every sin makes it applicable only to an almost nonexistent case; human beings are not free from errors except those under God’s special protection.

Al-Mizan rejects the Muʿtazilite definition that a small sin is one whose punishment is less than a person’s total reward and a great sin one whose punishment exceeds it. Neither this verse nor any other Qur’anic text supports such a general doctrine of forfeiture, though certain sins can nullify deeds in particular cases. The verse likewise does not establish that expiating small sins becomes obligatory upon God when a servant avoids major sins.

Another account says that every forbidden act is great when committed with indifference, arrogance, or haughtiness toward the divine command, but small when done under anger, desire, or cowardice; a related view makes the greatest aspect of every sin contempt for the sharīʿah and includes repeated commission because it manifests disrespect. Al-Mizan accepts that arrogance and disdain intensify a sin and can make it great, but denies that this is the sole measure. Some sins are great in themselves: incest compared with looking at a stranger woman, and murder compared with beating, remain so without arrogance. Arrogance makes prohibition more severe and the disobedience more condemnable; fornication under overpowering lust and ignorance is not like fornication committed arrogantly while judging it harmless. Moreover, interpreting the verse as a promise to forgive merely the lesser aspects within every individual sin does not accord with its wording or style.

Al-Ghazālī’s reported synthesis distinguishes sins as great and small both in themselves and by their effects on the soul. Repeated minor sin may become great. Obedience gives the soul light and purity, while disobedience brings darkness and remoteness; where the darkness of sin overcomes the light of obedience, it extinguishes that light and the sin is great, whereas where obedience overcomes sin, it sacrifices an equivalent measure of reward and leaves diminished light, which he identifies with al-tahābut and the expiation of small sins. He also holds that perfect equivalence between good and evil would imply a person with neither light nor darkness, but regards the division of people into those in the garden and those in the fire as refuting this. Al-Rāzī rejects this explanation as based on erroneous Muʿtazilite principles.

The author of Tafsīr al-manār, in a reported criticism, reproaches al-Rāzī for opposing a Qur’anic distinction merely because of its association with the Muʿtazilites. He reports that Ibn ʿAbbās said great sins were nearer to seventy, or even seven hundred, rather than seven, and says that certain Ashʿarites denied the division into great and small sins through far-fetched interpretation in polemical opposition to the Muʿtazilites. He criticizes such partisanship as turning scholarship into a source of Muslim strife rather than attention to religious reality.

Al-Mizan finds al-Ghazālī’s account partly sound but defective. First, the classification based on cancellation of reward and punishment does not always correspond to the classification of acts in themselves. Great sins may reduce a large store of reward until a later small sin cancels the remainder; thus something great by one measure may be small by the other, and conversely. Second, obedience and disobedience can oppose or weaken one another in some cases, but neither the Qur’an nor the sunnah establishes an all-encompassing and unchanging rule of mutual cancellation. Virtue and evil may coexist, producing a divided personality: a person may commit serious injustice while sincerely maintaining other obligations, with opposing dispositions struggling until each becomes established and takes its turn in control.

Third, al-Ghazālī’s earlier theory would make voluntary avoidance of grave sins irrelevant, since one unable to commit them would still have his small sins cancelled by superior good deeds. Yet al-Ghazālī elsewhere says expiation arises only where a person has both urge and ability to commit a major sin but restrains himself; one who lacks the desire or ability does not receive this expiation. He also holds that a darkness in the heart must be removed by an opposite, corresponding good deed. These later statements make voluntary restraint from a desired major sin the condition of expiation, but that conclusion does not necessarily follow from his earlier account.

Al-Mizan concludes from the Qur’an that good and bad deeds may cancel or diminish one another in particular cases, but there is no proof that every evil affects every good, or the reverse, in this way. Moral and psychological conditions help to understand the Qur’anic realities of reward and punishment. Great and small sins, however, are distinguished by comparison with one another, independently of a theory of forfeiture: unjust killing is greater than looking at a stranger woman, and drinking liquor while claiming it lawful is greater than drinking it under the pressure of desire.

Since the verse is unrestricted, it promises one who avoids great sins the expiation of all small sins, past and future. This avoidance means that each believer avoids, as far as possible in his particular circumstances, the great sins within his power and toward which his heart is inclined; it does not require first intending the sin and then withdrawing. It would be untenable to make the general promise depend on a person being inclined and able to commit every major sin, an almost imaginary case. God therefore expiates the small sins of one who avoids the major sins available to him, whether or not the two sins have any reciprocal relation.

The conditional wording indicates that avoidance itself has a role in the expiation. Otherwise the verse would have said simply that acts of obedience expiate evils, as in surely good deeds take away evil deeds (11:114), or that God forgives small sins without qualification. In sum, a sin is great when its prohibition is expressed severely or accompanied by a threat of fire or something similar, whether in the Qur’an or the sunnah; these signs are not exclusive criteria.
verses.32:
Al-Mizan explains coveting as the inward wish that what another possesses were one’s own. The verse forbids coveting the additional bounties and legally assigned rights that God has given exclusively to one group, particularly men or women: men’s plurality of wives and larger inheritance share, and women’s dower and maintenance. Rather than fastening oneself upon those who possess such advantages, one should turn to God and ask Him from His treasures. The prohibition is advisory, intended to protect the preceding legislation: persistent desire becomes hidden envy, then speech and action, and collective envy produces corruption. By describing the recipients as “some of you” over others, the verse calls for submission to God’s decree and mutual affection, since the recipient is not an alien body.

“Men shall have the benefit of what they earn and women shall have the benefit of what they earn” supplies the reason. Although al-iktisāb particularly denotes what one acquires for oneself, “earning” here is not confined to voluntary labour or commercial gain; otherwise the verse would concern only envy of others’ earnings and would not fit the inheritance and marriage context. It means acquisition or entitlement, whether through activity or an inherent characteristic. Each sex receives the financial and non-financial advantages suited to its social position and characteristics, and each owns what it acquires. Thus men’s inheritance and marital rights, and women’s inheritance, maintenance, and dower, are not to be coveted as though they were arbitrary possessions; God does not will injustice to His servants.

“Ask Allah of His grace” redirects the inseparable human desire for distinction and livelihood from others’ possessions to God, in whose hand all grace lies. Grace is left indefinite in order to teach two things. First, one should ask God for what is truly best without prescribing the desired object or the means by which it should come, since a person may ardently seek wealth, children, honour, or health only to find its attainment ruinous. Second, one must not ask for an excellence exclusively assigned to others in a way that would negate the divine reason for a creative or legislative distinction and nullify its regulations. One should ask God to fulfil one’s need as He deems best. “Surely Allah knows all things” confirms that He knows the underlying reasons for His allotments and does not err in His decisions.

Al-Mizan then holds that unequal human capacities to acquire life’s advantages are a natural and perennial fact. Earlier domination of the weak by the strong generated hatred and revolt; even after arbitrary tyranny was curtailed by law, economic disparity preserved the same disorder under another form. Communism tried to abolish private property and distribute the fruits of labour, but, in the commentary’s view, destroyed individual free will, conflicted with nature and instinct, and could not eliminate the human drive to work for distinction. Replacing material incentives with immaterial glory does not solve this: if such glory is not believed real it cannot motivate, and if it is believed real it has the effect of material incentive. Democracy’s criticism of communism and heavy taxation likewise did not prevent affluent classes from luxury and oppression; authority over collected wealth can yield the same benefits as ownership.

The underlying failure of both systems, Al-Mizan argues, is their aim of material enjoyment by every means, an aim inseparable from conflict and corruption. Islam instead leaves people free in matters to which their nature leads, raises the standard of the deprived through taxes upon the affluent, restrains the affluent through prohibiting extravagance and displays that widen social distance, fosters unity and good manners, and redirects competition from material distinction to the honour of piety. It teaches people to seek every desired bounty from God: and ask Allah of His grace; surely the most honourable of you with Allah is the one among you who is most pious (49:13); Therefore fly to Allah (51:50). Turning to God does not entail idleness, but leads people to the genuine causes of their aims without neglecting livelihood or happiness; the claim that Islam discourages material acquisition is therefore, in the commentary’s view, ignorant and false.
verses.33:
Al-Mizan takes al-mawālī, “heirs,” as those possessing a form of al-wilāyah, and reads the verse, together with the preceding verse, as a concise summary of the detailed inheritance laws. It commands that every entitled person receive his or her due share of what parents and near relatives leave. Thus the heirs are all those already enumerated in the inheritance verses—children, parents, brothers, sisters, and others—and the three categories in this verse correspond to parents, near relatives, and spouses.

Accordingly, “those with whom your right hands have ratified agreements” means husband and wife, whose marital relationship is established by the marriage formula; the wording alludes to the custom of ratifying an agreement by shaking hands. God has appointed heirs for every male and female to inherit the property left by parents, relatives, and spouses. The preposition min may connect inheritance to the property itself or to an understood verb, “they shall inherit,” without changing this result. “So give them their portion” orders that the prescribed inheritance shares be delivered, and “surely Allah is a witness over all things” emphasizes the command.

The commentary rejects interpretations that make al-mawālī agnates outside the principal heirs, or make min explanatory of the heirs themselves, because the wording does not support them. It also rejects construing the ratified agreements as pre-Islamic inheritance alliances, whose one-sixth share would require abrogation by and the possessors of relationship are nearer to each other in the ordinance of Allah (8:75), or as a continuing command merely to help, advise, or support such allies. Likewise, it rejects references to the Medinan brotherhood, allegedly later abrogated by inheritance law, or to adopted sons who should receive a bequest. None of these readings is supported by the verse’s text or context.
verses.34:
Al-Mizan interprets the verse’s “maintainers” as those responsible for and given authority over another’s affairs. The verse grounds men’s maintenance of women in what it presents as men’s greater prudence and capacity for strenuous public tasks, together with their financial obligations of dower and maintenance. Because those grounds are stated generally, the opening principle is not limited to husbands and wives: it assigns men authority in collective affairs such as rule, judgment, defence, and war. The following description of good women, however, turns specifically to marriage and does not narrow the preceding social principle.

Within marriage, obedience and “guarding the unseen” concern the conjugal rights created by the husband’s maintenance of his wife. A wife is to observe those rights in his presence and protect them in his absence, avoiding sexual betrayal and safeguarding the property entrusted to her for domestic life. The preferred reading of “as Allah has guarded” is that God has protected the husband’s rights by establishing his authority and obliging this obedience; another possible reading makes the wife’s duty an exchange for the rights God secured for women, including dower and maintenance.

This marital authority does not erase a woman’s independent will, ownership, management of her property, or ability to protect and pursue her personal and social rights. A man has no general right to interfere with her proper individual choices, except where an unlawful act is intended. The husband’s claim is confined to matters arising from the conjugal relation and the reciprocal rights attached to his financial maintenance.

Al-Nushūz is refusal to submit in that sphere, and fear of it means that signs of recalcitrance have appeared. The three responses are sequential and progressively more severe: admonition comes first; if it fails, separation in the sleeping place follows; only if that also fails does beating follow. The gradual order comes from the escalating character of the measures, not merely from the conjunction joining them. “Leave them alone in the sleeping places” most plausibly means displaying displeasure by turning away and withholding contact in the shared bed, rather than moving to a separate bed altogether.

If obedience resumes, the husband must seek no pretext to trouble or oppress his wife. The reminder that God is High and Great rebukes the abuse of strength: true grandeur belongs to God, so a man must not let his relative power deceive him into imagining superiority or justify continued action against her.

The publisher’s note adds the following clarification: The literal and apparent meaning of the word yaḍribuhunna used in the verse is “strike them” or “beat them” but the word has other meanings and the correct and appropriate meaning should be applied to conform to the verse contextually and according to the broader Qur’anic teachings.
verses.35:
Al-Mizan explains al-Shiqāq as breach or enmity. When a breach between spouses is feared, the appointment of one judge from each side reduces injustice and arbitrariness. If husband and wife sincerely seek agreement, without obstinacy, and relinquish the contest of power by entrusting reconciliation to the two judges, harmony will follow. Although their willingness and acceptance of the judges’ decision are the apparent means, the verse attributes reconciliation to God because He is the real cause, joining causes to their effects and giving each person his due; hence, “surely Allah is Knowing, Aware.”

The commentary maintains that the Qur’an gives primacy to sound intellect over pleasure-seeking and excessive passion, while not neglecting pure emotions—such as compassion, marital love, and enjoyment of lawful adornment and provision—so long as they conform to reason. Because Islamic law protects intellect, it prohibits what confuses its judgment or social operation, including liquor, gambling, fraudulent transactions, lying, slander, and backbiting.

On this basis, Al-Mizan argues that broad social affairs requiring intellect free from emotional influence—rulership, judiciary, and war—are entrusted to men rather than women, who are said to be more governed by emotion. It presents “Men are the maintainers of women” as God’s ordinance, confirmed by prophetic pronouncements and by the Prophet’s practice: he appointed no woman ruler, governor, or judge, and did not call women to active fighting in war.

This does not, in the commentary’s account, deny women freedom in matters not hindered by emotion, such as learning, teaching, trade, nursing, and medicine. Prophetic traditions do not prohibit these, and the Qur’an implies their lawfulness through women’s independent will and action, including ownership, management, and development of property, and their capacity to bring or testify in legal cases and therefore to appear before a judge. Their freedom, however, ends where it conflicts with the husband’s right: she must obey him in his presence, protect his interests in his absence, and any right of hers that obstructs his rights ceases.
verses.36:
Al-Mizan understands the command to worship Allah without associating anything with Him as practical monotheism: every good deed, including the benevolence enjoined here, must be done solely for God’s pleasure and the reward of the hereafter, not in pursuit of one’s own desire. The later condemnation of miserliness and charity done for display shows why: both conduct is association, since it makes wealth, praise, or another desired object equal to God. Such practical polytheism arises from forgetting the Day of Reckoning; were the Last Day truly believed, it would not be forgotten. Following desire is thus worshipping it, while sincere worship seeks God’s pleasure and reward rather than desire.

The emphatic form ihsānāʾ means doing good to parents and all the following classes to one’s utmost ability. Near of kin means close relatives. Al-Mizan takes “the neighbor of (your) kin” as the physically near neighbor and “the alien neighbor” as the more distant one; traditions narrated from the Prophet set neighborhood at forty arm-lengths and at forty houses, probably describing the two categories separately. A translator’s note, however, judges this distinction far-fetched, suggesting instead a related neighbor versus an unrelated one, and adds that such reports likely describe ordinary social usage rather than enforceable measurements. “The companion at your side” includes companions in travel, residence, and similar settings. The wayfarer, literally the “son of the way,” need not be poor, stranded, or without provisions. “Those whom your right hands possess” means male and female slaves, whom one is also obliged to treat well.

Al-Mizan explains al-Mukhtāl as one absorbed in haughty self-conceit and al-Fakhūr as boastful. Pride and boastfulness accompany excessive attachment to wealth and glory, so God does not love such a person because his heart is attached to something besides Him. The following references to the miser and the ostentatious giver respectively expose craving for wealth and for fame. The verse begins with these traits, rather than their ensuing evil acts, to make clear why they are unloved.
verses.37: Al-Mizan explains that the niggardly bid others to niggardliness through their conduct and example, even without verbal commands. Because they are wealthy, people seek their favor and imitate them, a tendency reinforced by human greed. They hide God’s bounty by acting and presenting themselves as needy: annoyed by requests for help yet afraid openly to refuse or to let attention turn to their wealth, they pretend to be poor. The verse’s “unbelievers” refers to these concealers of divine bounty; this accords with the root sense of al-kāfir, one who hides the truth by rejecting it.
verses.38: Al-Mizan explains that spending to show people is polytheism, whether in charity or any other good work, because the person relies more on people and their appreciation than on God. It is also practical polytheism: he seeks no reward in the hereafter, hoping only for the worldly return of his apparent charity. One who performs good deeds for display is Satan’s associate, and Satan is an evil associate.
verses.39: Al-Mizan says that the question is one of pity or amazement. Refusal to spend benevolently in God’s way comes from a lack of true belief in Allah and the Last Day, even if a person professes such belief. “And Allah knows them” prepares for the following verse and is more suitably read as a circumstantial clause.
verses.40:
Al-Mizan explains that mithqāla dharratin means even an injustice equal to the weight of an atom; al-dharrah may mean a small red ant or an almost imperceptible particle of dust floating in the air. The variant readings hasanatan and hasanatun mean respectively that God multiplies a good deed even if it is only that minute weight, or that He multiplies any good deed. The feminine pronoun in wa in taku may be due either to the feminine predicate hasanatan or to mithqāl’s construction with the feminine dharrah.

In context, the verse supplies a reason for regretting their failure to believe and to spend benevolently. Had they done so, although God knows them, He would not neglect or leave unrewarded even the smallest amount spent; if it were a good deed, He would multiply it. And God knows better.
verses.41: Al-Mizan refers the meaning of the witness brought from every people, and of the Messenger as witness over these, to its earlier discussion of witnessing over deeds in ... that you may be witness for the people ... (2:143), reserving further detail for a more suitable place.
verses.42:
Al-Mizan holds that “disobey the Messenger” means disobeying his administrative orders, not disobeying God in matters of sharīʿah. Their wish that the earth be levelled with them is an indirect wish for death and nonexistence, like the unbeliever’s wish to be dust.

The clause that they shall not hide any word from Allah is apparently joined to their wish and explains it. When they stand before God, none of their secrets can remain hidden: their deeds will be present, their limbs and organs will testify, prophets, angels, and others will bear witness, and God encompasses them on every side. With their evil deeds exposed, they will wish to be nonexistent. Al-Mizan adds that their false oath in On the day that Allah will raise them up, then they will swear to Him as they swear to you, ... (58:18) will be a reflex of their worldly habit of lying, not an attempt to conceal anything from God on that day.
verses.43:
Al-Mizan explains that “prayer” here means the mosque: believers must not approach it while intoxicated, until they know what they are saying, nor in a state of major ritual impurity, except while travelling, until they have washed themselves. If sick or travelling, or after coming from the privy or touching women, and unable to find water, they should use clean earth, wiping part of their faces and hands; Allah is Pardoning, Forgiving.

The mosque is called “prayer” because the clause “until you know (well) what you say” is suited to prayer, in which worshippers stand before and address God. Intoxication, which makes them unaware of their speech, is therefore improper. Since prayer is generally offered congregationally in the mosque under the Prophet’s established system, the expression also concisely conveys the rule barring one in major ritual impurity from entering it.

“Until you know (well) what you say” states the reason for forbidding liquor whose intoxication lasts until prayer-time; it does not mean that one may drink provided one is sober when praying. The ruling on major ritual impurity while travelling is explained under (5:6).
verses.44:
Al-Mizan holds that these verses were revealed about the Jews, or about people who secretly associated with them and adopted their counsel. The Jews are presented as a concrete example of those who refuse spending in God’s way and are marked by pride, boasting, niggardliness, and showiness. Although given only a portion of the Book, rather than the whole as they claimed, they chose error over guidance and wished believers to share their deviation.

The commentary explains that they appeared as sincere friends and helpers, offering advice that could seem attractive, but sought to divert Muslims from the right way by inducing them to withhold benevolence. They knew that such conduct would frustrate the believers’ progress and success. Therefore, believers must not be deceived by their apparent goodwill, obey their commands, or be carried away by their false and flattering speech. Allah knows their enmity better than the believers do, and His guardianship and help make their pretended friendship and assistance unnecessary.
