verses.46:
Al-Mizan explains “Among the Jews” as specifying either those previously described as having been given a portion of the Book or the enemies previously mentioned. Their “perverting words from their meanings” may mean altering the text by deletion, insertion, or displacement; misinterpreting the words and prophecies of Moses and other prophets, including prophecies concerning the Messenger of God and the Christ; or, more particularly, misusing words through the expressions that follow.

On the last reading, they used words normally expressing obedience and courtesy in improper, mocking ways. “We hear” conventionally implies obedience and is completed by “We hear and obey,” whereas “We hear and disobey” is disgraceful. Likewise, they said “Hear without listening!” and used “Raʿina.” The believers used Raʿina to ask the Messenger of God to attend to what they wished to say, but the Jews exploited a disrespectful sense which it reportedly bore in their language. Thus they made falsehood appear as truth and ridicule appear as politeness, twisting their tongues in order to revile the religion.

The preferable expressions—“We hear and obey,” “Listen,” and “Unzurna”—are described as better and more upright not because their expressions had any real goodness, but in comparison with the imaginary benefit the Jews supposed they gained through taunting and verbal distortion. The conditional form indicates that they will not in fact utter the words of faith.

Their curse is caused by their unbelief, not a curse consisting in unbelief itself; disbelief could itself be removed through belief. Rather, because of their unbelief, God cursed them in a manner that made them cling to faithlessness. “They will not believe except a few” may mean that only a small number will believe, or that there will be belief in which believers are few. It cannot mean an insignificant or worthless quantity of belief: belief may be deep or transient, perfect or imperfect, but is not properly called “little.” Both inward belief and outward Islam are recognized. The general curse and condemnation concern Jewish society as such, while the exception preserves the fact that a few individuals are not covered by it; it does not overturn the decree concerning that society.
verses.47:
Al-Mizan reads the address as an invitation to all the People of the Book to believe in the revealed Qur’an, which verifies what they possess, together with a threat of definite divine punishment should they rebelliously reject it. The “people of the Sabbath” were Jews who violated the Sabbath and were cursed and transformed; thus the threat of being cursed like them means metamorphosis.

“Before We alter faces then turn them on their backs” does not mean effacing physical faces. A face is what a person advances with toward his aims, and its alteration means that his direction is reversed: the more he proceeds toward what he considers worldly or religious good, the more he retreats into evil, corruption, and failure. The masculine pronoun in “or curse them,” though apparently referring to “faces,” further indicates that faces signify persons insofar as they pursue their ends. The verse therefore describes a divine management of the soul by which thought becomes crooked, truth is shunned, and falsehood is sought.

The two punishments are genuine alternatives. Alteration of faces changes the condemned people’s aims without substantially changing their bodies; the curse of the Sabbath-breakers changes their bodily form from human to animal as well as changing their aims. Although the threatened group will continue in rebellion, the indefinite plural “faces” indicates that the punishment will not encompass every individual. Its unspecified scope makes the warning effective, since each person whose conduct fits the description must fear that he may be among those punished.

The commentary rejects the view that physical faces will be turned backward in the last days or on the Day of Resurrection, because “or curse them” conflicts with it. It considers the explanation of perpetual worldly disgrace and frustrated hopes not far-fetched, but unsupported by the opening of the verse; exile and return from exile likewise do not fit its context. The interpretations may nonetheless be combined insofar as reversal from truth to falsehood necessarily deprives people of the blessings of true religion and, consequently, of the blessings of worldly life—security, ordered safety, independence, sovereignty, and fruitful success—except to the degree that religious discipline remains among them. “The command of Allah shall be executed” means that His decree cannot fail and has already been realized through their curse, divine wrath, and enduring mutual enmity and hatred.
verses.48:
Al-Mizan takes this verse as explaining the preceding command to believe in the revelation verifying the earlier Book. To reject it is to associate something with God; the resulting unforgiveness brings the worldly consequences previously threatened: altered faces and divine curse. In contrast, the similar wording in (4:116) concerns consequences in the hereafter, though each verse considered by itself can include both worldly and otherworldly consequences.

Divine forgiveness is not arbitrary, but follows wisdom. Polytheism cannot be forgiven because creation, as divine mercy, rests upon worship and servitude, and there can be no true worship with polytheism. Sins other than polytheism may be forgiven through the intercession of rightful intercessors—the prophets, the waliyys, the angels, and good deeds. The verse does not concern repentance: repentance is incompatible with continuing disbelief, and through repentance every sin, including polytheism, is forgiven.

Here polytheism includes disbelief, even where the Qur’an does not formally call the disbeliever a polytheist. Thus People of the Book who reject the revelation verifying what they possess become unbelievers and associate their inherited scripture with God, since God did not command them to cling to it in the manner they do. Similarly, one who believed in Moses but rejected Jesus in reality disbelieved in God and associated Moses with Him. This explains the wording that God does not forgive “that any thing should be associated with Him,” rather than simply saying that He does not forgive polytheists.

“To whomsoever He pleases” excludes the notion that anyone can compel or influence God’s judgment. It also means that forgiveness of sins other than polytheism is not due to every sinner: if all sinners were certainly forgiven, commands, prohibitions, sharīʿah, and the divinely ordered path of spiritual advancement would be futile. At least some perpetrators of every sin must be punished, without contradicting the general promise of forgiveness. God may forgive or not forgive sins other than polytheism, through a good servant’s intercession or a good deed, and His decision is always grounded in reason.
verses.49:
Al-Mizan distinguishes purification through good deeds, which is praiseworthy, from verbal self-praise, which is immoral even when true. The verse concerns the People of the Book, especially the Jews, whose claims to be God’s sons, beloved ones, and exclusive friends, and whose claim that the Fire would touch them only briefly, reveal the self-complacency and arrogance that prevent submission to truth and revelation. They are not called People of the Book at this point because persistent self-purification is incompatible with true knowledge of the Book.

Purifying and declaring someone pure belong exclusively to God. A person may possess excellence, but cannot rely on it or claim independence from God; all that he is and has, including every excellence, belongs to God. To attribute purity to oneself therefore amounts to associating oneself with the Lord. This self-appreciation is a fundamental evil that develops into pride and, when the person gains power, into oppression, violation of inviolable things, and attacks on others’ lives, honour, and property. When it becomes a social custom or national character, it corrupts society and destroys humanity.

God alone bestows superiority and grace and may praise His virtuous servants. In this context, divine purification principally means God’s verbal attribution of excellence, although the expression in itself can include actual purification as well. His statement that they will not be wronged “the husk of a date-stone” means that His purification is entirely true and just, without excess or deficiency; the phrase denotes something utterly insignificant.

No one should praise himself for a genuine or supposed virtue, because excellence belongs to God. Nor should one attribute excellence even to others except as God has praised them; genuine excellence is what religion recognizes as such. This does not require ignoring God-given virtues or withholding due respect: the ignorant must submit to and respect the scholar, while the scholar must not boast of knowledge. The same rule applies to every true human virtue. The commentary also rejects self-reliance as a religiously recognized virtue; the Qur’anic teaching is reliance on God and deriving strength from Him, for all power and might belong to Allah.
verses.50:
Al-Mizan explains that their claims to be God’s children, beloveds, and friends are lies against Allah, because He has not granted them such distinction. Indeed, verbal attribution of excellence to oneself is a lie against God even if the alleged excellence is real, since it treats the person as sharing with God what belongs to Him alone, although He has no partner in His Kingdom.

This alone makes self-praise a manifest sin. Sin is a blameworthy act that prevents or delays attainment of goodness; this disobedience is a branch of polytheism that keeps a person from divine mercy and leads into disbelief.
verses.51:
Al-Mizan explains al-Jibt as that in which there is no good, or anything worshipped apart from God, and al-Tāghūt likewise as a false object of worship. The verse concerns some People of the Book who supported unbelievers against believers and judged the path of the polytheists to be more correct and straight than that of the believers. They did so despite knowing that the believers followed the monotheistic religion revealed in the Qur’an, which verified their own revelation, whereas the polytheists followed idols and false deities.

By assigning a share of truth to idols and false deities, they acknowledged and believed in them, thereby committing polytheism. For this God cursed them. Reports concerning the occasion of revelation support this reading: Meccan polytheists asked some People of the Book to judge which religion was better, and they decided for the polytheists against the believers. Their having been given a portion of the Book intensifies the condemnation, since scholars of a Book exposing the falsity of idols should be furthest from believing in them.

verses.53:
Al-Mizan takes “or” as connected to the preceding discourse, not as an unrelated “rather,” nor as implying an omitted alternative concerning a superior right to prophethood. The sequence is: do they have a right to judge as they wish, a share in the Kingdom, or envy the people? This makes the three questions connected and orderly.

“The Kingdom” includes authority over both spiritual and material affairs: prophethood, mastership, and guidance, as well as people and property. The preceding judgment against the believers suggests their claim to spiritual authority, while their refusal to give people even the insignificant speck in a date-stone points to material control. The verse thus asks whether they have any share in the comprehensive kingdom God gave His Prophet. Had they possessed it, their niggardliness and evil nature would have made them withhold even the most worthless thing from people.
verses.54:
Al-Mizan treats this as the third alternative in the rebuke of the Jews for preferring the polytheists’ religion to that of the believers. At first “the people” could refer to the believers, and God’s grace to prophethood, the Book, and religious knowledge and realities. But the reference to Abraham’s progeny restricts “the people” to Abraham’s descendants; it therefore refers to the Prophet, through whom the grace received by others came. The word “people” may conventionally be used for a single person.

The statement that God gave Abraham’s progeny the Book and wisdom cuts off the Jews’ hope that this grace could be removed from Muḥammad. Abraham’s progeny may mean the Prophet alone, the Prophet with his progeny and Ishmael and similar descendants, or Abraham’s descendants through Ishmael and Isaac insofar as they include the Prophet. It cannot mean the Children of Israel alone, for that would support rather than refute the Jews’ envy. Nor can “the people” mean the believers generally: not all believers descend from Abraham, and following Abraham’s religion gives nearness to him but does not make one his descendant.

The “grand kingdom” has a comprehensive meaning, including spiritual authority, prophethood, and real mastership in guiding people, rather than mere worldly dominion. God does not characterize a kingdom as grand unless it entails spiritual superiority or religious excellence. Since prophethood and mastership are not separately mentioned alongside the Book and wisdom, they are included in the term “grand kingdom.”
verses.55:
Al-Mizan explains that some believe in Muḥammad while others turn away from him. The latter phrase may also mean that they prevent others from believing in him; on this reading, the Jews not only refused the revelation sent to the Prophet but also exerted themselves to hinder people from God’s way. Hell’s burning is threatened because they obstructed faith in the divine Book and kindled the fire of mischief against the Prophet and the believers.

The following verses explain this threat: those who disbelieve in God’s signs enter the Fire, where their skins are repeatedly replaced after being thoroughly burned so that they continue to taste the chastisement. In direct contrast, those who believe and do good deeds enter everlasting gardens with rivers beneath them, pure mates, and dense shade. The two groups are thus utterly opposed in their hereafter: gardens and shade for believers, and blazing fire and burning for those who turn away and hinder others.

verses.58:
Al-Mizan connects the command to return trusts and judge justly with the preceding condemnation of Jews who judged the polytheists better guided than the believers. The Book entrusted to them contained the divine signs and religious realities, and they had been charged to teach its knowledge rather than conceal it from those entitled to receive it. “Trusts” therefore includes not only material deposits but also spiritual trusts, such as true divine knowledge which scholars must convey to deserving people.

The Jews betrayed this trust by concealing the knowledge of monotheism and the prophecies of Muḥammad’s advent when disclosure was due. They also perverted judgment by deciding for idolatry against monotheism. The verse consequently commands people generally to restore trusts to their proper owners and to judge justly.

Although the immediate apparent meaning establishes two legal duties—returning deposits and the qādī’s obligation to judge justly—general Qur’anic legislation is not restricted to fiqh. Jurists may derive rules concerning monetary trusts and judicial cases from it, while theologians may derive from it principles concerning the foundations of religion.
verses.59:
Al-Mizan reads the verse as reinforcing Islamic society by preserving unity and removing disputes through referral to God and His Messenger. “Obey Allah and obey the Messenger” is both the basis of the sharīʿah and the premise of this referral. Obedience to God means obedience to all realities and laws conveyed through the Messenger. The Messenger must be obeyed under two divinely granted authorities: his legislative explanation, through revelation other than the Qur’an, of what the Qur’an states generally; and his administrative and judicial decisions, made by the authority God gave him. Consultation may involve the community, but the final decision belongs to the Prophet.

The repeated imperative—“obey Allah and obey the Messenger”—is not mere emphasis. It distinguishes the connotation of obedience to God from that of obedience to the Messenger, even though obeying the Messenger is in reality obeying God because God made it obligatory. The Messenger is obeyed both in what he expounds by revelation and in what he decides by divinely granted wisdom.

Ulu al-amr have no revelation, yet their judgments and orders must be obeyed as the Prophet’s are. They are omitted from the command to refer disputes to God and the Messenger because the dispute is among believers, not over their executive orders. It concerns identifying God’s ruling from the Qur’an and sunnah. Thus ulu al-amr have no authority to originate legislation or repeal a Qur’anic or sunnah rule: in judicial and general matters they disclose the decisions of God and His Messenger, while in executive matters they direct affairs within their wilāyah. Once they state what the Qur’an and sunnah require, argument ends.

Because obedience to the Messenger is commanded without condition, he cannot command what opposes God’s actual command; otherwise God would impose a contradiction. He is therefore maʿsūm, sinless and free from error. The same unrestricted wording and the conjunction of ulu al-amr with the Messenger establish their ʿismah as well. The verse contains no qualification such as obedience only when they do not command sin or when their error is not known. Such a limitation cannot be imported from the tradition, “No creature is obeyed in disobedience of the Creator,” or from analogous cases of obedience to officials or a mujtahid. A valid theory is not thereby proved to be the apparent meaning of this verse. When the Qur’an commands the less consequential obedience of parents, it expressly limits it in the case of polytheism (29:8); an essential command governing mankind’s felicity would not omit an equally necessary proviso. Since the Messenger cannot sin or judge wrongly, joining ulu al-amr with him in one unconditional obedience entails that they too cannot do so.

Al-amr here means the believers’ religious and temporal affairs, not simply a command as opposed to a prohibition. “From among you” means that they are raised from within the community; it does not mean they are ordinary believers without ʿismah. The plural ulu al-amr requires a number of such persons, but they may succeed one another, each being obeyed in his own time. This is not an improper use of a plural for a singular; it is a series of commands addressed to a plurality, like honoring the scholars of a town.

The commentary rejects the proposal that ulu al-amr are a collective of influential people—ahl al-halli wa al-ʿaqd—such as scholars, commanders, rulers, commercial and political leaders, or editors. If every member must be sinless, no such group has ever existed. If sinlessness is ascribed to the collective while members can err, it improperly makes a real attribute inhere in an abstract collective. If God merely protects their consensus from error, their case is said to resemble a mutawātir report; but this has no proof. The reported saying, “My ummah will not unite on error,” even if accepted, concerns the entire ummah, not its influential leaders, and means that right guidance will remain among the ummah, not that every collective decision of leaders is correct.

Ordinary collective deliberation cannot guarantee truth: historical experience shows that influential bodies can err. If Muslim leaders possessed an unfailing, supernatural collective protection, it would be a continuing miracle parallel to the Qur’an, and the Qur’an and Prophet would have defined its members, jurisdiction, responsibilities, and mode of operation. The community would have asked about it and invoked it in the major disputes after the Prophet, yet this did not occur; nor was the interpretation known to the early exegetes. Nor can such inerrancy result merely from Islamic training, for a whole composed of fallible judgments is not thereby infallible. The political errors, oppression, bloodshed, violations of honor and property, and neglect of religious laws that followed the Prophet further refute the alleged immunity of influential leaders.

The commentary also rejects the view that fallible leaders must be obeyed because their occasional errors are outweighed by social unity and welfare, even when their rulings reinterpret or alter religious law to meet changing circumstances. That view lets political judgment override explicit religious law and reduces Islam to a changing social system, rather than a religion with enduring beliefs, morals, and legal rules. Likewise, the suggestion that the verse concerns rulers, including unjust rulers obeyed when no alternative exists to avert harm, fails: the Qur’an forbids obedience to the unjust, oppressors, and unbelievers. A permission necessitated by fear is not an unconditional command joined to obedience to God and His Messenger. Nor can an obligation of this fundamental kind be directed to a person who does not exist or only rarely exists.

Thus ulu al-amr can only be persons within the ummah who are free from sin and error in speech and deed and whose obedience is obligatory; they can be known only by explicit divine designation, directly or through the Prophet. This accords with reports from the Imāms of Ahl al-bayt that they are ulu al-amr. The interpretations identifying them as the rightly guided caliphs, expedition commanders, or scholars fail because those groups are not sinless and because the claims lack evidence.

Against objections, Al-Mizan maintains that the sinless Imāms have been identified in the Qur’an, sunnah, verses of Guardianship and Purity, and reports such as the Ark and the Two Precious Things. Recognition is necessary for every object of obedience, whether an influential leader or an Imām; it is not a condition that removes the obligation itself. The present inability to reach a sinless Imām results from the ummah’s own conduct, not from God or the Messenger, and does not abolish the obligation. The same practical objection applies to the supposed collective leaders, who do not now govern a single united Muslim ummah.

Referral to God and the Messenger does not exclude referral to the Imām. The dispute in the verse is not a dispute with ulu al-amr or among them, nor a dispute over their executive commands; it is believers’ disagreement over religious laws. Those capable may infer the rule from the Qur’an and sunnah; otherwise, in the Prophet’s presence they ask him, and in his absence they ask the error-free Imām. No one but God and His Messenger legislates or abrogates religious law, and ulu al-amr are equal with all others in being unable to manipulate it.

The proviso, “if you believe in Allah and the last day,” strongly ties referral to faith: contravention exposes a defect of belief and the concealed disbelief of hypocrisy. “This is better and very good in the end” may indicate either referral in dispute or obedience to God, the Messenger, and ulu al-amr. Al-taʾwīl, rendered “in the end,” is the underlying good upon which the command rests and which is realized by fulfilling it.
verses.60:
Al-Mizan explains that al-zaʿm means to think or claim, whether or not the claim accords with reality, unlike al-ʿilm, knowledge that conforms to fact. Although al-zaʿm is often used of false claims, falsity is not part of its essential meaning.

Al-tāghūt originally denotes exceeding proper bounds and is commonly used for an exceedingly rebellious oppressor or tyrant who rejects divine worship and transgresses the limits set by reason or sharīʿah; hence it is applied to whatever is worshipped besides God. “What has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you” means the revelations sent to God’s messengers, an expression suited to the issue of referring disputes to the divine Book and its laws. Their command to deny tāghūt is therefore contained in those revealed books.

“Have you not observed” answers why obedience and referral to God, the Messenger, and those vested with authority were commanded, while expressing pity at people who claim belief in the revealed books but seek tāghūt’s judgment. Those books were sent to judge human disagreements, as stated in Mankind was but one nation; so Allah sent the prophets as bearers of good news and warners, and He sent down with them the book with truth, that it might judge between the people in that in which they differed ... (2:213). Resorting instead to one who rebels against divine religion abandons God’s books and laws despite the command to deny tāghūt. Their conduct follows Satan’s influence and serves his desire to lead them into a far-reaching error.
verses.61:
Al-Mizan explains that taʿālaw, “come,” is an imperative derived from “to rise,” and that the call to come to what God revealed and to the Messenger means coming to God’s law and to the one who judges by it. Although they are summoned to both the Book and the Messenger, the verse addresses the Messenger alone when describing their utter aversion.

These people profess belief in revelation and therefore cannot openly reject God’s Book, but their open turning away from the Messenger exposes their hypocrisy. Accepting God’s command while hesitating over or rejecting the Messenger’s command is an unqualified form of hypocrisy; God and His Messenger cannot be separated in this way.
verses.62: Al-Mizan takes the verse as a warning that turning away from God and His Messenger and seeking the judgment of tāghūt will certainly bring misfortune, caused by that very conduct. It also foretells their subsequent excuse: overwhelmed by the consequences, they will come swearing by God that their recourse to a judgment other than the divine Book and the Messenger was intended only to bring social good, concord, and an end to disagreement. God knows best.
verses.63:
Al-Mizan holds that this verse rejects the hypocrites’ excuse. Though God does not expressly describe the contents of their hearts or call their motive evil, His instruction to the Messenger to turn aside from them and admonish them sufficiently exposes their claim; He would not command this concerning one whose intention and account were true.

The Messenger is to address them with words that penetrate their hearts, make them recognize the evil of their conduct, and show them that their hypocrisy, once exposed, will bring God’s wrath and punishment.
verses.64:
Al-Mizan regards the verse as a comprehensive refutation of the hypocrites’ resort to tāghūt, their turning from the Messenger, and their sworn claim to seek good and concord. All of this is disobedience to the Messenger, whatever excuse accompanies it. Every messenger is sent to be obeyed by God’s permission; the Prophet’s obedience is therefore unconditional and is itself obedience to God, as the verse later declares: whoever obeys the Messenger, he indeed obeys Allah.

One must not suppose that obedience to God alone is required and that the Messenger may be bypassed whenever someone thinks the same public good can be achieved otherwise. This does not make the Messenger a partner in God’s worship; rather, God Himself authorized his obedience. The question sometimes put when the Prophet decided an important matter—whether it was God’s order or his own—reflects the mistaken attitude being refuted.

Instead of futile oaths and excuses, they should have returned in repentance: after wronging themselves by disobeying and turning away from the Messenger, they should have sought God’s forgiveness and asked the Messenger to seek forgiveness for them. Then they would have found God Oft-returning to mercy and Merciful.
verses.65:
Al-Mizan explains that, though the verse first rebuts hypocrites who claim belief while seeking Satan’s judgment, its general language extends to all who imagine that merely accepting revealed teachings and commands constitutes faith. True faith requires complete outward and inward submission to the Prophet’s judgment: one must neither turn from it in conduct nor feel straitness in the heart when it conflicts with one’s desire. Since God empowered the Messenger to judge by what He taught him, resentment of the Prophet’s judgment is resentment of God’s judgment.

This submission to the Messenger is submission to God’s legislative and creative decree. It is a stage of faith that brings higher virtues, especially surrender to God’s command, and frees one from inward constraint and verbal or inward objection. Although the immediate wording concerns judgment in disputes, its meaning is comprehensive: it covers the commands of God and His Messenger, legislation and creation, and every judgment, system, and action proceeding from the Messenger. A person who truly believes cannot reject or be troubled by any of these; such resistance is, to that extent, associating others with God, as in And most of them do not believe in Allah without associating others (with Him), (12:106).
verses.66:
Al-Mizan understands “they would not have done it except a few of them” as describing the community collectively: as a society, they would not obey commands that seem grievous because they touch what hearts cling to, such as life and home. The exception of a few prevents the mistaken impression that not even one true believer would obey; it does not alter the collective judgment.

Accordingly, “Kill yourselves or go forth from your homes” concerns collective killing by the group and its collective departure from towns and villages, not each person’s killing himself or leaving his individual house. It resembles therefore turn to your Creator (penitently), and kill your people [lit.: yourselves] (2:54), which is likewise addressed to a group.

The change from “prescribed” to “admonished” shows that divine commands are, in their reality, compassionate directions to human good and bliss. Had they obeyed, it would have been better for them in all worldly and otherworldly matters, for the latter follows from the former, and it would have strengthened their hearts and souls through true faith.
verses.67: Al-Mizan explains that the promised great reward follows their strengthening through firm faith. Its indefiniteness corresponds to the unrestricted promise that obedience would be “better for them.”
verses.68: Al-Mizan states that God would guide those who obey to the straight path, whose meaning was explained under Guide us to the straight path (1:6).
verses.69:
Al-Mizan explains that the promise concerns obedience to both God and the Messenger. Those who obey will be with the people upon whom God has bestowed favors—the prophets, truthful ones, witnesses, and good ones—but will not thereby become prophets or members of those ranks. They will enjoy their company, as the final phrase, “and excellent are these as companions,” indicates. The favored are the people of the straight path, as in Guide us to the straight path, the path of those upon whom Thou hast bestowed favors (1:6–7), and the favor specifically denotes mastership and guardianship.

Prophets receive revelation and news of the unseen, though people know of them only through their social achievements. Al-shuhadāʾ in Qur’anic usage means witnesses to people’s deeds, not martyrs in battle; the good ones are those worthy of divine favors.

Al-Siddīq is an intensive form of al-sidq, truth, which pertains to both speech and action. Truthful action conforms to one’s words and manifests firm belief, while truthful speech conforms to reality. Because speech is itself an action, one truthful in action speaks only what he knows to be real: both his report and what it reports are true. Such a person acts only upon what he knows to be right rather than desire, says only what he knows to be true, thinks only what is true, sees realities as they are, speaks truth, and acts rightly.

The ranks are therefore ordered: prophets, who are leaders and chiefs; truthful ones, witnesses of realities and people’s deeds; witnesses, who witness deeds; and good ones, qualified to receive divine favors. Rafiqā is an accusative of specification, meaning excellence in companionship and explaining its singular form; alternatively, it may be circumstantial, meaning that each is an excellent companion.
verses.70:
Al-Mizan says that the distant demonstrative dhālika and the definite predicate al-fadl together magnify the promised grace, as though it were grace in its totality. The verse concludes with God’s knowledge because the preceding ranks of faith and belief can be known only by divine knowledge.

The commentary also notes that these verses repeatedly shift between first, second, and third person without impairing their coherence. Believers are first directly addressed and then spoken of in the third person; God shifts from the third person to the first-person plural and back; and the Messenger shifts from third-person reference to direct address and back again. These ten shifts follow the context and preserve the connected flow of the discourse.
verses.71:
Al-Mizan explains that “take your precaution” means taking the means of protection—especially arms—and making complete preparation for jihād before proceeding against the enemy. The conjunction “then” makes going forth consequential upon this preparation.

To go forth “in detachments” means that groups depart separately, whereas going forth “in a body” means moving together. These are not optional alternatives for the fighters: a small detachment suits a lesser enemy, while a large enemy requires the believers to go out together, with equipment proportionate to the operation.

In view of the following verse about those who hang back, the command warns believers not to lay down their arms, slacken their effort, or become lax in jihād. Such inertia lowers morale and zeal for truth and forfeits the opportunity to cleanse the earth of disbelief and polytheism.
verses.72:
Al-Mizan takes “among you is he who would certainly hang back” to mean that the tardy people were among the believers addressed by the verse, not merely hypocrites who professed faith outwardly. The surrounding exhortations to believers to fight, together with their quoted words—such as calling absence from misfortune a benefit from Allah and asking why fighting was ordained for them—show that some measure of faith existed in their hearts.

Some exegetes identify them as hypocrites who were counted among believers because of social affiliation, common lineage, or their inclusion in the laws of sharīʿah after uttering the two witnesses. Al-Mizan rejects this as contrary to the Qur’an’s apparent meaning without valid reason. It attributes the interpretation to an excessive good opinion of every early Muslim who met and believed in the Prophet, an opinion challenged by both historical conduct and the Qur’an’s severe remarks about them.

No human community is wholly composed of unwavering believers; reports make an exception for the martyrs of Karbalā. The early Muslim society likewise contained hypocrites, people with spiritual diseases, followers of desire, and people of manifest weakness, despite being an excellent society led by the Messenger of God, pervaded by faith, and governed by religion. The Qur’an describes its collective virtues, but makes promised forgiveness and great reward conditional for individuals upon faith and good deeds (48:29).

The misfortune in the verse is being slain or wounded; the one who held back calls his absence a divine benefit because otherwise he too would have suffered.
verses.73:
Al-Mizan explains “grace from Allah” as spoils of war, wealth, and similar gain. The verse dramatically portrays the weak faith of those who stayed behind: although believers are united by faith in God and His revelation more strongly than by family, guardianship, allegiance, or friendship, they react to the believers’ gain like strangers wishing they had shared in it.

They call worldly wealth “a mighty good fortune,” yet regard the believers’ being slain, wounded, or otherwise distressed as a misfortune. This reversal discloses the weakness of their faith and their lack of felt fellowship with the believers.
verses.74:
Al-Mizan explains that those who “sell this world’s life for the hereafter” exchange worldly life for the hereafter. Following the rebuke of those who hold back from jihād, the verse recalls that believers accepted Islam by making this exchange, as expressed elsewhere: Surely Allah has bought of the believers their persons and their properties for this, that they shall have the garden (9:111).

Fighting in Allah’s way yields one of two good outcomes: being slain in His way or overcoming His enemy, and either brings a great reward. By omitting defeat and retreat, the verse indicates that a fighter in Allah’s way does not retreat or flee.

Being slain is mentioned first because martyrdom has the greater and more certain reward. A victorious fighter is entitled to a great reward but may forfeit good deeds through later sins and evil acts; martyrdom ends worldly life and begins the hereafter, leaving no such risk. Thus the martyr certainly receives the reward in full, whereas the victorious fighter may only hope to receive it fully.
verses.75:
Al-Mizan explains that “the weak” is joined to the name of Allah: the question urges believers to fight both in Allah’s way and for weak believing men, women, and children. For sincere believers, God’s call alone should suffice; for others, the suffering of their weakened fellow believers should also stir them to fight with zeal and a sense of honor.

Islam initially negates relationships based on blood or other causes, retaining faith as the fundamental bond; after conversion, other relationships are restored within Islam. A Muslim must therefore sacrifice wealth and life for a Muslim brother joined to him by faith, and for Muslim male, female, and child relatives. Such sacrifice for their safety is itself in Allah’s way.

The weak are true believers, humiliated, oppressed, and tortured by polytheists. Their prayer that Allah remove them from a town “whose people are oppressors” refers generally to the people’s oppression and torment of them, not merely to those people’s wrongdoing against themselves. They appeal not to clan, leaders, or people, but to their true Lord and seek from Him a human guardian and helper—namely the Prophet and the brave believers with him.

Al-Mizan further distinguishes rightful honor from blameworthy bigotry. The human instinct to defend what one holds inviolable, including women, children, dignity, and national honor, is praiseworthy when it follows truth and blameworthy when unjustified. Islam accepts the principle required by nature but removes its base and worldly impulses, directs it toward God, and permits it to operate in its original settings within monotheism. It thus makes honor for one’s people and rights serve God’s pleasure, purifies it from corrupt desire and emotion, and turns it from conflict toward concord and peace. Its regulated forms are harmonious manifestations of monotheism and following truth.
verses.76:
Al-Mizan says that the verse compares the motives of the two sides in fighting: believers fight in Allah’s way, which leads to and depends on God, while unbelievers fight in Satan’s way. This superiority gives believers further reason to fight.

By following Satan, the unbelievers have left Allah’s guardianship and have no guardian or friend but Satan, the friend of polytheists and those who worship other than God. Satan’s strategy is weak because it is the way of tāghūt, opposed to God’s way, while all power and strength belong to God alone. This weakness encourages believers to fight Satan’s friends, though it does not deny Satan’s hold over those who follow their desires.
verses.77:
Al-Mizan explains “Withhold your hands” as refraining from fighting. When the Muslims initially suffered the unbelievers’ oppression, they were impatient to fight; God instead commanded prayer and zakāt so that religion and faith might first be established firmly. Fighting before they possessed the requisite strength and arms would have endangered the whole structure of religion.

The verse censures those same believers: formerly eager for combat when unable to meet the enemy, a party of them became afraid of merely human opponents when fighting was ordained, fearing them as—or more than—they should fear Allah. Their question, “why hast Thou ordained fighting for us,” is apparently joined to this fear. It may either disclose their inward state or report their actual words.

Their request for postponement to a “near end” does not mean merely a little more life before being killed. Even a natural death would leave them only a short life; they resent being exposed to a quicker death. Their attachment to this vanishing worldly provision makes them prefer it to the lasting, real life of the hereafter.

God therefore answers that the provision of this world is short, while the hereafter is better for one who guards against evil, and no one will be wronged even the husk of a date-stone. The commentary takes “for him who guards (against evil)” as indirectly rebuking them: as believers they ought to be people of piety, through which the good of the hereafter is attained, rather than prefer the world’s brief life to the dignity of jihād and martyrdom. They need not fear injustice from God.
verses.78:
Al-Mizan explains that the “lofty towers” are an example for every secure refuge from calamity: death decreed by God cannot be escaped. Thus, staying away from the battlefield, or the absence of a command for jihād, would not have kept these people safe from death.

The benefit and misfortune mentioned are those encountered as the Prophet established religion through jihād: victories and war-booty on one side, and death, wounds, and hardship on the other. The same weak believers credited the former to Allah but blamed the latter on the Prophet, treating him as an ill omen or charging him with bad judgment and mismanagement. Their words may have been spoken explicitly or inferred from their conduct.

The commentary rejects attempts to make the verse concern Jews, hypocrites, or both, because its context identifies the speakers with the weak believers already under discussion. Their attitude resembles that of earlier peoples toward their prophets, including those who ascribed evil fortune to Moses and those with him. God’s reply, “All is from Allah,” refutes their division: all such events are arranged by God alone, to whom all things submit in their existence, continuance, and coming occurrences. The closing question expresses astonishment at their failure to grasp this plain reality.
verses.79:
Al-Mizan says that the verse addresses the Prophet in the singular in order to explain a reality that applies generally to human beings, including prophets and others. Things naturally welcomed—health, bounty, security, and comfort—are from Allah. Things naturally disliked—disease, humiliation, poverty, and mischief—are, in this respect, caused by man and are not attributed to God; this does not contradict the universal sense in which good and evil both emanate from God, considered from another angle.

The Prophet’s distinction is solely that God sent him as a Messenger, charged with conveying the message. He has no independent power to bring people misfortune or to withhold good from them. The statement therefore indirectly refutes those who called him an ill omen and said of misfortune, “This is from you”; Allah is sufficient as witness.
verses.80:
Al-Mizan takes “Whoever obeys the Messenger, he indeed obeys Allah” as reaffirming that the Prophet was sent only as a Messenger. Obedience to him on account of his Messengership is obedience to Allah; one who turns away is not under the Prophet’s custody. “Whoever obeys the Messenger” points to the reason for the declaration, and the wording preserves the same theme through its shifts between addressing the Prophet and speaking of the Messenger.

The commentary then distinguishes al-Hasanah—good, merit, benefit, and beauty—from al-Sayyiah—evil, sin, ugliness, and misfortune. Beauty first appears in the perception of a well-proportioned human form and is extended to mean a thing’s conformity with its natural purpose; ugliness is the lack of that conformity. The same measure applies to actions and social qualities: justice, appropriate beneficence, education, and sound advice accord with human felicity, while injustice and transgression do not. Some such values are enduring, such as justice and injustice, whereas the appropriateness of particular acts varies with time, place, and circumstance.

Al-Mizan rejects the claim that ethical values are wholly relative. Its error is to confuse the fixed meaning of justice with its changing practical applications. People may alter their social customs, but do not accept being called unjust; even when they excuse an oppressor, they do not concede that oppression is justice. Good and evil are consequently relative to human perfection and felicity, but this relation may be permanent in some cases and changing in others. Help, for example, is good when given to one who deserves it and bad when given to one who does not.

Good is positive, while evil and ugliness are privative: a thing or action is evil insofar as it lacks conformity with felicity. Apart from this relation, the same event or act may receive opposite descriptions. An earthquake devastating a community is evil for it but good fortune for its enemies; a calamity is good, in the religious view, when it strikes unbelievers who spread mischief, but evil when it strikes a believing community. Food is lawful when it is one’s own and unlawful when taken without permission; intercourse is lawful in marriage and sinful outside it. The physical act is the same, but its relation to divine command differs.

According to the Qur’an, every thing other than God is His creation, and God has made good every thing that He has created: “[God] Who made good every thing that He has created (32:7).” Created existence is therefore inherently good and harmonious with its intended purpose; no creature can defeat God’s purpose or weaken Him. In this comprehensive creational sense, every blessing and even every calamity are attributable to God, which is the sense of “All is from Allah” in (4:78). A calamity seems evil only when viewed from the other angle—its incompatibility with the nature, interest, or felicity of the person or thing harmed by it.

The Qur’an nevertheless attributes a person’s misfortune to that person: “Whatever benefit comes to you, it is from Allah, and whatever misfortune befalls you, it is from yourself (4:79).” Misfortune is not a created evil. It is the withholding of mercy or generosity where what is created fails to accord with a recipient, and this withholding is called calamity from the standpoint of the one harmed. God grants and withholds according to the recipient’s capacity, condition, and measure: “He sends down water from the cloud, then the valleys flow (with water) according to their measure (13:17).” Each thing seeks what agrees with its own condition.

For human beings, in matters subject to free choice, happiness and distress are therefore closely tied to their choices. Following the proper path leads to happiness, while deviation brings turmoil and distress. Pure intentions and righteous actions preserve or affect blessings; insincerity and evil actions lead God to withhold mercy. Thus, “And whatever affliction befalls you, it is on account of what your hands have wrought, and (yet) He pardons most (of your faults) (42:30).” This does not imply that God has forgotten that all things are His good creation: what comes to a person is good in itself, but becomes that person’s misfortune because it conflicts with that person’s aims and desires through that person’s wrong choice. God does not initiate evil, harm, or misfortune for the person.

Though 4:79 directly addresses the Prophet, its meaning includes all people and applies to social as well as individual affairs. A society has an existence, will, and choice distinct from those of its members; accordingly, later generations may bear the consequences of predecessors’ evil and even innocent members may share a society’s punishment, unlike the case of individual responsibility. The Prophet’s wounds and the Muslims’ losses at Uhud illustrate this: attributed to the community, they resulted from its disobedience to God and His Messenger; attributed to the sinless Prophet personally, they were a divinely ordained trial in his mission, a grace that raised his spiritual rank.

Benefits may in one respect be connected to people’s faith, patience, and good deeds, but no creature can reach a good or its intended end unless God grants it power and guidance. Hence all good is from God both because every created thing is good and because He owns all good, while others possess it only when He gives it to them. Evil, as such, is not created and cannot be attributed to God; it is the name for His withholding of mercy in consequence of what people’s hands have done. The commentary refers the distinct question of attributing obedience and disobedience to God to its discussion of (2:26), and concludes that the issue becomes clear only by keeping separate the different senses of good and evil, bounty and punishment, and the distinct realities of individuals and societies.
verses.81: Al-Mizan explains that the nominal statement “Obedience” has an omitted subject: “Our business is obedience,” meaning total obedience. When called to jihād, these people profess such obedience, but after leaving the Messenger’s presence some secretly plan by night either to do the opposite of their own assurance or of his command. God therefore orders the Messenger to disregard them and trust in Allah, who suffices as protector. The commentary finds no evidence that they are hypocrites; the context concerns the believers of weaker faith mentioned earlier.
verses.82:
Al-Mizan treats the verse as an interrogative exhortation to meditate on the Qur’an. Although al-Tadabbur may mean repeatedly pondering a single verse or considering verses one after another, the latter is more fitting here, because the argument concerns the Qur’an’s freedom from discrepancy. One should assemble all verses relevant to a subject—Meccan and Medinite, decisive and ambiguous—and see that its earlier and later parts verify one another. No verse negates another, and there is no unevenness in its style, meanings, or themes.

This complete harmony demonstrates that the Qur’an is from God. Everything other than God, especially human beings, is subject to movement, change, gradual development, and a continual pursuit of perfection. A person normally judges later opinions and works better than earlier ones; even a long book, poem, or lecture will usually vary in quality among its parts. Such variation is intrinsic to created things. Thus “many” in “many a discrepancy” is explanatory, not restrictive: if the Qur’an came from other than God, discrepancies would necessarily be abundant by the nature of created production; the verse in fact negates every discrepancy, few or many.

The meditator finds a book encompassing human affairs: genesis and resurrection, creation and existence, virtues, social and personal laws, stories, lessons, and admonitions. Revealed piecemeal over twenty-three years amid war and peace, ease and hardship, day and night, it retained its unmatched rhetoric, knowledge, wisdom, and legal coherence. Its details agree with its foundations, and its laws rest on pristine monotheism, whose divinely given wisdom appears in the particulars of the sharīʾah. Natural intelligence must therefore recognize it as the speech of God, the One, the Subduer, not the work of one affected by time and development.

The commentary further infers that the Qur’an is accessible to normal understanding and is not subject to abrogation, nullification, completion, refinement, or anyone’s judgment and control. Such things would entail alteration, which its freedom from discrepancy excludes. Consequently, the sharīʾah of Islam continues until the Day of Resurrection.
verses.83:
Al-Mizan condemns the thoughtless spreading of reports of security or fear. The verse indicates that adverse propaganda endangered the believers by leading them to disobey the Prophet; the following command that he fight even without helpers confirms this. The reports were false rumors brought to Medina by agents of the disbelievers to create discord and sap the courage of believers of weaker faith. God saved them from following the Satans who circulated such discouragement.

The commentary identifies the episode with the Lesser Badr. After Uhud, the Messenger called the believers to meet the disbelievers, while others sought to frighten and turn them away by reporting that the polytheists had assembled against them. This was Satan’s plan through his friends. The present verse accordingly censures that same conduct among the weak believers.

Referral in this verse differs from referral to Allah and the Messenger in a disputed legislative matter. News concerning security and fear cannot be referred to God’s Book for a factual decision; it must be referred to the Messenger and those in authority, who can determine whether it is true or false and right or wrong. Istinbāt is drawing a matter from ambiguity into clarity and knowledge. “Those among them who (can) draw out the truth” may mean the Messenger and those in authority, which is the obvious reading: if investigation serves religion and society, they discern the reality. It may instead mean the believers who seek the matter’s truth and learn it from them.

Al-Mizan holds that ulu al-amr has the same meaning as in (4:59) and rejects four alternatives. Commanders of fighting detachments govern only particular troops in particular battles and cannot resolve rumors affecting general security. Scholars possess expertise in traditions, jurisprudence, recitation, and theology, not necessarily in the political affairs whose mishandling can bring collective ruin, humiliation, killing, or captivity. Identifying ulu al-amr with Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthmān, and ʿAlī has neither Qur’anic nor definitively accepted traditional proof: if the command applied only during the Prophet’s life, their special status should have been publicly known then; if it continued after him, it would have expired with them, though the verse gives no such limitation. Nor can it mean influential people who “tie and open,” for no formal body of ahl al-halli wa al-ʾaqd existed in the Prophet’s time; identifying them with his consultees fails because he consulted hypocrites as well. A report related by al-Nasāʾī, al-Ḥākim, who declares it correct, al-Ṭabarī, and others identifies ʿAbdu al-Rahmān b. ʿAwf among those exposed with his group by the preceding admonition, so such persons could not be the proper authorities for these sensitive reports. The remaining and preferred interpretation is that ulu al-amr are the Twelve sinless successors of the Prophet.

The concluding warning apparently also concerns Lesser Badr: Abū Sufyān sent Naʾīm b. Masʾūd al-Ashjaʾī to Medina with reports of a vast hostile force so that the Muslims would not go to Badr. Following Satan meant accepting this report and failing to go. The exception “save a few” naturally denotes the Prophet and the few nearest to him who initially remained steadfast, while most people wavered, made excuses, and tried to avoid departure before others eventually joined them.

The commentary rejects other explanations of the exception. It rejects restricting divine grace and mercy to guidance through the order of referral, with a few naturally pure believers excepted, because the wording concerns a favor already completed and gives no basis for that restriction. It also rejects the notion that only weaker believers needed such grace, since the Qur’an affirms that none would become pure without God’s grace and mercy, and even the Prophet required divine strengthening. It likewise rejects interpretations that make grace and mercy the Qur’an and the Prophet, or victory, and those that attach the exception to “they spread it” or “draw out the truth,” or treat it as a merely verbal exception meaning that all would have followed Satan. It calls these explanations literary affectation and distortion.
verses.84:
Al-Mizan explains taklīf as the burdensome imposition of duty; citing Majmaʾ al-bayān, it explains tankīl as an exemplary punishment that deters the offender and warns others. The “then” in the command to fight follows from the preceding believers’ apathy toward jihād. The Messenger is commanded to fight the disbelievers even if alone, without being disheartened by their refusal: he is accountable only for his own deed, not for their duty. His responsibility toward others is to rouse the believers to ardor, in the hope that Allah may restrain the disbelievers’ fighting.

The commentary preserves the force of “maybe”: ʿasā expresses hope, whether in the speaker, the addressee, or the circumstances, and need not mean certainty merely because God uses it. The verse thus further rebukes those sluggish toward jihād. The Prophet is to leave such people to their choice and not be discouraged by them, while urging the believers; whoever wishes may answer the call, and whoever wishes may disobey God and His Messenger.
verses.85:
Al-Mizan explains that al-Nasīb and al-kifl both mean a share, even though the latter is translated as “responsibility.” Intercession is mediation intended to remedy a deficiency or obtain a benefit; consequently, the intercessor necessarily shares in the good or evil that results, receiving reward or blame.

The verse therefore warns believers to consider carefully what they support and prohibits interceding for a harmful cause. Those who pleaded that the double-faced polytheists should not be fought should have understood that an unchecked small evil can grow and spread until it becomes destructive. Bad intercession includes pleading for people engaged in oppression, transgression, hypocrisy, polytheism, and mischief on earth.
verses.86: Al-Mizan holds that every greeting must be answered with one better than it or with its equivalent. Although this is a general command, its present context particularly concerns an offer of peace made to Muslims.
verses.87: Al-Mizan explains that the certain gathering on the Resurrection Day grounds the preceding commands concerning good and bad intercession and the response to greetings. God will gather all people and reward or punish them for accepting or rejecting His commands; believers therefore must observe these injunctions rather than turn away from greetings offered to them.
verses.88:
Al-Mizan connects this verse to the warning that one who makes a bad intercession shares its evil. The believers had divided over the double-faced polytheists: one party wished to fight them, while the other pleaded that they not be fought. This intercession would leave a tree of mischief to grow with the polytheists’ strength until it bore its destructive fruit.

God had returned these people to straying as punishment for their evil deeds after they had emerged from it. Intercession cannot guide one whom God has left to stray, for such a person cannot find the path of guidance. The final statement is addressed directly to the Prophet rather than the believers, showing that those who interceded lacked the understanding required to grasp this reality; otherwise they would not have interceded. The Prophet, by contrast, possessed true and clear knowledge of it.
verses.89:
Al-Mizan explains that these people not only disbelieved but advanced further in disbelief until they wanted the believers to disbelieve and become like them. Muslims are forbidden to take them as friends unless they leave their homes and migrate in Allah’s way.

“But if they turn back” means that they are to be asked to migrate: if they do so, they may be taken as friends; if not, the believers are to seize and kill them wherever found, and neither befriend them nor seek their help.
verses.90: Al-Mizan identifies two exceptions to the preceding command to seize and kill those who turn back. The first consists of those who reach a people bound to the Muslims by a covenant. The second consists of disbelievers unwilling either to fight the Muslims or to fight their own people; they withdraw from the believers and offer peace, being neither with them nor against them. Both groups are excluded from that command.
verses.91:
Al-Mizan reads the verse as a forecast of another group resembling the second group previously excepted. They seek security from both the Muslims and their own people, but they are hypocrites, so their covenants and offers of peace cannot be trusted. The verse replaces the former group’s positive conditions—withdrawal, non-fighting, and an offer of peace—with negative ones: if these people do not withdraw, offer peace, and restrain their hands, they are to be seized and killed. This warns believers to remain on guard.

The commentary then explains that every people has customary greetings, such as bowing, nodding, hand gestures, or removing a hat. Such forms generally express submission, abasement, and a subordinate’s relation to a superior; they are remnants of slavery and of idolatry nurtured by that system. Since Islam aims to erase idolatry and its rites, it instituted a greeting free of these defects.

The Islamic greeting, al-Salām (peace, greeting), declares that the greeted person is safe from transgression against his rights and has nothing to fear from the greeter concerning the natural freedom bestowed by the Creator. Mutual security in life, honour, and property is the first requirement of a cooperative social order, and every social trouble arises from one of these three matters. God therefore prescribed this salutation when people meet, taught the Messenger to use it even with believers although he was their chief, and commanded him to offer peace to others as well.

Al-Mizan notes that “Peace” was already used in pre-Islamic Arabia. Lisan al-ʾArab reports that, alongside other formulas, it signified mutual peace and the absence of fighting; Islam then directed people to use the formula of peace alone and to say it openly. Its appearance in the Qur’anic accounts of Abraham, including his greeting to his father [that is, uncle] and his exchange of peace with the messengers, shows that it was, like hajj, a remnant among the Arabs of Abraham’s pure religion. God also uses peace as His greeting to prophets and messengers, describes it as the greeting of the honoured angels, and makes it the greeting and speech of the people of the Garden.
verses.92:
Al-Mizan explains that al-Khatāʾ, without elongation, means the opposite of intentional killing. “It does not behove” negates any demand or inclination in a believer to kill another believer within the sanctuary of faith, while also stating a legal prohibition: God has never permitted, and will never permit, such killing. The exception for mistake is a real, joined exception, not an isolated one. It removes the prohibition where the killer did not intend to kill a believer—for example, where he intended no killing at all or believed the victim to be an unbeliever whose killing was justified—but does not authorize unintentional killing. The contrary claim that a joined exception would imply that accidental killing is commanded or allowed is therefore unfounded.

One who unintentionally kills a believer must free a believing slave and pay blood-money to the victim’s heirs, unless they remit it as alms. If the slain believer’s heirs belong to hostile fighting unbelievers, only emancipation is required, since such an unbeliever does not inherit from a believer. If the slain believer belongs to a people bound to Muslims by any covenant, including al-dhimmah, both blood-money and emancipation are required; the priority given to blood-money in the wording stresses fulfilment of the agreement. One unable to free a slave must fast two consecutive months.

The fast is a merciful penance for one financially unable to emancipate a slave. Alternatively, “a penance from Allah” may describe all the prescribed reparations: they cleanse the killer from the stain of accidental killing, warn against carelessness, replace society’s lost free person by adding another free person, and compensate the slain person’s family through blood-money. Al-Mizan concludes that Islam regards freedom as life, slavery as a kind of murder, and full indemnity as equivalent to a man’s average earnings. The exact legal definitions of intentional and unintentional killing, emancipation, indemnity, heirs, and covenant are to be found in sunnah and works of fiqh.
verses.93:
Al-Mizan defines al-Taʾammud as intending an act in its particular aspect. Since one act may have several aspects, it may be intentional in one respect and unintentional in another: shooting at what one thinks is an animal is intentional hunting but, if it is a man, unintentional killing; striking a child to discipline him may likewise result in unintentional killing. Intentional killing of a believer therefore requires intending to kill him, knowing that the act will kill, and knowing that the victim is a believer.

The verse threatens such a killer with abiding eternally in hell, God’s wrath and curse, and a great punishment. Yet the broader wording of Surely Allah does not forgive that any thing should be associated with Him, and forgives what is besides that to whomsoever He pleases (4:48), and surely Allah forgives the faults altogether (39:53), may qualify this threat. Thus it does not establish an irreversible final decree, and forgiveness through repentance or intercession remains possible.
verses.94:
Al-Mizan explains that marching forth “in Allah’s way” means going out for jihād, and that al-Tabayyun here means investigating in order to distinguish a believer from an unbeliever. One must not deny the faith of a person who offers the believers’ greeting of peace; some reciters read al-Salām, meaning submission or surrender.

The prohibition against coveting worldly goods condemns greed for wealth and war-booty. The gains with God are superior because the gains of the hereafter are limitless and enduring. Believers themselves formerly shared this worldly tendency before God bestowed faith and turned them toward what is with Him; therefore the repeated command to investigate stresses their duty to distinguish properly between believer and unbeliever.

The commentary holds that the verse evidently concerns an actual killing of a believer, though it does not show that it was intentional. Apparently, a believer mistakenly killed a polytheist who had greeted him with peace, suspecting that he professed Islam merely to save his life. The admonition is that Islam judges by outward appearance, while what lies in hearts is known only to God, the Subtle, the Knower. Killing one who presents himself as Muslim without proper inquiry resembles the conduct of one pursuing wealth and booty on petty, unacceptable pretexts. Having received true faith and guidance, believers must abandon the motives and conduct of the days of ignorance.
verses.95:
Al-Mizan explains that al-Darar is a bodily defect—such as blindness, lameness, or sickness—that prevents participation in jihād. Striving with property means spending it to overcome the religion’s enemies, while striving with one’s person means fighting in God’s way.

The comparison concerns believers who held back when their participation was not vital because the Muslim force was already sufficient. Thus, although God promises good to all, the verse exhorts believers to hasten to jihād and other excellence. Those physically unable to fight are exempted, and their good intention may compensate for their inability; nevertheless, fighting, martyrdom, or victory over God’s enemies remains a great distinction over non-participation.

“And to each Allah has promised good” may include the strivers and those who held back, whether injured or uninjured. “Good” may mean a good outcome or recompense. The assurance prevents a holder back from supposing that the preceding preference of the strivers has nullified his faith and other good deeds. Yet believers must not be content with this promise and become indolent: the strivers receive a far greater recompense, namely high degrees, pardon, and mercy.

The changing descriptions of the strivers are deliberate. At first, jihād is fully qualified as striving in Allah’s way with property and persons, because it has value only when undertaken for God rather than desire, through sacrifice of wealth and life. The second mention retains property and persons to show the reason for superiority before the promise of good to all; the final mention needs no qualification because the matter has already been made clear.

Likewise, the singular “rank” does not conflict with the later plural “degrees.” In the first occurrence, darajah merely specifies that their superiority is one of rank, without deciding whether it consists of one degree or many. In the second, “(High) degrees” explicates, or stands for, the “great recompense” bestowed on the strivers: it declares that their reward comprises many high ranks from God. Al-Mizan rejects as unsupported the attempts to assign the singular and plural respectively to disabled and able holders back, worldly and otherworldly benefits, or spiritual status and the grades of the Garden.

In “(High) degrees from Him,” the pronoun apparently refers to God, as “pardon and mercy” describe the degrees and plainly come from Him; alternatively, it may refer to the preceding great recompense. These ranks are manifestations of divine pardon and mercy. Mercy is the bestowal of bounty, while pardon removes impediments to receiving it; each rank is mercy in itself and, by preparing for a higher rank, is pardon in relation to that higher rank. The conclusion, “and Allah is Forgiving, Merciful,” therefore accords with the promised pardon and mercy.
