verses.97:
Al-Mizan notes that tawaffāhum, translated “cause to die,” may be an aorist, originally tatawaffāhum with one “ta” omitted for ease of pronunciation, or it may be read as a past tense.

The injustice of those whom the angels cause to die is the harm they inflicted on themselves by turning from the divine religion and neglecting its practices while living among polytheists, unable to learn religious tenets and fulfil what belief in God’s lordship requires. This fits the Qur’anic description of the unjust as those who hinder from Allah’s way and seek to make it crooked. The angels’ question, “In what state were you?” asks about the state of their religion and, as traditions indicate, points generally to questioning in the grave.

Their reply, “We were weak in the earth,” is not a direct answer but an excuse: powerful polytheists had oppressed them and prevented them from learning sharīʾah and acting upon it. But their weakness resulted from remaining under polytheist domination. Since God’s earth beyond that territory was vast and the oppressors had no authority there, they could have left and freed themselves through emigration. Their condition was therefore due to their own wrong choice, not genuine weakness.

“Was not Allah’s earth vast (enough), so that you should have emigrated therein?” is a rebuke; the first question may also be a simple enquiry, since it is addressed elsewhere to both the unjust and the pious, but the second is certainly reproachful. Calling it God’s earth may indicate that He gave the earth its vastness before calling people to faith and good deeds. Because the earth is described as vast, emigration is said to occur “therein”: one migrates from one of its places to another. After this questioning, God judges that their abode is hell, an evil resort.
verses.98:
Al-Mizan holds that the exception for weak men, women, and children is isolated and defines genuine weakness. Unlike those previously condemned, these people cannot free themselves from oppression by emigration. They have no hīlah—no means or device to attain their end—and find no way out of their enemies’ grasp. The “way” includes both an actual route, such as the route to Medina, and every means by which oppression may be ended.

The verse shows that ignorance of religious tenets is excused by God only when it results from an inadequacy or weakness to which the ignorant person has not contributed. Ignorance of religion and inability to establish its rites is otherwise an inequity not forgiven; the exception extends to all who truly cannot avert their danger or ignorance.

This genuine inability has two forms. First, a person may lack access to religious instruction, be forcibly prevented from observing sharīʾah, and be unable to emigrate to join Muslims because of mental weakness, sickness, physical disability, poverty, or similar causes. Second, a person may be unaware of the established truth, without hostility or aversion to it, and would accept it if he knew it; circumstances beyond his control may have overpowered his thought and left him in oblivion. Such a person too lacks the means and way to escape ignorance.

The unrestricted wording covers unavoidable ignorance and oblivion, in accordance with: Allah does not impose upon any soul a duty but to the extent of its ability; for it is (the benefit of) what it has earned, and upon it is (the evil of) what it has wrought (2:286). What a person does not know is beyond his ability just as what he is forcibly prevented from doing is beyond it. The criterion is that he must not have caused the inability: ignorance arising from negligence or wrong choice is his sin, whereas ignorance caused by factors outside his power is neither intentional opposition to truth nor arrogance.

A genuinely weak person is thus empty-handed, having earned neither good nor evil; his judgment rests with his Lord. The following promise that Allah may pardon them, indicates this awaiting of the divine command, and His mercy is ahead of His wrath.
verses.99:
Al-Mizan explains that the weak have earned no sin because they could not remove their ignorance. Yet failure to earn good is itself sufficient for infelicity, and every person—good, evil, or empty-handed—remains in need of God’s pardon, which effaces the traces of evil and infelicity. The verse therefore offers them hope of pardon.

Although it says “it may be” that Allah will pardon them, the immediately following declaration that Allah is Pardoning, Forgiving makes it almost certain that forgiveness will encompass them on the Day of Judgment. Their separation by exception from the unjust, whose abode is hell, confirms this hope.
verses.100:
Al-Mizan explains murāghaman, rendered “place of refuge,” through its association with rubbing a nose in dust, an idiom of displeasure, embittering, and spite. One who emigrates in Allah’s way—seeking His pleasure through complete religious commitment in knowledge and practice—will find many places to which he may turn if prevented from observing religion in one place. By leaving, he frustrates and angers the adversary, and he will also find abundant resources.

The addition of “many a place of refuge” makes “in Allah’s way” necessary: the refuge is particularly needed by one who wishes to continue on God’s way. The verse consequently continues the admonition of believers living among polytheists, urging them to emigrate and assuring them of provision. Emigrating to Allah and His Messenger means going to the place of Islam, where one can learn the Book of God and the sunnah of His Messenger and act by them. “Death overtakes him” is a metaphor for death, possibly sudden death, catching a person; “his reward is surely incumbent upon Allah” similarly conveys the certainty of a good and abundant recompense. The ending, “and Allah is Forgiving, Merciful,” reinforces this assured promise of full reward.

The commentary reads verses 95–100 as classifying professed believers by residence in the place of Islam or of polytheism and assigning each group its recompense. Among believers in the land of Islam are strivers with property and persons, those who hold back without disability, and those held back by disabling injury: good is promised to all, but the strivers have superior ranks. Among those living in the land of polytheism are the unjust who do not emigrate and whose abode is hell; genuinely weak men, women, and children who have neither means nor a way out and are not unjust; and those who set out emigrating to Allah and His Messenger but die en route, whose reward is incumbent upon God.

The purpose is first warning, then encouragement to emigrate to the land of Islam, assemble there, strengthen Islamic society, cooperate in righteousness and piety, and raise the word of truth, tawhīd, and the flag of religion. Though initially describing Arabia between the Prophet’s emigration to Medina and the conquest of Mecca, the classifications apply in every age. Dār al-Islām was Medina and its surrounding Muslim-dominated regions, where Muslims could freely observe their religion despite the presence of polytheists and others. Dār al-shirk was Mecca and its surroundings, dominated by idol-worshippers who prevented Muslims from practising their religion and subjected them to severe oppression in the hope of turning them from Islam.

The governing principle remains that a Muslim must live where he can learn Islamic belief, perform religious rites, and follow sharīʾah; he must emigrate from a country where he cannot learn religious realities or find a way to live by Islamic principles. Present labels of Dār al-Islām and Dār al-Shirk do not determine the matter, since their real meanings may have been discarded and religion reduced to citizenship or Islam to a name. Qur’anic consequences follow the reality of Islam, not its name, and Muslims must follow the spirit of its rules rather than merely their letter.
verses.101:
Al-Mizan explains that, in journey, shortening the prayer incurs no sin or impediment. Although “there is no blame on you” appears to grant mere permission, its legislative context indicates obligation, just as the same expression in connection with going round Safā and Marwah does not remove the compulsory character of al-Tawāf. Legislation need only disclose that an order has been laid down, without detailing every aspect of it.

The fear mentioned is a proviso on the ruling: al-Fitnah, when connected with disbelievers and polytheists, denotes such atrocities as killing and torture, and here means fear that the enemy will attack and put Muslims to the sword. Thus the Qur’an states the case in which shortening was first ordained, namely fear of the disbelievers’ harm. The rule was subsequently extended to every legal journey, even without fear, through the sunnah of the Prophet.
verses.102:
Al-Mizan explains the verse as prescribing the congregational prayer of fear through the example of the Prophet acting as its imām. In danger, the whole body of Muslims must not pray together: one party prays behind him while carrying its arms, and the other guards them and their possessions. Once the first party has prostrated and completed its prayer, it goes to the rear to relieve the guards; the second party then comes forward to pray with the Prophet, likewise taking its precaution and arms.

“Take their precaution and their arms” treats precaution metaphorically as a defensive weapon. The arrangement is necessary because the disbelievers await Muslims’ inattention to their weapons and luggage in order to launch a sudden united attack. Rain or sickness permits laying down arms, but does not permit neglecting precaution, since the disbelievers seek the Muslims’ weak points. Allah has prepared a disgraceful chastisement for the unbelievers.
verses.103:
Al-Mizan holds that remembering Allah while standing, sitting, and reclining enjoins continuous remembrance in every state and place. In context, becoming secure contrasts with journeying; it means returning home, and “keep up prayer” therefore means offering the full four rakaʾāt, whereas the prayer in fear and danger was shortened.

Prayer is a prescribed and imperative ordinance. Although al-Mawqūt may indicate an obligation at fixed, known intervals, the commentary argues that, in this context, its apparent import is especially that prayer is a confirmed, permanent obligation: it cannot be abandoned, waived, altered, or replaced by an alternative, unlike fasting, which may at times be changed to redemption.
verses.104: Al-Mizan explains that believers must not weaken in pursuing the enemy. Both sides suffer pain alike, so believers are not at a disadvantage; rather, they can hope for victory and forgiveness from Allah, their guardian. Their enemies have no guardian and no hope to encourage and impel them toward their aim. Allah knows what benefits His servants and is Wise in His commands and prohibitions.
verses.105:
Al-Mizan explains judging between people as resolving their disputes through judicial decisions, and presents this as a principal purpose for which the Book was revealed. The verse grants the Messenger divine authority to judge: beyond teaching him laws and rights, God creates in his mind the sound opinion by which he can determine which rule applies to a particular contested case.

The command not to be an advocate for the treacherous is joined to the command to judge. An advocate speaks for a claim, and defending dishonest people would annul the right of those entitled to it. Because the command to judge is unrestricted, treachery here likewise means every transgression against others’ rights, not merely breach of a deposited trust.
verses.106:
Al-Mizan takes al-istighfār here in its literal sense of seeking concealment or protection: the Prophet is commanded to ask God to shield him from the natural tendency to incline to desire or violate another’s rights, so that he neither supports the treacherous nor comes under their influence. This is not because he committed, or was about to commit, a sin. Rather, although maʾsũm (protected, sinless), he always needs God’s protection and aid in subduing desire.

The later assurance that the plotters cannot harm him establishes that they could not induce injustice, partiality, or the following of desire in his judgments. It would be gross injustice for a judge to distinguish between strong and weak, friend and foe, believer and unbeliever, or near and distant. This protection concerns praiseworthy and blameworthy acts of obedience and disobedience; it does not mean that every judicial verdict rendered under procedural rules invariably coincides with the hidden reality. Rules such as requiring proof from the claimant and an oath from the defendant generally distinguish truth from falsehood, but not in every case.

The commentary therefore rejects the view that the Prophet sought forgiveness because he had intended to defend the treacherous man against a Jew, since this would imply that the plotters had influenced him harmfully. The commentary adds that acting unfaithfully toward one’s soul may mean that sin’s consequences return to the sinner; and, since believers are like one soul and share responsibility for protecting one another’s property, usurping or stealing a believer’s property may be treachery toward oneself. The wording describes persistent, deeply rooted treachery and sinfulness. Thus judges must not support persistent deceivers, whether their treachery is small or great; but someone treacherous in one matter may still be defended when he is right in another case.

verses.108:
Al-Mizan sees this verse as further indicating that the connected verses concern the same event described in (4:112): a concealed crime, such as theft, whose blame could be shifted onto an innocent person. “They hide themselves from men” does not mean that they can literally conceal themselves from God; rather, it apparently alludes to their lack of shame before Him.

They secretly plotted by night so that they could deny involvement before people, speaking what displeased God. God’s being with them at that particular time exposes their conspiracy, while His encompassing all that they do gives the general reason they cannot escape Him, including when they committed the crime.
verses.109: Al-Mizan explains that the question exposes the futility of pleading for treacherous people. Even if such advocacy benefits them in this worldly life, it has no value before God; in the hereafter, where they will truly need an advocate and protector, no one will plead their case, manage their affairs, or explain away their misdeeds.
verses.110:
Al-Mizan reads the verse as an invitation to the treacherous to return to God and seek forgiveness. “Evil” and “injustice” may distinguish harm done to others from injustice ascribed to one’s own soul, or may indicate an ascent from a lesser to a graver sin; God knows better.

Together with the next two verses, it describes sin from three angles: the sinner himself bears and records his sin, yet may repent and find God Forgiving, Merciful; sin cannot be transferred to another through false accusation; and accusing an innocent person after committing a fault or sin adds a fresh calumny and manifest sin to the original offense.
verses.111: Al-Mizan treats this verse as a preamble to the prohibition of falsely accusing another. Every sin is committed against the perpetrator’s own soul and is written in his own account, not in that of the person he accuses, even if that person undertakes to bear it. God is Knowing of the actual sinner and Wise: He holds no one responsible except the one who committed the crime and does not place its burden upon another.
verses.112:
Al-Mizan notes al-Rāghib’s view that al-khatīʾah commonly concerns an unintended result, sometimes arising from a lawful cause and sometimes from an unlawful one. The commentary, however, argues that al-khatīʾah is an adjective used as a noun whose faʾīl form suggests a settled and enduring mistake. Originally it denoted an unintentional error such as manslaughter, but its sense expanded to acts a person should not intend if he retained natural uprightness, including every disobedience and its effect.

Because this verse attributes al-khatīʾah to earning, that is, wilful action, it means an intentional fault—an act a right-minded person ought not to have intended—not a merely inadvertent error. Sin is an act whose harmful effects deprive a person of goods and virtues and degrade him socially, such as drinking liquor, gambling, or theft. Thus “fault” and “sin” are distinct yet both are wilful: the verse concerns one who commits an enduring fault, such as unlawful murder or theft, then throws its blame upon an innocent person.

Al-ramiyy, rendered “accuses,” literally means shooting an arrow; describing calumny as a burden forms a metaphor. The false accuser shoots the innocent victim and thereby loads himself with a crime he cannot cast off, one that bars him from good throughout life. The differing names for disobedience in these verses—sin, fault, evil, injustice, treachery, and misleading—each suit its particular context.
verses.113:
Al-Mizan understands the group’s attempt to mislead the Prophet as their effort to induce him to defend the treacherous people for whom they pleaded; this fits the people of Abū Tuʾmah. Their design harms only themselves, for every sin is a form of delusion, and cannot harm the Prophet in knowledge or action.

God’s revelation of the Book and Wisdom, and His teaching the Prophet what he did not know, are the basis of al-ʾIsmah (sinlessness, infallibility). Al-ʾIsmah is a distinctive divine knowledge that prevents sin and error. Ordinary beneficial knowledge and virtues may usually restrain their opposites, but can be eclipsed when another faculty or desire overpowers awareness; al-ʾIsmah, by contrast, can never be overpowered. It rules the other faculties according to its wisdom and so fully guards its bearer from error and straying. This knowledge is not the ordinary sort acquired from teachers.

The Book and Wisdom are a first category of divine knowledge: revelation sent down to the Prophet, including the cognitions beneficial in this world and the next, and the Book revealed to settle human disagreements. “He has taught you what you did not know” is a second category, distinct from that revelation: a particular knowledge created by divine inspiration in the heart, without an angel’s mediation, through which the Prophet forms judgments in particular litigations on the basis of his own divinely guided opinion. Traditions report that the Prophet and the Imāms possess the Holy Spirit, which supports them and protects them from sin and error; the commentary connects this with the Spirit in (42:52) and, in relation to the Imāms, with (21:73).

The commentary consequently rejects interpretations that reduce the Book and Wisdom to the Qur’an and its commandments, or to the Qur’an and sunnah, and identify the further teaching simply with the sharīʾah, unseen knowledge, or stories of earlier prophets. The concluding statement recalls the greatness of God’s favor upon the Prophet.
verses.114:
Al-Mizan defines al-najwā as secret counselling or whispered talk, derived from being alone with someone; it may also denote those who whisper. The verse resumes the condemnation of their night-time plotting, but extends it to secret consultations at any time. Likewise, the subsequent warning concerns hostility to the Messenger whether or not it follows secret consultation.

The exception is isolated: there is good in counselling that enjoins charity, goodness, or reconciliation. Calling such secret counsel an “enjoinment” is metaphorical. Charity is included within goodness but is mentioned separately because it is its most prominent and perfect example and naturally calls for confidential discussion.

Secret counsellors therefore fall into two classes. Those who seek God’s pleasure by urging goodness or reconciling people receive a mighty reward. Others secretly plan hostility to the Messenger and follow a way other than that of the believers; God leaves them to their chosen course and makes them enter hell.
verses.115:
Al-Mizan explains al-mushāqqah as metaphorically taking the opposite side of another; hostility to the Messenger after guidance has become clear is therefore disobedience to him. Following other than the believers’ way clarifies that hostility, because the believers’ unified way is obedience to God and His Messenger. It is the path of piety, mutual cooperation in goodness, and freedom from the disobedience and social friction that divide the Islamic community.

To turn such a person to what he has himself turned to means that God lets him continue upon the path he chose, apart from the believers’ way. This abandonment in the world and his entry into hell in the hereafter are parts of one divine decree; hell is the evil final resort.
verses.116: Al-Mizan takes this verse as explaining the preceding threat: hostility to the Messenger is associating something with God. Disobedience to God and His Messenger is disbelief and, in other words, polytheism, which God does not forgive. The clause that He forgives what is other than this to whom He pleases completes the statement while emphasizing the enormity of hostility to the Messenger.
verses.117:
Al-Mizan explains “females” as denoting passivity and susceptibility to influence. The verse calls idols and everything worshipped besides God “females” because they are created, acted upon, and powerless to bring about what their worshippers seek. Their femininity thus signifies the utter passivity of every creature in relation to the Creator. This is preferable to restricting the expression to particular goddesses such as Lāt, ʿUzzā, and Manāt, since some beings worshipped besides God are male.

“Calling” here metaphorically means worship, since people worship a deity by calling on it to fulfill their needs. Worshipping anything other than God is in reality worshipping the rebellious Satan, because it is done in obedience to his suggestion. Al-Marīd means one stripped of every good.
verses.118: Al-Mizan explains God’s curse on Satan as his removal from mercy, which accounts for his being called rebellious. Satan’s claim to take an appointed portion of God’s servants points to his assertion that he will lead people astray except the purified servants. Yet even those who stray remain God’s servants: they cannot discard that servitude, and God remains their Lord, deciding concerning them as He wills.
verses.119:
Al-Mizan reads Satan’s leading astray as a general statement followed by examples: he induces worship of other than God, sin, and vain desires that distract people from their obligations; he commands the slitting of cattle’s ears, an Arab practice of the Days of Ignorance by which certain camels and bullocks were made unlawful to eat; and he commands alteration of God’s creation. Thus he encourages people to prohibit what God has made lawful.

Alteration of God’s creation may include castration, other mutilations, sodomy, and lesbianism; possibly, it means more broadly opposing natural law and abandoning the upright religion. Obeying Satan’s commands is calling upon him and counts as taking him for a guardian instead of God. Yet Satan possesses no true guardianship: God alone is the guardian, even if someone chooses Satan as his guardian, and this choice brings manifest loss.
verses.120: Al-Mizan explains the manifest loss of taking Satan as guardian as exchanging real happiness and the perfection proper to creation for false promises and imaginary desires. Satan’s promises are his direct temptations, while vain desires arise from those temptations and captivate the mind through imagined beauty. The verse calls the promises, rather than the desires, deception. The final outcome for those who follow them is hell, from which they will find no refuge.
verses.121: Al-Mizan explains the manifest loss of taking Satan as guardian as exchanging real happiness and the perfection proper to creation for false promises and imaginary desires. Satan’s promises are his direct temptations, while vain desires arise from those temptations and captivate the mind through imagined beauty. The verse calls the promises, rather than the desires, deception. The final outcome for those who follow them is hell, from which they will find no refuge.
verses.122:
Al-Mizan contrasts Satan’s deceptive promises with God’s true promise: believers who do good will enter everlasting gardens beneath which rivers flow. The shift to the proper name “Allah” and to third-person pronouns marks the greatness of the matter, while “We will make them enter” indicates that believers will soon stand before God, their guardian, who does not conceal Himself from them.

The following verse returns to the issue of litigants who expected their profession of Islam to oblige God and His Messenger to favor them regardless of right and wrong. It joins such Muslims to the People of the Book, who likewise imagined privileged standing before God. These are vain desires, mental fictions without reality: recompense depends on deeds, so evil earns evil and good earns good.

“Whoever does evil, he shall be requited with it” is general, encompassing prescribed worldly punishments and punishment in the hereafter. No guardian or helper—not even the Prophet, an Imām, or the honor of Islam and religion—can avert the punishment God has prescribed for wrongdoing, in this world or the next, except as the next verse states.

verses.124:
Al-Mizan explains that entry into the garden is conditioned on faith, for the reward corresponds to good deeds and an unbeliever has no good deed to his credit. Yet the phrase “whoever does from good deeds” broadens the promise: “from” indicates some good deeds, so the garden is promised to every believing person who performs some good. What he leaves undone or the sins he commits may be remedied by repentance or intercession, since God forgives what is other than associating partners with Him to whom He pleases.

The verse expressly includes males and females without distinction. It repudiates ancient religious and social claims that women’s virtuous acts earn no reward, or that women are inherently deficient and receive less than men. Both sexes equally deserve divine grace, and “they shall not be dealt with a jot unjustly” means that women, like men, receive their full shares without either excess or deficiency.
verses.125:
Al-Mizan presents these verses as answering an implicit question: if merely calling oneself Muslim or belonging to the People of the Book does not ensure benefit or protection from the consequences of one’s acts, what is the honor of religion and faith? Religion’s goodness remains certain: the best religion is complete submission to God, doing good to others, and following Abraham’s upright, natural faith. Abraham was the first to embody this submission, beneficence, and upright religion, and God took him as a friend.

Divine friendship, however, is not like human friendship, which can override right and wrong and permit favoritism or despotism. God owns all that is in the heavens and earth and encompasses everything, while nothing encompasses Him. Unlike earthly rulers, whose authority depends upon and can be overcome by their subjects and rival groups, God surrenders none of His freedom or power. The closing declaration of His universal ownership and encompassing power establishes this distinction.

verses.127:
Al-Mizan explains al-fatwā and al-Futyā as a reply, or the opinion contained in a reply, concerning difficult matters; when attributed to God here, it is God’s decision. Read with the earlier verses of the chapter, this verse was apparently revealed after them in response to general questions about the unfamiliar Islamic laws governing women’s inheritance and marriage, not specifically questions about orphan girls.

“Allah makes known to you His decision concerning them” means that the right to decide belongs to God, not the Prophet, and that God had already conveyed His ruling in the earlier revelations. “And that which is recited to you in the Book” is joined to “them,” as al-Farrāʾ allows, and refers to the earlier-revealed rules concerning female orphans; al-tilāwah includes reciting the words and explaining their meaning. The alternative reading of al-fatwā as explanation is possible, but the other proposed grammatical constructions are arbitrary and unsuitable for Divine speech.

The female orphans mentioned were deprived under a prevailing custom: guardians took both them and their property, marrying a beautiful girl to enjoy her beauty and wealth, but refusing either to marry an unattractive girl or let another man marry her, thereby retaining her property. “What is appointed for them” is the Divine Decree inherent in human creation: the right to marry at the proper age and to manage one’s own property. Preventing either is deprivation of what God appointed. “While you desire to marry them” means while you are averse to marrying them, with ʿan understood as omitted. “The weak among children,” joined to female orphans, were likewise neglected and denied inheritance because they could neither ride nor fight in defence of women.

The command to deal with orphans equitably extends beyond female orphans and weak children to every orphan and every aspect of an orphan’s affairs, including property. God’s knowledge of every good deed both encourages obedience to these rules, which are for people’s own good, and warns against violating them.
verses.128:
Al-Mizan holds that this ruling, though not part of the original enquiry, is relevant to women’s affairs. It applies when a wife fears—not only when she has actually suffered—ill-usage or desertion, so reconciliation should begin as soon as its signs appear. The reconciliation intended is that the wife may forgo some or all of her matrimonial rights in order to preserve affection, harmony, and the marriage; reconciliation is better.

Avarice, al-shuhh, is ingrained in human nature to protect self-interest and avert loss. Thus the wife may be reluctant to surrender rights such as clothing, maintenance, accommodation, and conjugal relations, while a husband wishing to separate may withhold affection and harmony. They therefore incur no blame if they settle by one party’s relinquishing rights.

The commentary addresses the final admonition especially to men: they must continue to do good and avoid evil, remembering that God knows their conduct. They must not oppress women in domestic life or frustrate them until they abandon their due rights merely to preserve family peace.
verses.129:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse further clarifies the earlier command, “But if you fear that you will not do justice (between them), then (marry) only one.” Exact justice is the precise middle between extremes, and is beyond human power in marital relations because the inclinations of the heart, especially love, are not fully controllable. The husband must nevertheless not incline wholly to one wife and leave another “in suspense”: she receives no attention as a wife, yet is not free to marry another.

Practical justice is wājib (necessary): a husband must treat his wives equally and fulfil their rights without excess. Doing good to all of them, without dislike or ill-treatment, is sunnah; this was the Messenger of God’s conduct with his wives. The prohibition of total inclination shows that the verse does not deny every possibility of justice. What is unattainable is perfect, exact justice without any excess; what the law permits is practical justice, in which slight inclinations are tolerated.

Al-Mizan therefore rejects the claim that these verses prohibit polygamy. The qualifying prohibition itself, the Prophet’s sunnah, polygamy practised in his presence, and the uninterrupted Muslim practice all refute that reading; to make the permission to marry “two and three and four” a merely imaginary, inapplicable supposition would reduce Divine speech to a riddle.

The closing words press men to seek reconciliation whenever discord appears. Reconciliation belongs to piety, and piety brings God’s forgiveness and mercy, reinforcing the preceding declaration that reconciliation is better and the exhortation to do good and guard against evil.
verses.130: Al-Mizan explains that if husband and wife divorce, God will render each independent of the other through His Ampleness in matters connected with marriage, including harmony, intimacy, maintenance, and clothing. Neither has been permanently reserved for the other; separation does not mean that either can never find another spouse, since marriage is a widespread human practice to which people are naturally inclined. God’s being Ample-giving and Wise, and His ownership of whatever is in the heavens and earth, explain His power to make both free from want.
verses.131:
Al-Mizan says that the verse strongly enjoins piety throughout every stage and circumstance of marital life, as it had been enjoined on those given the Book before this community. Obedient piety is gratitude for Divine favours; abandoning God-consciousness is either open disbelief or hidden disbelief in believers who disobey God.

If people neglect this command, their disbelief neither harms God nor makes Him need their piety: all that is in the heavens and earth belongs to Him, and He is Self-sufficient, Praise-worthy. The three consecutive repetitions of God’s ownership serve different purposes: the first explains why He can make separated spouses free from want; the second answers “if you disbelieve” by declaring His independence from them; and the third begins the new subject that explains the following warning, “If He pleases, He can make you pass away.”
verses.132: Al-Mizan explains God’s ownership as His protective governance of His servants’ affairs. He is sufficient as Protector and needs no assistance. If He is displeased with a people’s deeds, He can make them pass away and replace them with others, or hold them back while others advance; this connects the verse to the following warning: “If He pleases, He can make you pass away O people!”
verses.133:
Al-Mizan reads the verse in light of the command of piety addressed both to this ummah and to the People of the Book before it. Since God is Self-sufficient and owns all things, failure to obey His command does not affect Him. If people do not worship Him and adhere to piety as He wills, He can hold them back and bring forward others who will do what pleases Him. The verse thus concerns the possible replacement of impious people by pious ones.

Al-Baydāwī reports in his tafsīr that, when this verse was revealed, the Messenger of God patted Salmān’s back and said, “Surely they are his people.” Al-Mizan regards this report as supporting this interpretation. It rejects the contextual applicability here of the view that the verse means God may destroy humanity and replace it with other people or another creation, though that explanation may fit: Do you not see that Allah created the heavens and the earth with truth? If He pleases He will take you off and bring a new creation. And this is not difficult for Allah (14:19-20).
verses.134: Al-Mizan says that one who abandons piety and Divine enjoyment in pursuit of worldly reward is confused, since both worldly and otherworldly reward are in God’s hand. Others understand the verse as urging people to seek the higher reward, or both rewards, rather than the lower alone. More apparently, and God knows better, it means that the rewards and felicity of both worlds are with God; therefore even one seeking only worldly felicity must strive to draw near to Him. Real felicity cannot be attained without fear of God and piety, which are obtained only through the religion He has ordained. Religion is the exclusive path to true felicity and happiness, for no reward can be attained unless God grants it; He is Hearing, Seeing.
verses.135:
Al-Mizan explains al-qist as justice: to stand with it is to enforce and maintain it fully, without being diverted by desire, sentiment, fear, greed, or similar motives. Such justice is the nearest and most perfect means of following and preserving truth; truthful testimony is one of its consequences.

Although the verse concerns the rule of evidence, it first sets out the broader ideal of maintaining justice and then applies it to testimony. A person can bear witness for God’s sake only by becoming a maintainer of justice. Testimony is for God when it is given truthfully to demonstrate and revive truth, as indicated by the prohibition against following low desires and thereby deviating.

Testimony must not be altered or concealed because it harms the witness, parents, or near relatives. This applies whether the testimony is directly against them—for example, against one’s father in a dispute—or harms them indirectly.

The dual pronoun in “them both” refers to the rich and the poor as alternative conditions of the same person, who may be rich at one time and poor at another, not to an actual plurality. God is nearer to the rich in his wealth and to the poor in his poverty. Thus, neither a rich person’s wealth should induce partiality nor a poor person’s need induce one to twist the truth for his benefit. One must testify for God and leave their care to Him, who is more merciful to their circumstances. His requiring truth and justice is itself mercy: when justice is established and truth made manifest, humanity attains felicity, the rich are strengthened, and the poor’s condition improves.

Though a rich or poor person may sometimes gain from distorted or withheld evidence, in the long term it weakens truth, kills justice, enlivens oppression, and strengthens falsehood and injustice, an incurable disease that destroys humanity. The warning against low desires therefore identifies the danger of abandoning truth and justice by failing to testify for God’s sake; it may also mean, do not follow low desires in order to deviate from truth.

Swerving in testimony means twisting it, while turning aside means withholding and concealing it. According to another recitation, “wa in talū,” the phrase means that if people are charged with giving testimony, whether they fulfil that duty or turn aside from it, God knows what they do and will recompense them.
verses.136:
Al-Mizan explains the renewed command to believe as an order for believers to extend their faith to all its detailed, mutually connected objects: Allah, His Messenger, the revealed Book, angels, previous Books, messengers, and the last day. God’s knowledge and power entail creation, guidance to felicity, resurrection and recompense; these in turn require messengers who bring glad tidings and warnings, and Books that settle disputes and explain creation, resurrection, sharīʿah, and law.

Faith in any one of these realities is incomplete without faith in all of them. Accepting some and rejecting others is disbelief when openly expressed and hypocrisy when concealed. A believer may enter this hypocrisy by separating from believers, drawing near to unbelievers, and endorsing their accusations, objections, or mockery against religion and its people; the following verses therefore describe and threaten such hypocrites.

The commentary rejects, as unsuitable to the context, the interpretations that the command means merely inward faith corresponding to outward profession, steadfastness in an existing faith, or an address specifically to believing People of the Book; the last is the least suitable. In the latter clause, the conjunction “and” means “or”: disbelief in any one of Allah, His angels, His Books, His messengers, or the last day is remote error, not only disbelief in all of them collectively. Other Qur’anic verses likewise declare disbelief in any one of these essentials to be disbelief.
verses.137:
Al-Mizan first observes that, read by itself, the verse concerns those who repeatedly apostatize: belief followed by disbelief, renewed belief, renewed disbelief, and then an increase in disbelief. So long as this condition remains, they are not forgiven or guided, because their profession of faith is an unserious display and they treat the divine command as a plaything. Yet this is the normal course, not an absolute denial of every possible exception: one who truly believes and remains firm may be forgiven. The related passage (3:86-90) shows that repentance is accepted after apostasy when joined with amendment, whereas the repentance of those who increase in unbelief is not accepted. Their repeated apostasy after witnessing the Messenger’s truth and receiving clear proofs manifests deeply rooted obstinacy, arrogance, and oppression; consequently, return and repentance are normally not expected from them.

In its context, however, the verse apparently supplies the reason for the preceding declaration that disbelief in any essential of faith is remote error, and it applies to the hypocrites threatened in the following verses. Its precise application follows the interpretation of the preceding command to “believe.” If that command calls for inward faith corresponding to outward profession, the alternating belief and disbelief describes hypocrites who say one thing to believers and the opposite to unbelievers. If it commands steadfastness, it describes repeated apostasy. If it addresses the People of the Book, it may refer to belief in Moses, disbelief through calf-worship, belief in ʿUzayr (Ezra) or Jesus, disbelief in him, and increased disbelief through rejecting Muhammad and his revelation.

But on Al-Mizan’s preferred reading—faith must encompass all its detailed realities—the verse explains the hypocrite’s condition. One who leaves the believers’ society, keeps intimate company with unbelievers, attends their gatherings, and confirms their calumnies and mockery of true religion and its leaders, appears a believer among believers but becomes an unbeliever by endorsing falsehood among unbelievers. Continuing in this way increases disbelief until it is rooted in him. His unstable condition also ordinarily prevents repentance, since even remorse does not endure. Repentance is nevertheless accepted if he repents with a firmness that changing circumstances and desires cannot shake; hence the stringent conditions later stated: repentance, amendment, holding fast to Allah, and sincerity in religion to Him. And God knows better.
verses.138:
Al-Mizan takes the verse as a threat against hypocrites characterized by taking unbelievers as guardians instead of believers. This trait is not confined to people wholly devoid of inward faith: some believers, including some in the Prophet’s time, maintained secret and intimate relations with unbelievers or cut themselves off from the believers’ society.

The commentary therefore finds some support for understanding the hypocrites here as believers who preferred unbelieving friends and guardians to believers. The subsequent warning not to sit where Allah’s communications are denied and mocked, although addressed to believers, threatens such hypocrites. Likewise, the statement that they remember Allah only a little indicates that they did remember Him, which would not describe those who had no faith in their hearts at all.
verses.139: Al-Mizan reads the question as a negative interrogation: they do not truly obtain honor from unbelievers, for all honor belongs to Allah alone. Honor proceeds from sovereignty, and sovereignty belongs only to God, who gives and removes kingdom and exalts and abases whom He pleases (3:26).
verses.140:
Al-Mizan connects this prohibition with the earlier command in “The Cattle” (6:68) to withdraw from those engaged in false discourse about Allah’s communications until they change the subject. Although that Meccan verse addresses the Prophet in the singular while this Medinan verse is addressed more generally, it shows that some Qur’anic addresses directed to the Prophet are intended for the whole ummah.

The reason for not sitting with those who deny and mock Allah’s communications is that remaining with them in that state makes one like them. Accordingly, Allah will gather hypocrites and unbelievers together in Hell.
verses.141:
Al-Mizan identifies another trait of the hypocrites: they keep connections with both believers and unbelievers, waiting to profit from whichever party gains advantage. When believers attain victory, they claim fellowship in order to share in the gains; when unbelievers have an opportunity, they claim that they had mastery over them and restrained them from the believers’ faith, in order to claim a share of their gains as well.

The believers’ success is called a “victory,” perhaps because Allah has promised it, while the unbelievers’ success is called merely a “chance,” indicating its insignificance. For, despite temporary success, Allah has promised ultimate victory to believers and is their Guardian; this may also explain why victory is ascribed to Allah but the unbelievers’ chance is not.

Though addressed to believers, the judgment on the Day of Resurrection includes hypocrites and unbelievers. Allah will judge in favor of believers and against unbelievers, and will never give the latter a way against the former; thus unbelievers have no hope of triumph on the last day. The declaration may also extend to this world: believers will remain victorious so long as they fulfill the requirements of faith, as in: And be not infirm, and be not grieving, and you shall have the upper hand if you are believers (3:139).
verses.142:
Al-Mizan explains al-Mukhādaʾah as continuous or intensified deception. The hypocrites seek to deceive Allah—that is, the Prophet and the believers—by feigning faith, remaining near believers, and attending their gatherings in order to gain worldly benefit through unreal belief and deeds. Yet Allah is deceiving them in recompense: He leaves them free to pursue these showy acts and evil intentions without hindrance, so that their very hypocrisy becomes the means of His requital.

Their sluggish, ostentatious prayer and scant remembrance of Allah are further marks of hypocrisy. Prayer is the highest act of worship through which Allah is remembered. Had their hearts truly inclined to their Lord, they would pray attentively and eagerly, not for people to see them, and would remember Allah often.
verses.143:
Al-Mizan, citing al-Ṭabrisī in Majmaʿ al-bayān, explains mudhabdhab as something suspended and moving pendulously between two extremes without attachment to either. This precisely describes hypocrites: they move between faith and disbelief, belonging exclusively neither to true Muslims nor to open unbelievers.

Their wavering results from Allah’s causing them to err from the path; having been led astray, they cannot find the true way.
verses.144:
Al-Mizan explains that the verses forbid believers to prefer friendship with unbelievers to friendship with believers, because Allah counts such conduct as hypocrisy and threatens hypocrites with the lowest stage of the Fire, where they have no helper. Al-sultān means proof. Al-darak denotes descending stages, in contrast to al-daraj, ascending steps; hence the Garden has ascending ranks, while the Fire has descending stages.

These verses summarize the preceding discussion and make it almost certain that it exposed believers of weak faith and diseased hearts as hypocrites, or at least joined them to hypocrites. Believers are warned not to approach this course, lest they furnish Allah with proof against themselves. Then He may leave them to error and deception, wavering in this life, before joining them to unbelievers in Hell’s lowest stage, without help or intercession.

The verses show, first, that divine abandonment, deception, and other forms of displeasure are recompense for proof supplied by people’s own deeds. Divine Majesty does not initiate evil or misfortune without a cause from their side: He does not cause to err by it (any) except the transgressors (2:26). Second, Hell has descending degrees of lowliness and ignominy, and chastisement intensifies as one descends.

Al-Mizan explains that the verses forbid believers to prefer friendship with unbelievers to friendship with believers, because Allah counts such conduct as hypocrisy and threatens hypocrites with the lowest stage of the Fire, where they have no helper. Al-sultān means proof. Al-darak denotes descending stages, in contrast to al-daraj, ascending steps; hence the Garden has ascending ranks, while the Fire has descending stages.

These verses summarize the preceding discussion and make it almost certain that it exposed believers of weak faith and diseased hearts as hypocrites, or at least joined them to hypocrites. Believers are warned not to approach this course, lest they furnish Allah with proof against themselves. Then He may leave them to error and deception, wavering in this life, before joining them to unbelievers in Hell’s lowest stage, without help or intercession.

The verses show, first, that divine abandonment, deception, and other forms of displeasure are recompense for proof supplied by people’s own deeds. Divine Majesty does not initiate evil or misfortune without a cause from their side: He does not cause to err by it (any) except the transgressors (2:26). Second, Hell has descending degrees of lowliness and ignominy, and chastisement intensifies as one descends.
verses.146:
Al-Mizan understands this as an exception to the threat that hypocrites occupy the lowest stage of the Fire. Those described have separated from hypocrisy and joined the believers; therefore the verse says that they are “with the believers” and then promises all believers a mighty reward.

Hypocrisy cannot be removed without all four conditions. Repentance is returning to Allah, but it has no value unless one amends what has been corrupted in thought and deed. Amendment does not suffice unless one holds fast to Allah—following the divine Book and the sunnah of the Holy Prophet—because no path leads to Allah except the one He has established, while all other paths are Satan’s. Even this adherence is ineffective without sincerity in religion to Allah, since polytheism is unforgivable. When these conditions are fulfilled, people become true believers, free from the taint of polytheism, protected from hypocrisy, and rightly guided; “Those who believe and mix not their faith with inequity, those are they for whom is security and they are (the ones) guided aright” (6:82).

Here “believers” means pure believers sincere in faith. The stated qualities encompass the characteristics which the Qur’an assigns to believers without qualification. The wording “with the believers,” rather than “among the believers,” indicates that such people become attached to believers as soon as these qualities appear in them, but do not become part of them until the qualities are firmly rooted in their hearts.
verses.147:
Al-Mizan holds that the verse, like the preceding passage, is apparently addressed to believers, though it speaks to them as if they lacked faith. Allah has no need to chastise them: punishment is invited only by abandoning gratitude and faith, not by any need, benefit, or injury on God’s side.

Gratitude means giving Allah His due rights in return for His favors, together with true belief in Him. Allah appreciates the virtue of those who thank and believe, and, being Knowing, puts everything in its proper place. Thus chastisement originates from people’s own side. The same is true of what brings punishment—error, polytheism, sins, and mistakes—for these are done by people, not originated by Allah; if they originated from Him, their resulting punishment would also be from Him, since an effect is related to its cause.
verses.148:
Al-Mizan explains al-Jahr as excessive manifestation to sight or hearing; here it means openly or loudly speaking. Evil speech includes any words that hurt the person spoken of, such as cursing, abuse, or imputing bad qualities, whether true or false. Allah’s not loving such speech metaphorically expresses His displeasure and thus a legislative prohibition or dislike, since divine love and hatred are not human emotions.

The exception for one wronged permits the oppressed person publicly to speak against the oppressor concerning the injustice suffered and the character that led to it. It does not permit allegations unrelated to that oppression or qualities absent from the oppressor. “Evil speech” is unrestricted, encompassing cursing, descriptions of injustice, and other hurtful speech; it should not be confined to a particular kind. The ending, “and Allah is Hearing, Knowing,” reinforces the prohibition for one who has not been wronged, for Allah hears every utterance and knows what people do.
verses.149:
Al-Mizan relates this verse to the preceding one: it commends openly expressing good, including gratitude for a benefactor, and forgiving evil rather than publicly speaking against one’s oppressor. Open good may be deeds, such as visibly spending on a deserving person, or words, such as praising and thanking a benefactor; such publicity encourages others to do good and strengthens religion.

Secret good is likewise commendable because it protects against dissimulation and brings one nearer to sincerity: If you give alms openly, it is well, and if you hide it and give it to poor, it is better for you; and this will remove from you some of your sins (2:271). Pardoning evil means concealing it in speech—neither describing the oppressor’s wrongdoing nor disgracing him publicly—and in action, by not returning similar mistreatment even where sharīʾah permits retaliation. The pardoner thereby acquires a Divine attribute of perfection, since Allah pardons His servants while able to punish them; doing good openly or secretly, especially favoring the needy in every condition, is also among the Divine attributes.
verses.150:
Al-Mizan identifies those who believe in some messengers and reject others as the People of the Book: the Jews, who believe in Moses but reject Jesus and Muhammad, and the Christians, who believe in Moses and Jesus but reject Muhammad—God’s mercy be on all of them. Though they suppose that they believe in God and only disbelieve in a few messengers, the verse declares them unbelievers in God and all His messengers.

Their claim, “We believe in some and disbelieve in others,” means that they seek to differentiate between God and His messengers. Since a messenger is sent by God, rejecting him rejects God’s choice and therefore His Divinity. Their desired middle way lies between believing in God and all His messengers and disbelieving in both: they accept some messengers while rejecting others. Yet the only way to God is belief in Him together with all His messengers, for a messenger has no authority over himself or his mission and acts wholly under Divine guidance. Belief in him is belief in God, and rejection of him is rejection of God.

By separating belief in a prophet from belief in God, they treat the messenger as independent of God and remove him from his proper central position; but a person cannot be a messenger if faith or disbelief in him is unrelated to faith or disbelief in God. Belief in such an independent messenger amounts to ascribing someone to God. Thus they are truly unbelievers, for whom God has prepared a disgraceful chastisement.

verses.152: Al-Mizan contrasts the disbelievers who differentiate between God and His messengers with those who believe in God and all His messengers without distinction; this completes the division of people into two groups. It notes the shift from the first-person plural in “We have prepared for the unbelievers a disgraceful chastisement” to the third-person singular in “He will grant them their recompense.” Probably, the first-person attribution of punishment makes its certainty especially manifest, whereas this is less clear in the third person; the same reason explains the pronoun shift in the preceding verse. Addressed to the Prophet, the verse gives glad tidings: he knows that God will surely fulfil His promise and grant this recompense.
verses.153:
Al-Mizan explains that “the People of the Book” includes both Jews and Christians: both made the demand for a book to descend from heaven, although the particular crimes subsequently listed were committed by the Jews. The two communities share their Israelite root, to whom Moses and Jesus were sent, and share such traits as despotism, falsehood, recklessness, and disregard for covenants. Thus the address may concern them jointly, while a punishment or crime peculiar to one group is assigned to that group. This common root also explains why Jesus is included with Moses among the messengers mentioned later.

Their request came after they had heard the Qur’an revealed in Mecca and Medina. They nevertheless refused to regard it as a divine book or adequate proof of the Prophet’s mission, despite its challenge and claim to miraculousness. The commentary therefore treats their demand as a foolhardy expression of obstinate refusal to submit to truth, like demands for further signs made by the Quraysh. God’s answer rests, first, on the fact that people marked by disbelief despite clear proofs, violation of sacred covenants, falsehood, and injustice do not deserve to have such demands granted; and, second, on the fact that the Qur’an itself bears the witness of God and His angels and repeatedly challenges its opponents.

Their predecessors asked Moses for something still greater: that Allah be shown to them manifestly, so that they might see Him with their eyes. This was the height of ignorance and transgression, for which lightning seized them. They then worshipped the calf despite clear signs and the demonstrated falsity of attributing bodily and transient qualities to God. God pardoned them after Moses commanded their repentance through their killing one another, stopping it before all were destroyed; Moses’ clear authority was shown in the enforcement of his orders upon them and upon al-Sāmirī and his calf.

God also raised the mountain over them in connection with the covenant He took from them, commanded them to enter the door prostrating, prohibited transgression of the Sabbath, and took from them a firm covenant. Apparently, this covenant includes these matters and others, since the Qur’an repeatedly speaks of covenants made with the Children of Israel.

verses.155:
Al-Mizan holds that “therefore” connects this verse to the preceding account and introduces the humiliating recompense prepared for them in this world and the hereafter, while also listing further evil traits. Their breaking of the covenant covers both violations recorded in the Qur’an and others; their disbelief in Allah’s communications includes their many acts of disbelief during Moses’ lifetime and afterwards, including the demand to see Allah manifestly and the worship of the calf. Though those examples were previously mentioned before covenant-breaking because they suited the reply to the demand for a heavenly book, covenant-breaking comes first here because the context concerns recompense after their acceptance of the call to truth.

Their unjust killing of prophets refers to Zachariah, John, and other unnamed prophets. Their saying, “Our hearts are covered,” means that their hearts were allegedly veiled from hearing the prophetic call and accepting truth. By this they sought both to reject the call and to shift responsibility to God, as though their condition were beyond their own choice or as though they could hear no call but Moses’. The reply, “Nay! Allah has set a seal upon them owing to their disbelief,” does connect the sealing of their hearts to divine creation, but not in the sense they claimed. Rather, it is God’s requital for their own disbelief and denial of truth. As a society and nation they are under this punishment and will not believe in the Prophet, although a few individuals may enter Islam.
verses.156: Al-Mizan explains that the grievous calumny against Mary was the assertion that Jesus was the product of fornication. It combined disbelief with false accusation, even though Jesus spoke soon after his birth: “Surely I am a servant of Allah; He has given me the Book and made me a prophet.” (19:30).
verses.157:
Al-Mizan states that the verse first reports their claim to have killed the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, then completely refutes it by denying both killing and crucifixion. The two denials are joined so that no one may suppose that, although they did not kill him by an ordinary means, crucifixion nevertheless caused his death. The verse therefore explicitly establishes that Jesus did not die at their hands, whether by crucifixion or otherwise.

Rather, it appeared to them so: they seized and killed or crucified someone other than the Messiah. In the turmoil of such a mob, the intended person could escape and another be taken, particularly since the Roman soldiers did not fully know Jesus’ appearance and circumstances. Traditions also say that God put Jesus’ likeness upon another person who was then seized and killed in his place.

The commentary reports an alternative historical proposal from some research scholars: recorded accounts of Jesus and his contemporaries may fit two persons called the Messiah, separated by more than five hundred years. On that view, the true Messiah was not killed, while a later false Messiah was crucified; the present Christian calendar would then be doubtful, and the Qur’anic “appearance” could refer to the resemblance between Jesus and the crucified Messiah.

Those who differ concerning Jesus or his killing have only doubt, no knowledge, and follow conjecture based on reports from others. “Certainly they killed him not” may also mean, “they did not kill him; I give you the confirmed news.” Al-Mizan rejects as untenable the suggestions that “him” refers to knowledge, meaning that they did not eliminate doubt from knowledge, or to conjecture, meaning that they did not verify it; the wording does not bear either meaning.
verses.158:
Al-Mizan reads Allah’s raising of Jesus to Himself in light of: And when Allah said: “O Jesus I am going to take you away completely and cause you to ascend unto Me” (3:55). It refutes the claim that he was killed or crucified: the very Jesus against whom that claim was made, with his body, was raised and rescued from their plot. Thus Jesus was raised body and soul, not merely as a soul after death; otherwise the contrast expressed by “Nay!” would have no force, since a soul might be raised after murder or natural death.

This raising was a rescue from their hands. The verse by itself does not determine whether Jesus then died naturally or by a means other than murder and crucifixion, or remained alive through a perpetual life whose mode is unknown. Either divine act is possible and belongs to the same category as the Qur’an’s plainly affirmed extraordinary events concerning Jesus and the miracles of Abraham, Moses, Sālih, and others. Reinterpretations made on the assumption that miracles would violate the general order of cause and effect cannot set aside these Qur’anic affirmations. The next verse, however, proves or points to Jesus’ continued life and that he has not yet died.
verses.159:
Al-Mizan holds that the pronouns in “believe in him” and “he shall be” refer to Jesus. One interpretation makes “before his death” refer to each individual of the People of the Book: before dying, every one of them recognizes that Jesus was Allah’s servant and messenger, although such faith at death does not benefit him; Jesus will nevertheless testify against them all on the Day of Resurrection.

Another interpretation makes the pronoun refer to Jesus and relies on traditions that he is alive and will descend before the Resurrection, when Jews and Christians will believe in him. Taken by itself, however, this would unjustifiably restrict “there is not one of the People of the Book” to those alive at his descent, excluding all who died between his raising and return. The verse’s two parts instead show that all will believe in Jesus before death and that he will witness over them all. In conjunction with Jesus’ statement, And I was a witness over them so long as I was among them; when You did take me up You were the watcher over them and You are witness over all things (5:117), this indicates that Jesus will not die until after all those over whom he testifies have believed. He is therefore alive and will return. Those absent from his return may believe at their own deaths, while those present must believe, willingly or under compulsion.

Placed after the denial of Jesus’ killing and crucifixion and the statement that Allah raised him, the verse indicates that he has not died. Otherwise there would be no useful point in stating that all would believe in him under compulsion. This supports understanding their belief as occurring before Jesus’ death.

Verses that may appear contrary do not overturn this conclusion. The promise to make Jesus’ followers prevail over disbelievers until the Day of Resurrection does not say that the disbelievers will remain People of the Book in that identity. The sealing of Jewish hearts means that true, accepted belief will not belong to all of them collectively; if they believe, it may be only a few, while this verse merely affirms belief itself rather than its acceptability. And Jesus’ statement that Allah watched over “them” after taking him up concerns “the people,” not specifically Christians or the People of the Book; as one of the ulu al-ʿazm Messengers, his testimony encompasses Israelites and others alike. Thus the related verses show that Jesus neither was killed nor crucified nor died a natural death.

Al-Mizan calls al-Zamakhsharī’s suggestion in Tafsīr al-kashshāf very strange: that, when Jesus descends, God will revive all People of the Book in their graves so that they believe in him without benefit, as in al-rajʾah (partial return). It also rejects al-Zajjāj’s view that they collectively profess belief in a Messiah yet to appear, because the passage concerns their claim to have killed and crucified Jesus, not their expectation of a future national restorer; on that reading, “before his death” and Jesus’ testimony would be unnecessary. The claim that the verse concerns belief in Muhammad before each person’s death is likewise unsupported: Muhammad is not mentioned in the preceding context, and the interpretation does not suit its subject. Although some traditions give this meaning, they do so according to the principle of the Qur’an’s flow, not as the apparent exegesis of this passage.
verses.160: Al-Mizan explains that “Wherefore” makes the prohibition of certain good things a consequence of what has preceded. “Inequity,” used as a common noun, either magnifies their injustice or leaves its particulars unspecified because identifying them serves no important purpose. It refers not to every wrong mentioned in the passage, but to some grave transgressions for which good things formerly lawful to the Jews were forbidden in the sharīʾah of Moses revealed in the Torah. It cannot include later acts such as slandering Mary. Their hindering many from Allah’s way denotes their repeated deviation from His way, including taking interest despite its prohibition and wrongfully devouring people’s property.
verses.161: Al-Mizan takes their taking of forbidden interest and wrongful consumption of people’s property as continuing the statement that certain good things were forbidden to them. Their inequities brought two punishments: in this world, the prohibition upon all of them of some things previously made lawful; and in the hereafter, a painful chastisement prepared specifically for the unbelievers among them.
verses.162:
Al-Mizan reads the verse as an exception and correction concerning some among the People of the Book. “The firmly rooted in knowledge” and “the believers” are, apparently, both qualified by “among them”: the firmly grounded and true believers from the People of the Book believe in what was revealed to the Prophet and what was revealed before him. Their faith arises from recognizing that his prophethood and revelation are of the same kind as the revelation given to Noah, the prophets after him, and the prophets from the progeny of Abraham and Jacob. This explanation suits believing People of the Book better than Arab believers whose forefathers had not been warned.

“Those who keep up prayers” and “those who give the zakāt” are conjoined to “the firmly rooted in knowledge.” The accusative form of “those who keep up prayers” serves to emphasize praise, as does the following phrase. “The believers in Allah and the Last Day” is the subject of the promise of a mighty reward. In the Qur’an of Ibn Masʾūd, “those who keep up prayers” was in the nominative, in which case all four descriptions are the subject of that promise. Al-Tabrisī reports in Majmaʾ al-bayān that Sībawayh and the Basran grammarians understood the accusative as praise. He also reports narrations from ʿĀ’ishah and from some others that attribute ungrammatical wording to scribes or expect Arabs to correct it, and the report that Ibn Masʾūd’s text used the nominative; he dismisses the reports alleging scribal error as unworthy of attention, because the Companions, who learned the Qur’an from the Prophet, could not have taught erroneous recitations.

The exception contrasts these people with those People of the Book who demanded a book from heaven despite the Book and Wisdom brought by the Prophet confirming earlier divine communications. In reality, he brought only what preceding prophets brought and lived among his people as they lived among theirs. The general body of the People of the Book lack a disposition to follow truth, are not firm even in truths entrusted to them by solemn covenants, neglect clear signs, and hinder others from truth. Those excepted, by contrast, are firm in knowledge and disposed to follow truth; hence they recognize the identity in principle of the Qur’anic revelation and earlier revelations. The following verse, “Surely We have revealed to you as We have revealed to Noah and the prophets after him”, supplies the reason for their belief.
verses.163:
Al-Mizan explains that this verse gives the reason the knowledgeable believers among the People of the Book accept the Prophet: his revelation presents no new claim or fundamentally new order, but belongs to the one system of revelation given to Noah and the prophets after him, including Abraham, his progeny, and the named prophets. Noah was the first prophet to bring a Book and a sharīʾah. Prophets differed in their particular modes of revelation: David received Zabūr [Psalms], Moses was directly addressed, and prophets such as Ishmael, Isaac, and Jacob received revelation without being given a Book.

Despite these differences, all were messengers bringing good news of divine reward and warning of punishment. They were sent to complete Allah’s proof against people by teaching what benefits and harms them in this life and the hereafter, so that no one might retain an argument against Allah after the messengers came. “The tribes” means the prophets from Jacob’s progeny. Zabūr is said to mean “the written,” synonymous with al-mazbūr.
verses.164:
Al-Mizan notes that “messengers” may be read as the object modified by “givers of good news and warners,” or all three expressions may be circumstantial descriptions. Allah sent both messengers previously mentioned and others not mentioned, and He spoke directly to Moses.

The messengers brought glad tidings and warnings so that people would have no argument against Allah after their coming. Reason by itself is insufficient to guide people to the right path unless prophets bring divine laws. Since Allah possesses unlimited might and wisdom, no one can prevail against Him in argument; conclusive proof belongs to Him.
