verses.166:
Al-Mizan treats this as an independent exception following the rejection of the People of the Book’s demand for a book from heaven. Since the Prophet’s revelation is not different in kind from what earlier prophets brought, anyone who professes belief in those prophets is bound to believe in him. Allah and the angels testify that what was revealed to him was revealed “with His Knowledge,” and Allah suffices as witness.

The phrase “with His Knowledge” is decisive. Mere descent from heaven would not alone establish the claim, since satanic agencies might present a false path in place of divine guidance or mingle falsehood with revelation. But Allah knows what He reveals, encompasses His Messenger, and guards him from Satan’s deception, as stated in: The Knower of the unseen! So He does not reveal His secrets to any, except to him whom He chooses as a messenger; for surely He makes a guard to march before him and after him, so that He may know that they have truly delivered the messages of their Lord, and He encompasses what is with them, and He records the number of all things (72:26-28). Satanic inspiration of its allies remains possible in other cases, but not as a corruption of this protected revelation.

The angels also witness because revelation came through them. Gabriel revealed the Qur’an to the Prophet’s heart by Allah’s command, and the description of the honored, strong, trusted messenger who is obeyed indicates subordinate angels under his command; these are the angels described as holding purified, exalted books. Thus, as the means by which revelation was delivered, they are witnesses along with Allah.

Allah’s testimony to the Qur’an is also manifest in its challenges: humanity and jinn cannot produce its like even if they aid one another; reflection reveals that it has no discrepancies such as would be found in a work from other than Allah; and opponents are challenged to bring a chapter like it.
verses.167:
Al-Mizan says that, after establishing the Prophet’s messengership, the divine origin and continuity of his Book with earlier revelation, and the witness of Allah and the angels, the verse declares the far error of those who disbelieve in him and hinder others, even if they are People of the Book.

The wording shifts from “Book” and its revelation to “Allah’s way.” This concisely supplies the premise that whoever disbelieves in this Book and prevents people from the revelation it contains is thereby one who disbelieves and hinders people from Allah’s way; such people have strayed into a remote error.
verses.168: Al-Mizan explains that the verse reaffirms the preceding reality: those who disbelieve and act unjustly will neither be forgiven nor guided except to the path of Hell, where they will abide forever. In this context, their injustice is their hindering people from Allah’s way. The verse may also state the reason for their having strayed so far.
verses.169: Al-Mizan explains that the verse reaffirms the preceding reality: those who disbelieve and act unjustly will neither be forgiven nor guided except to the path of Hell, where they will abide forever. In this context, their injustice is their hindering people from Allah’s way. The verse may also state the reason for their having strayed so far.
verses.170:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse addresses all people, whether People of the Book or others, because the Prophet’s messengership is universal and belief in him is incumbent on everyone. khayran lakum means that belief is inherently and inseparably good for those who believe.

Disbelief neither benefits its adherents nor diminishes God. Everything in the heavens and earth, in its existence and effects, belongs exclusively to Him; indeed, for a thing to exist is for it to belong to God, and nothing existing can be removed from His ownership. Reflection on this comprehensive ownership discloses the realities of belief and disbelief, obedience and disobedience.
verses.171:
Al-Mizan holds that the verse is apparently addressed specifically to Christians, although “People of the Book” can include Jews as well. That designation calls them to remain within what God revealed and to speak only truth about Him. The possibility that both Jews and Christians are addressed is supported by Jewish excesses, such as calling ʿUzayr God’s son and taking scholars and monks as lords; yet the context favors Christians, because the statement that the Messiah is only God’s Messenger apparently supplies the reason for forbidding the preceding excess in religion.

“Jesus son of Mary” identifies the Messiah unmistakably and demonstrates his human, created character, like that of one born from his mother. He is God’s Word conveyed to Mary: the creative word “Be,” by which he was brought into being without the normal causes of marriage and fatherhood. Everything is in a sense God’s word, but other things arise through normal causes; Jesus is called the Word because some of those causes were absent in his birth. He is also “a spirit from Him,” because spirit is from the command, and the creative word “Be” is a command.

Since Jesus is only God’s Messenger, the required belief is in God’s lordship and in all His messengers, including Jesus and their prophethood. “Three” denotes the Father, Son and Holy Ghost; Christians must desist from trinitarian belief. Belief in God and His messengers, and rejection of the Trinity, are good for them.

The declaration that God is far above having a son glorifies Him and is proved by His ownership and sole management of everything in the heavens and earth. A son resembles his father in the origin of his person, existence, and bodily development; but since every existing thing and its effects belong to God, nothing can resemble Him or be His offspring. “Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth” thus conveys that all other things belong to Him, while the heavens and earth themselves are also included in the argument. The verse’s commands and prohibitions guide people to their good in this world and the hereafter, and it closes by affirming that God is sufficient as Protector: He manages their affairs, guides them to their good, and calls them to the straight path.
verses.172:
Al-Mizan presents these verses as a further refutation of the Messiah’s divinity, whether he is considered God’s son or one of the three persons of the Trinity. Jesus is God’s servant and does not disdain worshipping Him; even the Gospels held by Christians explicitly state that he worshipped God. A son resembling his father in origin and constitution could not worship him, nor could he worship himself; likewise, one equal person of the Trinity could not worship the other two.

The mention of the near angels extends the argument to them, since Arabian polytheists called them God’s daughters. Jesus is called the Messiah, anointed and blessed, and the angels are described as near to God; these descriptions indicate why neither would disdain His worship. Had such disdain been possible, God would not have blessed Jesus or brought the angels near. The Messiah too is depicted as among those made near to God.

Their refusal to disdain worship follows also from their knowledge that every proud rejecter of God’s worship—human, jinn, or angel—will be gathered to Him and requited. Mere refusal arising from ignorance or weakness does not bring divine wrath; the refusal conceivable for the Messiah or the near angels, who know their Lord’s station, could only arise from pride. The gathering includes righteous as well as wicked servants, preparing for the division between believers who do good, whose reward will be fully paid and increased from grace, and the proud who disdain worship, who will receive painful chastisement. Their finding no guardian or helper besides God directly opposes belief in the divinity of the Messiah or angels.

Jesus is God’s servant and does not disdain worshipping Him; even the Gospels held by Christians explicitly state that he worshipped God. A son resembling his father in origin and constitution could not worship him, nor could he worship himself; likewise, one equal person of the Trinity could not worship the other two.

The mention of the near angels extends the argument to them, since Arabian polytheists called them God’s daughters. Jesus is called the Messiah, anointed and blessed, and the angels are described as near to God; these descriptions indicate why neither would disdain His worship. Had such disdain been possible, God would not have blessed Jesus or brought the angels near. The Messiah too is depicted as among those made near to God.

Their refusal to disdain worship follows also from their knowledge that every proud rejecter of God’s worship—human, jinn, or angel—will be gathered to Him and requited. Mere refusal arising from ignorance or weakness does not bring divine wrath; the refusal conceivable for the Messiah or the near angels, who know their Lord’s station, could only arise from pride. The gathering includes righteous as well as wicked servants, preparing for the division between believers who do good, whose reward will be fully paid and increased from grace, and the proud who disdain worship, who will receive painful chastisement. Their finding no guardian or helper besides God directly opposes belief in the divinity of the Messiah or angels.
verses.174:
Al-Mizan explains that al-Burhān is a verbal noun, though it is sometimes used for the argument or proof itself. The “clear light” is the Qur’an, as its being sent down shows; possibly the “manifest proof” is also the Qur’an, so that the two statements reinforce one another.

Alternatively, the light may mean the Prophet. This is supported by the verse’s connection with preceding proofs of his prophethood and of the Qur’an’s revelation from God, and by the subsequent command to hold fast by Him. Holding fast to God means accepting His Book and following His Messenger.
verses.175: Al-Mizan explains that believers who hold fast to God follow their Lord’s proof and the light sent down from Him. God admits them into His mercy—the Garden as their full reward—adds grace beyond it, and guides them to Himself on a straight path as the result of holding fast to Him. The verse recognizes only followers and transgressors; perhaps it omits the latter’s recompense because the preceding verse’s punishment already applies and need not be repeated.
verses.176:
Al-Mizan explains that al-istiftāʾ means seeking a legal decision, al-iftāʾ giving one, and al-kalālah a relative other than parents and children. “No child” includes both sons and daughters. Al-Ṭabrisī, in Majmaʿ al-bayān, reports the consensus that the parent is also understood to be absent; otherwise the verse would not have omitted the parent's prescribed share.

The verse assigns a sister half of her brother’s estate, while a brother in her place inherits her whole estate. It also entails corresponding shares between two sisters and between two brothers, since a difference would have been stated. Two sisters receive two-thirds, and where brothers and sisters inherit together, a male receives the share of two females; these shares do not vary according to whether the deceased is male or female. Thus, two brothers divide the whole estate equally, and a brother and sister inherit according to the two-to-one rule. Traditions, the commentary adds, have made these further cases clear.

These shares apply where the relatives are exclusively agnate or exclusively consanguine. If both classes occur together, as with a consanguine and an agnate sister, the agnate receives nothing. Finally, although the clause literally reads “that you err,” its idiomatic meaning is “lest you err,” expressing that Allah clarifies the law to prevent error.
